# HTF Liquidity Levels

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** drawing-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

HTF Liquidity Levels tracks previous daily, weekly and monthly extremes, emphasizing those price references that have not yet been revisited. Its purpose is to frame potential directional destinations or clusters during an intraday session. The author interprets those untouched levels as possible resting-order pools, but the indicator does not directly observe stop orders or order-book depth. A cluster is a price-geometry reference, not proof that price must move toward it. Tapped levels are visually distinguished and removed after the day ends.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Previous completed day/week/month extrema form a reproducible principal drawing; reaching a level highlights it and tapped references clear at day end. Cluster narratives and trade entries are not required for this level indicator.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Maintain prior day/week/month highs and lows and monitor whether price reaches them.
- Highlight touched levels and clear the touched subset at day end.

## Outputs and intended use

- Untapped higher-timeframe references and clusters support discretionary directional-bias planning.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Daily, weekly and monthly references are disclosed; no numeric defaults or controls are listed.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Historical extremes do not reveal actual resting order quantities.
- A supposed liquidity magnet can fail, and nearest-level/path arguments are qualitative.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Touch definition, session/timezone, retained history, cluster calculation, confirmation and trade rules are absent.

> SMA50 - the indicator compares the current price of the symbol to its Simple Moving Average (SMA) with the length of 50. If the current price is below the SMA, this price movement is considered a downtrend. If the price is above the SMA, it is an uptrend.

# Volume-based Support & Resistance Zones

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Volume-based Support & Resistance Zones marks high-volume swing extremes across several timeframes. It aims to highlight structural prices that may matter for reversal or for breakout-and-retest analysis. A zone extends from the fractal extreme to its candle close, combining a turning-point reference with the size of the rejection region. The author says larger zones are more significant, but that is a qualitative interpretation rather than a tested ranking. The indicator offers extensive history, drawing and alert controls without supplying a complete trading setup.

## How it works

- Require fractal highs with three successive higher highs followed by two lower highs, with inverse logic for lows.
- Gate fractals by volume above its configurable moving average.
- Draw extreme-to-close zones per timeframe, retain bounded history and suppress lower-timeframe zones on higher charts.

- Up to four timeframe zone sets, lines/labels/extensions and configurable alerts support level monitoring.

- Fractal sequence uses three rising and two falling highs; defaults for MA/timeframes are absent.

- Fractals confirm after the turning point; historical zone origins can appear earlier than availability.
- Older higher-timeframe origins may fall back to a bounded history position, especially on stocks.

# Stepped trailing strategy example

Version: 1.1.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: v1.0.0 to v1.1.0; explain the complete publication mechanism, objective and source gaps.

**Classification:** exit-example. Spec-only; no runnable repository implementation or measured performance.

## Idea and objective

Protect progressively more of a favorable move by advancing a stop at three profit milestones, without defining the entry signal.

## How it works

- The strategy describes one initial stop and three profit levels. The first two milestones change the protective stop; only the third explicitly closes the position for profit.
- This is a stepped state machine, not a continuously moving trail and not evidence that one-third of the position is sold at each milestone.

## Documented rules and trade lifecycle

- Start with the selected initial stop-loss.
- When the first profit level is reached, move the stop to break-even.
- When the second profit level is reached, move the stop to the first profit level.
- When the third profit level is reached, exit for profit.

## Parameters and stated settings

- One stop and three profit levels are described. Their numerical distances, sizing and long/short defaults are not supplied.

## Failure modes and caveats

- A bar can cross multiple milestones and a stop; assuming a favorable intrabar order can overstate results.
- A stop at the entry price is price break-even, not necessarily net break-even after costs.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Recover entry conditions, long/short handling, same-bar precedence, quantity handling and level definitions.
- The saved description does not establish partial profit-taking at the first two levels.

## Evidence and interpretation

The explanation above synthesizes the complete saved author description. Rules and numerical settings are attributed to that description; failure-mode analysis is our interpretation. The saved `script.content` field is empty. A public/open-source label does not supply the missing code. No order, bot or live integration is created by this card.

### E1: steps

> There are 1 stop loss and 3 profit levels.
> 
> When first tp is reached we move stop loss to break-even.

## How it works

- Fit local polynomial regression over a lookback, extrapolate one step and estimate fit RMSE. Use the preceding bar's forecast plus/minus multiplier times preceding RMSE for current bands, avoiding a current-fit center for that forecast comparison.

## Outputs and intended use

- Choose previous prediction, current regression or a colored ribbon as center display. The author suggests upper-band breaks as bullish momentum cues and lower-band or centerline crossings as possible exits.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

VQZL Z-Score adapts Volatility Quality Zero Line into a normalized regime gauge. The original VQZL apparently required instrument-specific adjustment; this version expresses its readings relative to their rolling mean and dispersion so the author can apply a more comparable scale across instruments. Readings near zero are interpreted as consolidation or choppiness, while larger departures suggest a trending environment. The intention is to keep trend traders away from ranges. It does not establish a trade direction from statistical extremeness alone, even though its bullish and bearish colors make directional readings visible.

- The underlying VQZL computation remains undisclosed despite the stated z-score transform.

## How it works

- Compute VQZL using the selected moving-average mode, then standardize it relative to a simple moving average and standard deviation over Z-Length.
- Assign colors according to adjustable positive/negative threshold levels, independently of the displayed threshold lines.

## Outputs and intended use

- A normalized zero-centered reading and gray/yellow/orange/green/red states indicate ordinary versus stronger departures.
- Use the result as market-regime context rather than a complete order prescription.

## Parameters and stated settings

- MA Mode controls VQZL smoothing; z-score averaging always uses SMA. Z-Length defines the comparison population.
- Built-in thresholds correspond to ±1.64, ±1.96 and ±2.58; the source also lists 1.28 and 1.44 as alternative reference values.

- Standardization can become unstable when dispersion is small and cannot remove instrument-specific distribution differences.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Market Structure Dashboard is a multi-timeframe market structure analysis indicator. It combines EMA trend detection, swing high/low tracking, market structure labels, Order Block detection, Fair Value Gap detection, liquidity sweep detection, volume analysis, volatility analysis, trading sessions, ICT killzones, a weighted trend bias system, and HTF levels into one unified dashboard. Each component is calculated independently across up to 7 configurable timeframes and displayed together in a single organized view.

> The core idea is that a trade setup becomes more reliable when multiple timeframes agree on direction. A bullish signal on a 5-minute chart carries more weight when the 15-minute, 1-hour, and daily timeframes also show bullish conditions. Analyzing each timeframe separately is both time-consuming and prone to error. The Market Structure Dashboard automates this process by calculating key metrics across all enabled timeframes and presenting them side by side.

> Each component operates independently while sharing the same underlying market structure logic. All features are calculated across up to 7 user-configurable timeframes and displayed in a unified dashboard. Detailed explanations for each component are provided in the sections that follow.

> ◇ Color coding shows green when price is above EMA (bullish) and red when price is below EMA (bearish).

> When a liquidity sweep occurs (price breaks a level then reclaims it), special arrows appear: ⤴ for a swept and reclaimed low, ⤵ for a swept and reclaimed high. A swept and reclaimed swing means price broke beyond the level, likely triggering stop-loss orders resting beyond it, but then reversed back inside the range. This suggests the breakout was a false move and the opposite direction may follow. Liquidity sweeps are explained in detail in the Liquidity Sweep & Reclaim Detection section below.

> ◇ Step 2: When price breaks above a swing high, the indicator identifies a bullish breakout. When price breaks below a swing low, it identifies a bearish breakout.

> ◇ Step 5: Mitigation is applied when price closes through the Order Block. Bullish OBs are mitigated when price closes below the zone. Bearish OBs are mitigated when price closes above the zone.

> ◇ Mitigation occurs when price wicks below the gap bottom for bullish FVGs, or above the gap top for bearish FVGs. Note that FVG mitigation is more sensitive than Order Block mitigation.

> The indicator draws from two established trading methodologies. Smart Money Concepts (SMC) focuses on identifying institutional footprints in price action through patterns like Order Blocks, Fair Value Gaps, and liquidity sweeps. Inner Circle Trader (ICT) methodology emphasizes time-based analysis through specific trading windows called killzones and the importance of previous day, week, and month highs and lows.

> The dashboard calculates a 9-period EMA (configurable) for each enabled timeframe. The EMA Trend column displays both direction and distance.

## Documented inputs and source details

> CT stands for "central tendencies" and is the real distinguishing characteristic of this indicator against other Monte Carlo based indicators.

> In statistics, Central Tendency is a single value that attempts to describe a set of data by identifying the central position within that set. It is the typical or expected value that the data clusters around. While the most common measures are the mean (average), median (middle value), and mode (most frequent), in a Monte Carlo simulation, the central tendency acts as the gravity points of the forecast. Because a random walk can technically produce infinite paths, with some shooting to the moon and others crashing to zero, the central tendency filters out those wild outliers to show you the m

> Instead of looking at the chaos of 200 individual spaghetti lines, the central tendency condenses that massive dataset into a clean, usable trajectory. It essentially represents the path of least resistance based on the historical volatility and drift the model has identified. By focusing on the median and its surrounding percentiles, you are shifting your perspective from "What could happen?" to "What is likely to happen?"

> Execute: Use the 25% (Solid Red) or 05% (Dashed Red) lines as buy the dip zones within a bullish forecast. Conversely, use the 95% (Dashed Green) as a logical place to take profits or tighten stops.

> Rel Volume: Shows how much effort the market is putting in compared to its 50-period average. High volume + high Win Prob is a high-conviction signal.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Efficient Work measures the ratio of price movement from close to close (resulting work) over the distance traveled to the high and low before settling down at the close (total work). The closer the two values are, the more Efficient Work approaches its maximum value of +1 for an up move or -1 for a down move. When price does not change, Efficient Work is zero.

> Higher values of Efficient Work indicate more efficient price travel between the close of two successive bars, which I interpret to be more significant, regardless of the move's amplitude. Because it measures the direction and strength of price changes rather than their amplitude, Efficient Work may be thought of as a sentiment indicator.

> Two progressively higher timeframes are used to calculate larger-context values for the oscillator. The rationale underlying the use of timeframes higher than the chart's is that, while they change less frequently than the values calculated at the chart's resolution, they are more meaningful because more work (trader activity) is required to calculate them. Combining the immediacy of values calculated at the chart's resolution to higher timeframe values achieves a compromise between responsiveness and reliability.

> • Bull/bear markers can be displayed. They occur whenever a new bull/bear state is determined by the "Main Line Coloring Conditions".

> It will generate an entry whenever a marker is displayed.

> • An aggregate line calculated using a weighed average of the three previous lines (see the Aggregate Weights section of Inputs to configure the weights).

> • The color of lines 2 and 3 are fixed but can be set in the "Colors" section of Inputs.

> • Repainting can be controlled separately for the chart's value and the higher timeframe values.

Lower thresholds (0.00001%-0.0001%) include more addresses with smaller stakes, revealing a broader holder base. Higher thresholds (0.01%-0.1%) focus on mega-whales. Fewer addresses at any threshold signals centralization. Healthy distribution shows many addresses at low thresholds and few at high ones, correlating with reduced volatility and organic price discovery.

# Dual Momentum (12-1)

> **Implemented in this session** from spec-only mechanism #18 of
> `research/STRATEGIES.md`. Its stated gap was "implementable now — needs code, not
> data", so the code was written and it was measured on the same 1,875 daily SOL bars
> and the same 70/30 split as every other measured card.
## What it is
Long when the return from `t-formation` to `t-skip` is positive. The skip is the
whole point: the most recent period tends to *reverse*, so including it dilutes the
signal.

## Equation
```
R_t = c_{t-skip} / c_{t-formation} - 1
target_t = 1 if R_t > 0 else 0
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/advanced.py::DualMomentum`. The skipped tail is excluded
from **both** ends of the return, so this is genuinely a 12-1 measurement rather than
a shifted full-window one — there is a test that fails if the skip stops binding.

## Measured on SOL

| Leg | Return | Sharpe | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-sample | +776.5% | 1.176 | — |
| **Out-of-sample** | **-65.3%** | **-1.303** | **37** |

For reference on the same split: buy-and-hold made **+565.2% (Sharpe 1.030)**
in-sample and **-70.8% (Sharpe -0.651)** out. That row reproduces the figure the
existing cards document exactly, which is how these new numbers are known to be
comparable to them.


The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos.*

The 12-1 construction is well documented, and it did **not** help: -65.3% and a
-1.303 Sharpe out-of-sample, slightly worse than `ts_momentum` at the medium horizon
(-51.1%). Skipping a bar cannot supply what single-asset momentum is missing, which
is the cross-sectional ranking that carries most of the published edge. On 37 trades
this clears the evidence floor, so it is a real result rather than an anecdote — and
the real result is that it lost.

## Re-evaluated under CPCV

`research/results/cpcv_results.csv`, 8 groups, k=2, 28 paths, all 25 registered configurations.

| Horizon | Median path Sharpe | Paths positive | Median path return | Trades | Rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| short | −4.633 | 0% | −39.2% | 728 | **25 of 25 — last** |
| medium | −0.319 | 43% | −37.2% | 212 | 23 of 25 |
| long | +0.358 | 57% | +5.5% | 156 | 9 of 25 |

**As a single strategy this is weak and the rating stands.** Zero of 28 paths positive at the short
horizon is the worst result in the study.

### The exception, which matters more than the row above

Paired with `vol_regime` in `all` mode at the long horizon, this is **the single best configuration
measured anywhere in this project**: median path Sharpe **+1.345**, **87%** of 28 paths positive,
median path return **+75.1%** over 52 trades (`research/results/cpcv_combos_results.csv`). It
survives ±10% perturbation on every parameter — **12 variants, 0 sign flips**, median never below
+0.904 (`research/perturb.py --horizon long --pair dual_momentum vol_regime --mode all`).

Both components are mediocre alone at that horizon (+0.358 here, +0.696 for `vol_regime`) and strong
together, which is the complementarity the pairing was chosen for: dual momentum states a direction,
the volatility regime states whether to act on it.

**This does not raise the rating of this card.** The pair sits atop a 295-configuration search whose
PBO is 0.650; a robust-under-perturbation row at the top of an anti-informative ranking is still a
row selected by an anti-informative ranking. The pair is documented here so the single's poor
standing is not mistaken for the mechanism being useless in combination.

## Caveats and limitations
- Momentum-crash risk survives the skip intact.
- Tested at one formation length. The window is the parameter that matters most and
  tuning it on this data would be the exact error `research/STRATEGIES.md` warns about.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy dual_momentum --interval 1d
```

## Documented inputs and source details

> The Half Causal Estimator is a specialized filtering method that provides responsive averages of market variables (volume, true range, or price change) with significantly reduced time delay compared to traditional moving averages. It employs a hybrid approach that leverages both historical data and time-of-day patterns to create a timely representation of market activity while maintaining smooth output.

> Traditional moving averages suffer from time lag, which can delay signals and reduce their effectiveness for real-time decision making. The Half Causal Estimator addresses this limitation by using a non-causal filtering method that incorporates recent historical data (the causal component) alongside expected future behavior based on time-of-day patterns (the non-causal component).

> The indicator operates through several coordinated steps. First, it stores and organizes market data by specific times of day (minutes/hours). Then it builds a profile of typical behavior for each time period. For calculations, it creates a filtering window where half consists of recent actual data and half consists of expected future values based on historical time-of-day patterns. Finally, it applies a kernel-based smoothing function to weight the values in this composite window.

> This dual approach allows the filter to respond more quickly to changing market conditions while maintaining smoothness. The name "Half Causal" refers to this hybrid methodology—half of the data window comes from actual historical observations, while the other half is derived from time-of-day patterns observed over multiple days. By incorporating these "future" values from past patterns, the estimator can reduce the inherent lag present in traditional moving averages.

> The benefit of using this "average future data" approach is that it counteracts the lag inherent in traditional moving averages. In a standard moving average, recent price action is underweighted because older data points hold equal influence. By incorporating time-of-day averages for future periods, the Half Causal Estimator essentially shifts the center of the filter window closer to the current bar, resulting in more timely outputs while maintaining smoothing benefits.

> This approach is particularly effective because market variables like volume, true range, and price changes tend to follow recognizable intraday patterns (they are positive values without DC components). By leveraging these patterns, the indicator doesn't try to predict future values in the traditional sense, but rather incorporates the average historical behavior at those future times into the current estimate.

# Session Edge Profiler | Flux Charts

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Session Edge Profiler measures completed-session behavior and compares the developing session with its own weekday-filtered history. It aims to replace generic claims about Asia, London or New York with instrument-specific evidence. The dashboard covers range, volume, directional persistence, daily extremes and explicitly defined structural counts. Its alert identifies unusually large range rather than a directional trade. The source provides enough parameterized lifecycle and metric rules to reproduce a substantive session-statistics specification, while realistic execution and future profitability remain outside its purpose.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** The source defines the financial computation and parameterized inputs sufficiently for a reproducible specification.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Track each enabled session’s OHLCV/events in New York time, commit completed records at the shifted trading-day boundary and filter history by selected weekday.
- Normalize session range by previous completed daily ATR; average normalized ranges and count historical values at/below the current normalized range for percentile.
- Bull means session close > session open. Continuation means its bullish/bearish direction matches the previous occurrence of that same session; exclude the first occurrence from the eligible denominator. Bull%=100×bull count/all sessions; Continuation%=100×matched count/eligible sessions. Volume share is session volume divided by summed completed enabled-session volume; daily-extreme flags compare session extremes with full trading-day extremes.
- At active-session bar t, bullish FVG is Low_t>High_(t−2), storing High_(t−2); bearish FVG is High_t<Low_(t−2), storing Low_(t−2). Later within the same session, invalidate/remove a bullish gap if close falls below its stored level or a bearish gap if close rises above its stored level. Survival%=100×(formed−invalidated)/formed at session end; later-session invalidation does not change that result.
- Confirm pivots with the chosen number of bars on each side. A subsequent close above a confirmed high or below a confirmed low increments the active-session swing-break counter and consumes that pivot so it cannot be counted again. A newly confirmed high above the previous tracked session high pivot increments HH; a newly confirmed low below the previous tracked session low pivot increments LL.

## Outputs and intended use

- Thirteen dashboard metrics, session boxes, live range/average/percentile label and high-percentile alert support session research.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Five default NY windows: Asia 19–02, London 02–08:30, NY AM 08:30–12, Lunch 12–13:30, PM 13:30–16. Day boundary 18:00 NY via six-hour shift.
- ATR length default 14, range 5–50; pivot strength default five each side, range 2–20. Weekdays default on, weekends off.
- Range alert exceeds 90th percentile. Tier cutoffs are 75/25 for percentile and 70/40 for FVG survival.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Live partial-session range is compared with complete historical sessions, so percentile is not time-of-session adjusted.
- Volume denominator is summed enabled completed sessions, not necessarily all market-day volume; overlaps can double-count.
- FVG survival means survival only until that session ends.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Tie/zero-denominator and interrupted-session edge cases need implementation choices; no trade-execution model is intended.

Required inputs: intraday ohlcv, daily ATR history, New York timezone/session calendar.

## Documented inputs and source details

> The Volatility Stop is a technical indicator that is used by traders to help place effective stop-losses. By using this indicator, traders are able to develop an equilibrium between profiting off trades and controlling risk within the market. Stop-loss needs to be significantly tightened in order to control risk, but it needs to be wide enough to give the market room to breathe in efforts to ensure the trader is not stopped out of the trade too early.

> To begin calculations for the Volatility Stop indicator, it is crucial to understand the top three concepts associated with volatility stop-loss: volatility measurement, safety multiple, and price anchor. Let’s analyze these concepts further.

> Safety multiple. By deciding on a safety multiple, traders add a buffer of sorts to the market to filter out noise. In addition, the safety multiple can signal how aggressive a trader is with their placement of stop-loss. For example, the safety multiple could be set at a multiple of 3, but is set based on trader preferences. Having a lower multiple will allow for a tighter stop-loss, with risk control projected able any potential profit. On the other hand, a higher multiple will project a stop-loss with more residual risk, but with larger market breadth. The multiple chosen, therefore has the

> Price anchor. The value that you are left with after deciding the volatility measure and the safety multiple will be the result of your stop-loss distance, specifically regarding price. For example, if you are using a standard deviation of 7 as your volatility measure, and a multiple of 3 as your safety multiple, the product of these values will be 21 (7 x 3 = 21). Next, choose your price anchor. For example, this can be the last closing price.

> The most common price anchors are listed as price bar highs, lows, and closes. In addition, Moving Averages (MAs) can also be used by traders as the price anchor. When entering a long- or short-position, setting the price anchor as the bar high or bar low, respectively, could project a tighter stop-loss. By using the closing price as the price anchor, traders will get a smoother result.

> The stop-loss distance can be determined by the value chosen from the anchor price. This will help traders ultimately determine where to place the stop-loss. The placement depends on the trader’s position (long or short position). From here, you subtract the product of the standard deviation value and the safety multiple from the price anchor value.

> There are many different volatility stop-loss methods out there to help traders find that distinct balance between profit and risk management. Let’s analyze a select few and see how strategies can come out of identifying the three key components of the Volatility Stop indicator listed in the Calculations section.

> Bollinger Bands. The Bollinger Bands indicator relies on standard deviation for both calculation and execution and is therefore a great tool to use in tandem with the Volatility Stop. The lower band can work particularly well as a stop-loss for a long position, although the indicator was not intended to aid stop-loss. The bands widen when volatility is reportedly high, and therefore traders should be mindful of the indicator’s projections, especially when the bands are moving away from price.

> The Volatility Stop indicator does come with a few drawbacks, one of which being that a trader must adjust input parameters. These parameters can be set to default, or adjusted by the trader given their preference.

> Those using the indicator often assume that current and future market volatility are rooted in historical volatility and therefore will follow suit. However, this is not always the case, and traders should be aware of the fact that historical volatility analysis may not affect current and future stop-losses.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Point and figure charts are another type of chart that relies solely on price movements rather than time intervals. In this sense, PnF charts are similar to Renko, Kagi, and line break charts.

> The "X"s and "O"s that make up each column occupy a space called the box size, which is a user-defined value. When the price moves enough in the same direction as the current column, a new "X" or "O" is added. When the price moves far enough in the opposite direction, a new column begins with either an "X" or an "O" (the opposite of the previous column).

> The required amount of price movement is determined by the reversal distance, calculated by multiplying the box size by another user-defined value: the reversal amount. The reversal amount specifies how many boxes the price must move for a new letter or column to be created.

> Breakouts: Breakouts occur when new boxes appear in one direction after a period of range-bound price action. This indicates a potential new trend.

> ATR length: Sets the look-back period (the default is 14)

> Percentage (LTP): The box size is based on a user-defined percentage of the most recent closing price. This percentage is rounded to the nearest minimum tick size and applied consistently. However, this method is subject to repainting, meaning it can change retroactively as new data comes in. Further information is available on this behavior.

# TASC 2026.05 The AutoTune Filter

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

AutoTune Filter estimates a dominant cycle from negative autocorrelation of high-pass-filtered data and uses that estimate to tune a bandpass filter. It aims to preserve cycle alignment while avoiding abrupt center-period changes. The author proposes turning-point context from the tuned filter’s rate of change, but cycle structure in recent data does not guarantee the next market oscillation.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Partly disclosed computation.** Highpass and bandpass recursions/bandwidth, ACF estimator/window endpoints, initialization and window default are not provided.

- Highpass and bandpass recursions/bandwidth, ACF estimator/window endpoints, initialization and window default are not provided.

## How it works

- Apply a two-pole highpass filter, calculate rolling autocorrelation over the cutoff/window length and choose the smallest lag attaining minimum correlation.
- Double that lag for candidate cycle length, limit per-bar period movement and use the result as a bandpass center.

## Outputs and intended use

- Display highpass data, minimum correlation, dominant cycle or final tuned bandpass; a zero derivative with positive/negative filter sign is proposed as local-high/low context.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Cycle estimate is twice selected lag and period change is capped at two per bar. Four output modes exist, with tuned bandpass default; Window controls ACF/cutoff.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Analytical: autocorrelation minima can be unstable in nonstationary data and an apparent half-cycle can reflect noise rather than persistent periodicity.

## Idea and objective

Responsive Linear Regression Channels chooses an analysis window from a desired time span and chart resolution, avoiding manual conversion into bars. It can show regression trend with RMSE envelopes or ignore slope and display average/standard-deviation references. ## How it works

- Convert selected day/month/year horizons into a lookback, optionally snap to day boundaries, or use a fixed bar window.
- Calculate regression with RMSE channels or mean with standard-deviation lines.
- For caller x,N calculate mean=sum(x)/N and population sigma=sqrt(sum((x-mean)^2)/N);draw mean plus/minus caller sigma multiples. Estimator convention is explicit study choice,not exact Pine parity. Smart lookback/regression/RMSE excluded.

> The Hammer is a single-candle bullish reversal pattern that appears after a downtrend. It has a small body near the top of the candle and a long lower shadow, at least twice the size of the body. The shape shows that sellers drove prices down during the session, but buyers pushed them back up before the close.

> Trend filter: In the indicator settings, choose how the prior trend is detected (based on SMA 50, or SMA 50 and SMA 200), or turn trend detection off.

> Like any candlestick pattern, the Hammer describes what has happened, not what will happen. The downtrend can continue after the candle forms, especially in a strong bear market. Candles with a similar shape appear often on lower timeframes, where many of them are noise. Traders often combine it with stop-loss levels, for example below the low of the lower shadow, to limit losses if the reversal fails.

> Length of the lower shadow: A longer lower shadow relative to the body shows a stronger rejection of lower prices.

# Delta Volume Channels [LucF]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Translate lower-timeframe directional-volume estimates into price-chart channels and configurable condition markers. The design emphasizes visual pressure and consolidation context rather than raw flow values or verified exchange aggressor volume.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Intrabar DV/DVpercent is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Classify intrabar volume by open/close direction, then prior-close change for flat bars, then last polarity. Summed up minus down volume forms delta; dividing by total intrabar volume gives delta percentage.
- A reference average and an average of a delta/relative-volume-weighted source define a channel. Their ordering sets bull/bear state; source-close position and both slopes strengthen that state.
- A divergence means disagreement of the two average slopes. Save divergence-bar levels, expand them on later divergences until breached, and reset with a new divergence after breach. Channel breakout direction combines with pressure strength for stronger states.
- Sign intrabar volume by close-open;flat body uses close-previous_intrabar_close;unchanged price carries last polarity. Sum U,D;DV=U-D;DV%=100*(U-D)/(U+D) for positive total. Caller supplies LTF/initial polarity and adequate observations. Weighted source/channels and marker filters remain outside scope.

## Outputs and intended use

- Filled channels, bar colors, divergence marks and optional raw-value tooltips support discretionary stop tightening or confirmation.
- Markers/alerts use caller-selected state transitions and filters at bar close. The author’s non-repaint claim is limited to that timing and is not independently verified.
- Usable scope: Intrabar DV/DVpercent. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Default reference is close ALMA length20, weighted line capped at five reference standard deviations.
- Divergence defaults use high/low boundaries; upside breach requires low above top and downside high below bottom. Precision, MA type/source/length, cap, volume weighting and marker filters are configurable.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Lower-timeframe polarity is a flow proxy; data coverage and volume-reporting quality constrain interpretation.
- Channel colors do not encode a complete trade policy; a weakened strong state need not predict reversal.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Exact relative-volume normalization, weighted-price transformation, cap lookback and complete marker-filter definitions are omitted.

**Classification:** risk-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

RedK Multi-Modal TrailingStop places several common stop-distance models behind one visual and alert interface. It aims to support management of an existing position, letting the trader change the stop method without changing how proximity and risk states are presented. A separate ATR-based distance gauge labels price as safe, watch or critical regardless of the selected stop model. # Simplified Percentile Clustering

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Simplified Percentile Clustering creates deterministic regime centers from percentiles and a mean instead of iterative k-means. It can classify one indicator or fuse several normalized indicators by their distances to corresponding centers, then interpolate toward the next closest regime. This is a clustering heuristic for interpreting market state, explicitly not a buy/sell model or forecast.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Standalone percentile centers/distance interpolation is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Build low/high centers halfway between lower/upper percentiles and mean, adding the mean as a middle center when selected.
- Average distances across enabled RSI/CCI/Fisher/DMI/Z-score/price-to-MA features and choose the closest combined center.
- Interpolate nearest and second-nearest cluster values using their distance ratio to show proximity transitions.
- For supplied feature/window compute low_pct,high_pct and mean mid. K=2 centers=((low_pct+mid)/2,(high_pct+mid)/2);K=3 adds mid between them. Given distances d1,d2 to the closest and second-closest feature-space centers, and their assigned cluster label/index values c1,c2,rel_pos=d1/(d1+d2);real_clust=c1+(c2-c1)*rel_pos. The interpolated output is in cluster label/index units, not feature-space centroid magnitudes. Require nonzero distance sum;feature fusion and normalization remain excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- Inspect colored regime histograms, bar colors and continuous transition line; use as an interpretable research feature or adaptive-filter context.
- Usable scope: Standalone percentile centers/distance interpolation. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Two or three clusters are supported; lookback, percentile cutoffs and feature toggles/standardization are configurable without full defaults.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Analytical: correlated features receive repeated influence, standardization choices alter distance and the prose’s 0/0.5/1 transition interpretation does not directly follow its nearest-distance ratio.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Compound Ratio Weighted Average (CoRa_Wave) is a moving average where the weights increase in a "logarithmically linear" way - from the furthest point in the data to the current point - the formula to calculate these weights work in a similar way to how "compound ratio" works - you start with an initial amount, then add a consistent "ratio of the cumulative prior sum" each period until you reach the end amount. The result is, the "step ratio" between the weights is consistent - This is not the case with linear-weights moving average (WMA), or EMA

> here are the formulas for our Compound Ratio moving average:

> index in the above formula is 0 for the furthest point out

> - for example, if you consider a Weighted Moving Average (WMA) of length 5, the weights will be (from the furthest point towards the most current) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -- we can see that the ratio between these weights are inconsistent. in fact, the ratio between the 2 furthest points is 2:1, but the ratio between the most recent points is 5:4 -- the ratio is inconsistent, and in fact, more recent points are not getting the best weights they should/can get to counter-act the lag effect. Using the Compound ratio approach addresses that point.

> - the outcome is, a moving average line that suffers very little lag regardless of the length, and that can be relied on to track the price movements and swings closely.

# Volume Profile [Makit0]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Makit0 Volume Profile plots session value references for discretionary stock/futures analysis, originally motivated by regular-session ES levels. It aims to show where session volume concentrated and to retain key auction references on the chart. Its value area surrounds the most heavily traded region, while session extremes and midpoint provide broader context. Crucially, the author says this implementation uses the current chart’s candles rather than finer intrabar data. Therefore its profile is resolution-dependent and should not be assumed to match a built-in tick- or lower-timeframe profile.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for session HIGH/LOW/MID reference lines with disclosed CT session windows and supported chart intervals. Volume distribution, POC and value-area construction remain outside this narrow range-line scope.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Independent session-range output: within the chosen CT session, track the maximum chart-bar high and minimum chart-bar low and draw HIGH, LOW and their midpoint (HIGH+LOW)/2. Use chart resolution compatible with session boundaries; these lines do not depend on volume allocation, POC or value-area calculations.
- Allocate session candle volume across price levels, identify maximum-volume POC and determine the value-area boundaries.
- Compute session high, low and midpoint and optionally extend all reference lines.
- Restrict processing/display to supported minute charts and selected session hours.

## Outputs and intended use

- POC, VAH/VAL and high/low/mid lines plus optional out-of-session shading support auction-context analysis.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Value area contains 70% of session volume. Supported minutes are 1,2,3,5,10,15,30.
- Sessions: RTH 08:30–15:15 CT default; GLOBEX 17:00–08:30; FULL 17:00–15:15.
- History defaults to one 12-hour period; levels/shading default on and line extension off.
- Narrow session-range scope uses RTH 08:30–15:15 CT (default), GLOBEX 17:00–08:30 CT, or FULL 17:00–15:15 CT; Show Range defaults true. MID is the range midpoint, not volume-weighted value.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Coarser chart resolution changes estimated price-volume distribution.
- Session definitions and daylight-saving alignment must match the instrument; many extended levels can obscure charts.

- Choose the lower-timeframe bar with greatest volume and mark its selected price as VPOC. Divide the parent candle into ten price lots, count lower-timeframe closes in each and mark the midpoint of the most occupied lot as TPOC.

- Default lower-timeframe map: chart <=30 minutes uses 1 minute; >30 minutes through 3 hours uses 5 minutes; >3 through 8 hours uses 15 minutes; >8 hours through 1 day uses 1 hour; >1 through 3 days uses 2 hours; >3 days uses 4 hours.
- Price source defaults to lower-timeframe close. Users can change source, interval and concentration thresholds. TPOC divides each candle range into ten price lots.

- This VPOC is the price of the highest-volume sub-bar, not necessarily the true most-traded price. Finer data improves granularity but reduces accessible history and slows loading.

# Oscillator Workbench — Chart [LucF]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Oscillator Workbench translates oscillator behavior into price-chart channels so traders can explore configurations in market context. It normalizes an oscillator’s position above or below its centerline, weights a price source with that percentage, and compares a weighted average with an unweighted reference. Separate divergence channels mark transition/consolidation regions without assigning an immediate bullish or bearish prediction. Direction follows later price breaches. The author suggests aligned strong states as one possible use, while emphasizing that settings must fit the reader’s methodology and that a neutral divergence region is generally a no-trade area.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for alternate close-RSI20 versus close-change divergence channels, including high/low expansion and whole-bar breaches. Default weighted-price channel, cap, strong-state labels and complex oscillator modes remain underspecified.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Track historical oscillator extrema separately above/below the centerline and convert relative position into signed weight; optionally include relative volume.
- Average original and weighted price sources with the same MA settings and cap weighted displacement.
- Detect mismatched slopes, form/expand a channel from divergence-bar prices until breached, and classify states by breach direction and oscillator-channel alignment.
- Independent alternate mode: use close-based RSI of length 20 and flag a divergence when the polarity of its one-bar change differs from close-to-close price-change polarity. At a divergence, save that bar high/low as channel top/bottom. Further divergences before breach expand top upward or bottom downward only when their extremes lie outside the current channel. After a breach, the next divergence starts a new channel.
- For default whole-bar breaches, bullish means the bar low is above channel top; bearish means the bar high is below channel bottom. An unbreached channel is neutral. Strong-state labels still require the separately underspecified weighted oscillator channel and are excluded from this usable alternate-channel scope.

## Outputs and intended use

- Oscillator channel, divergence levels, bar colors, optional closing-bar markers/alerts and Data Window raw values support exploratory analysis.
- Strong-to-ordinary trend-state weakening can motivate discretionary stop tightening, not an automatic reversal.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Thirty internal oscillators or an external plot with specified centerline are selectable.
- Defaults use close-based RSI 20 and ALMA 20, oscillator-only weight, three-standard-deviation cap, divergence-bar high/low and whole-bar breach conditions.
- Cap can instead use ATR; channel prices, divergence mode, bias estimation, coloring and marker filters are adjustable.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Early-history normalization is explicitly fragile. Volume-dependent choices fail when volume is unavailable.
- Realtime values change; the author says markers appear only at bar close, which does not independently verify all historical behavior.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

## Idea and objective

Liquidity Thermal Map presents historical candle-volume concentration as a horizontal heatmap rather than a bar-shaped volume profile. It aims to reveal high-interest price zones and a dominant point of control, with a separate directional-volume gauge. The term liquidity is the author’s interpretation of past traded activity, not a measurement of resting order-book depth. The tool is intended as background context for support/resistance, structural analysis and movement from dense into sparse-volume regions. Those uses remain discretionary because the source supplies no concrete trade trigger.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for the explicitly described bullish/bearish-candle volume totals, percentage shares and absolute imbalance over a chosen lookback. Doji assignment, zero totals, heatmap midpoint tolerance and conflicting price-side interpretation remain caveats.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Divide the lookback high-low range into evenly spaced price bins and accumulate candle volume near bin midpoints.
- Map bin totals to a thermal gradient and highlight the maximum-volume POC.
- Independent directional summary over the chosen lookback: sum volume of candles with close > open as Buy and close < open as Sell; report each side as its share of total traded volume and report absolute imbalance |Buy−Sell|. Equal-open/close volume assignment is not stated; no above/below-current-price regrouping is implied by this narrow candle-direction calculation.

- Close-based binning approximates actual volume by price.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA), introduced by Perry J. Kaufman in 1995, is a moving average that dynamically adjusts its smoothing behavior to the relative noise or choppiness in market movements.

> Kaufman designed the indicator as a generalized trend-following solution based on the idea that faster averages are more useful for tracking trends when the market price is moving quickly in one direction, and slower averages are better for avoiding whipsaws during periods of choppiness and volatility. As such, KAMA follows the market price at a faster rate when movements are efficient and directional, and at a slower rate when movements are choppy or inefficient.

> A traditional EMA calculates a fixed smoothing factor of 2 / (length + 1), where the length value controls the period for which the average responds significantly to changes in price.

> KAMA uses Kaufman's Efficiency Ratio (ER) to control its responsiveness. The ratio represents the absolute change in price over a period relative to the total bar-by-bar change (volatility) within that period:

> An ER value near 1 means that the total bar-by-bar change across the period is close to the overall change, indicating efficient price movement in one direction. A value near 0 means that the overall change is much smaller than the total bar-by-bar change, indicating choppy or inefficient movement over the period.

## Idea and objective

Fractional EMA Kalman Filter D7 conditions price through deliberately reactive fractional-EMA stages, then uses a single-state Kalman-style correction to form smoother estimates. It aims to flatten in sideways conditions while responding to structural changes through residual-dependent noise adaptation. Baseline and faster versions are plotted together to make the response tradeoff visible; “fractional” here describes sub-integer EMA lengths, not necessarily fractional calculus.

## How it works

- Use fractional EMA as measurement, calculate innovation as measurement minus state and weight the correction with K=P/(P+R).
- Update state and uncertainty using the printed recursion; derive Q/R from short/long residual-variance windows normalized by ATR and impose an R floor.

## Outputs and intended use

## Parameters and stated settings

- EMA lengths default 0.5/0.5; Q multipliers base/fast 0.002/0.005; R 50/50; R Gate 1/1.

## Documented inputs and source details

> This script implements the Points and Line Chart described by Mohamed Ashraf Mahfouz and Mohamed Meregy in the November 2025 edition of the TASC Traders' Tips, "Efficient Display of Irregular Time Series”. This novel chart type interprets regular time series chart data to create an irregular time series chart.

> The Points and Line (P&L) chart operates similarly to a P&F chart, using price change to determine when to plot points. However, instead of plotting the price in points, the P&L chart (by default) plots the closing price from RTS data. In other words, the P&L chart plots its points at the actual RTS close, as opposed to (price) intervals based on point size. This approach creates an ITS while still maintaining a reference to the RTS data, allowing us to gain a better understanding of time while consolidating the chart into an ITS format.

> Because the P&L chart forms bars based on price action instead of time, it displays displays significantly more history than a typical RTS chart. With this view, we are able to more easily spot support and resistance levels, which we could use when looking to place trades.

> ITS charts display data only after certain conditions are met. Since they do not plot at a consistent time period, they are called “irregular”.

> Typically, ITS charts, such as Point and Figure (P&F) and Renko charts, focus on price change, plotting only when a certain threshold of change occurs.

# Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) Filter

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

FFT Filter decomposes a selected series into frequency components, masks selected frequencies and reconstructs a filtered time-domain series. It supports either inspecting the latest window’s spectrum/reconstruction or applying the same operation in rolling windows and extracting each endpoint. The latter makes a causal windowed feature possible, while the full latest-window curve should not be mistaken for values historically available at every point.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** The selected-range FFT, frequency masking, inverse reconstruction and endpoint extraction are specified; caller-selectable settings define the computation.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Optionally standardize each input window by subtracting its mean and dividing by standard deviation, then perform FFT.
- Keep components in the selected index range, inverse-transform and display the reconstruction or use its final sample to form a rolling output.

## Outputs and intended use

- Inspect power spectrum, dominant-cycle table and selected pass components; suppress high-frequency noise or low-frequency trend according to purpose.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Source, Length, standardization, spectrum/table/row count, inverse display, rolling mode, Lowest/Highest Allowed N and filtering time range are configurable without numeric defaults. Zero-frequency mean is omitted from spectrum display.

- The source warns rolling history can exceed runtime limits; analytical: finite-window spectral leakage and endpoint effects can distort cycle interpretation. Standardization discards original level.

# Zigzag Cloud

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Zigzag Cloud measures price location relative to smoothed zigzag pivots rather than ordinary bar-by-bar prices. It combines an overall pivot average, separate high/low pivot averages and dispersion envelopes. The resulting cloud is intended to contextualize whether current price is relatively elevated or depressed compared with prior swings. It is an indicator specification at a conceptual level, not an entry/exit strategy, and the source does not disclose the pivot detector or full dispersion definitions.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Partly disclosed computation.** The listed core rules remain unresolved.

- Pivot construction and complete averaging/dispersion equations are absent.

## How it works

- Average the latest N zigzag pivots for the central line.
- Build adjacent averages using only pivot highs and only pivot lows.
- Add Bollinger-style upper/lower bands around the main average and outer bands derived from high- and low-pivot averages.

## Outputs and intended use

- Inspect the cloud and lines as relative price-location references.
- No automatic trade, breakout confirmation or reversal rule is stated.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Seven lines are described; the main Bollinger offsets use two standard deviations. N and averaging-type defaults are absent.

## Failure modes and caveats

- An evolving zigzag endpoint can alter averages unless confirmation is enforced.
- Swing-sampled dispersion differs from bar-sampled volatility.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Zigzag length/confirmation, mean type, N for each series and standard-deviation sample/basis are missing.

# Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) mean reversion test

Version: 1.0.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: first source-reconciled card.

> **Spec-only — no strategy implementation or performance result is claimed.**
> This card records a signal or research method. An indicator alone is not an order rule.

## Mechanism and equations

This publication documents the source-specific indicator named above. The
author-defined mechanism and any stated inputs are preserved in the passages below.
A similar component name does not make it equivalent to an existing strategy.
No missing equation or trading threshold has been supplied by inference.

## Documented inputs and source details

> The augmented Dickey-Fuller test (ADF) is a statistical test for the tendency of a price series sample to mean revert.

> Mathematically, the mean reversion property means that the price change in the next time period is proportional to the difference between the average price and the current price. The purpose of the ADF test is to check if this proportionality constant is zero. Accordingly, the ADF test statistic is defined as the estimated proportionality constant divided by the corresponding standard error.

> In this script, the ADF test is applied in a rolling window with a user-defined lookback length. The calculated values ​​of the ADF test statistic are plotted as a time series. The more negative the test statistic, the stronger the rejection of the hypothesis that there is no mean reversion. If the calculated test statistic is less than the critical value calculated at a certain confidence level (90%, 95%, or 99%), then the hypothesis of a mean reversion is accepted (strictly speaking, the opposite hypothesis is rejected).

> Length - The number of points in the rolling lookback window. The larger sample length makes the ADF test results more reliable.

> The VIX volatility index is known to exhibit mean reversion properties (volatility spikes tend to fade out quickly). Accordingly, the statistics of the ADF test tend to stay below the critical value of 90% for long time periods.

> It should be noted that the ADF test tells us only about the properties of the price series now and in the past. It does not directly say whether the mean-reverting behavior will retain in the future.

# Components

What each module is for, what it exposes, and what it depends on. `docs/codebase-overview.md`
is the flat file map; this page is the shape of the thing.

Dependency direction, strictly one-way:

```
extension/  (JavaScript)      soltui/  (Python)        mongo/  (Python)
     |                             |                        |
     | ports grid economics        | reads                  | reads all of it
     v                             v                        v
backtester/core/gridsim.py <-- backtester/ <-- research/ ---+
```

`backtester/` depends on nothing else in the repo. `research/` imports `backtester`.
`soltui/` reads the research side. `mongo/` imports both in order to load them and is
imported by neither, so dropping it changes nothing. `extension/` shares no code with any
of them — only an obligation, described below. `liquidity/` is self-contained (own venv, own
tests) and shares only files with soltui: it writes `~/.aero-lp/status.json` and `scout.json`,
and soltui's Liquidity tab reads them. The tab can also create/remove the daemon's `KILL`
flag. It never signs or imports the liquidity executor.

---

## `botmanager/`

The standalone `solbot` application separates durable bot specifications, typed default
resolution, command dispatch and SQLite persistence. Its CLI delegates to one registry.
An explicit supervisor runs independent grid reference-paper workers with lifetime
locks, generation fences and atomic cursor/fill checkpoints. It reuses the packaged
canonical simulator. Snapshot EOF remains a visible wait; prospective Jupiter data
and other new strategy runtimes follow later milestones. Read commands do not
initialize a data directory. Legacy discovery/control adapters
preserve the existing owner and distinguish unreachable or incompatible installations
from an empty inventory. See `botmanager/README.md` for delivered commands and limitations.

---

## `backtester/`

### `core/engine.py` — the bar loop

The single place execution ordering is decided, and the reason lookahead is structurally
impossible rather than merely avoided. Per bar, in this order: accrue borrow fees, execute
a fill scheduled for this bar at this bar's **open**, check liquidation against this bar's
range, ask the strategy for a target using data `<= i` only, then schedule the resulting
order for `i + fill_delay`.

```python
run_backtest(strategy, arrays, config) -> BacktestResult
```

`EngineConfig` carries mode, leverage, `fill_delay` (default 1 — the conservative choice),
`rebalance_threshold` and costs. `BacktestResult.exposure` is the **applied** exposure
(signed notional over equity), not the raw target — a distinction that matters to anything
comparing against it.

**Depends on:** `types`, `metrics`, `perps`. No I/O, no network.

### `core/types.py` — the lookahead guard

`BarWindow` is the guard. A strategy receives only this object, every accessor truncates at
bar `i`, and reading past `i` raises `LookAheadError`. Also `CostConfig` (fees, slippage,
borrow rates in **bps per hour** to sidestep the venue's deci-bps ambiguity), `Position`,
`Trade`, and `RunManifest` — everything needed to reproduce a run byte-for-byte.

### `core/strategies/` — the registry

```python
REGISTRY: dict[str, Callable]   # 25 strategies, name -> factory
FAMILY: dict[str, str]          # taxonomy: trend, mean-reversion, regime-filter, ...
build(name, **params) -> Strategy
```

Factories rather than instances, because several strategies carry state and a shared
instance would leak position state between runs. A strategy implements
`warmup_bars()` and `on_bar(history) -> float`, returning a target exposure in `[-1, 1]`
for the **next** bar.

Adding one requires a module plus one `REGISTRY` entry — no engine change — **and** a
`strategy_cards/<id>.md` in the same commit, whose machine-readable half is checked against
the code in both directions.

### `core/indicators.py`

Trailing-window functions, each returning a scalar for the current bar rather than a
series — strategies are called once per bar, so a series would be wasted work and would
invite indexing the wrong position. Exponential recursions use a capped lookback
(`EMA_CAP_MULTIPLE = 12`, chosen for a measured 2.4e-13 relative error) and a smaller
warm-up multiple (`EMA_WARMUP_MULTIPLE = 3`).

### `core/gridsim.py` — the ladder grid

Separate from the exposure engine and deliberately so: the extension's edge comes from
limit orders filling *intrabar* at known prices, which a target exposure cannot express.
Own bar loop, own entry point (`backtester.gridcli`).

**This module is a port of `extension/src/core/grid.js`.** A change to either one's
economics needs the matching change in the other, or the backtest becomes a confident
wrong number about the live strategy. Do not confuse it with the `grid` strategy in
`core/strategies/signals.py`, which is an exposure staircase, not a ladder of resting
orders.

### `core/data.py` and `core/fetch.py`

`CsvLoader` and `SyntheticLoader` both satisfy one `DataLoader` protocol, so tests need no
network. `validate_bars` checks schema, ordering and gaps; `checksum_frame` makes a run
traceable to its input. The explicit fetch modules write caches: Coinbase bars/minutes/ticks/products, Jupiter
spot snapshots and signed funding history. The simulation engine never fetches.

---

## `research/`

### `decide.py` — the per-bar readout

What every strategy, signal and indicator says about the last cached bar.

```python
replay_targets(strategy, arrays, *, mode, allow_short) -> np.ndarray
decide_strategy(key, arrays, ...) -> StrategyDecision
build_report(arrays, *, asset, interval, ...) -> dict
```

Strategies are replayed bar-by-bar from the start of history, because several are
path-dependent: a Donchian position opened on a breakout stays long through bars whose own
close would never have opened it. It imports the engine's own `_resolve_target` rather than
reimplementing the clamp, and its test suite asserts parity against a recording wrapper
around `run_backtest`.

### `cpcv_sweep.py` — and why `interpret()` exists

Combinatorial purged cross-validation over the strategy space. `interpret()` turns four
numbers into the reading a person should take from them, specifically to catch two
dangerous misreadings: a high positive-count with a high PBO ("lots of strategies work!"),
and a low PBO with a low positive-count. It has its own test file.

### `verify_numbers.py`

Re-derives every figure quoted in the research documents. Exit 0 means the prose matches
the code. This is the component's honesty gate — `research/`'s failure mode is overstating
a result, and this is what makes that detectable.

---

## `extension/`

### `src/core/commands.js` — one registry, three surfaces

Every action lives here. The Chrome message handler, `tools/cli.js` and
`tools/api-server.js` are thin adapters over it, and `test/surfaces.test.js` fails the
build if any surface drifts. Do not add a handler, CLI branch or HTTP route carrying its
own logic.

### `src/core/risk.js` — the rails

Every rail is a gate an order must pass. Two properties matter more than the list: a rail
documented but not enforced here is not a rail, and rails **fail closed** — a missing or
NaN state field must not silently disable one (see `normaliseState`).

### `src/core/engine.js` — reconcile, then plan

The venue's live order list is the source of truth at the top of every tick; local state is
a cache. An intent submitted but not found live becomes `unknown` and is **never**
auto-retried — that is exactly how a rung double-fires after a crash.

### `src/core/grid.js` and `pnl.js`

Ladder geometry and FIFO/paired-lot attribution. `grid.js` owns `expectedRoundTripUsd`,
which exists because the "exit at the level you bought at" bug shipped once: it captures
zero and pays two fees. Both files stay free of I/O and `chrome.*`.

### `src/jupiter/http.js`

The single HTTP layer: 4 attempts, full-jitter exponential backoff, a token-bucket request
budget charged **per attempt** so a retry storm cannot bypass it, 15s per-attempt timeout.
See `docs/external-calls.md`.

### `src/storage/`

Three implementations of one interface — `store.js` (IndexedDB: intents, fills, carry,
events), `fileStore.js` (mode-0600, for secret material), `memoryStore.js` (tests). The
intent journal is what makes the bot restart-safe: an intent is written before it is
submitted.

### `src/wallet/solana.js`

~150 lines that make a Solana dependency unnecessary, including the base58 zero-byte case.
Do not add a package to solve what this already solves.

---

## `mongo/`

A derived MongoDB store plus a runnable query reference. Full detail in
`mongo/README.md`.

`schema.py` holds the collection specs, `$jsonSchema` validators and indexes, and
`describe()` prints the layout with neither a server nor the driver present. `load.py`
builds every document and inserts it.

```python
schema.create(db, drop=True)                              # collections, validators, indexes
load.build_all(only=None, run_suites=False) -> dict[str, list[dict]]
```

Two constraints drive the design. **Time series collections accept no unique index**, so
there is no upsert key for a bar — `load.py` drops and rebuilds instead, and
`mongo/tests/test_load.py` asserts two consecutive loads leave identical counts, because
nothing else would catch a second load silently doubling every bar. And **every document
carries provenance**, because a figure that cannot be traced back to a file is not a
figure; that is the same reason `RunManifest` exists.

`decisions` documents are `research.decide.build_report()` output verbatim rather than a
Mongo-specific shape, so the store and the readout cannot disagree about what a strategy
said.

## `soltui/`

macOS menu-bar app plus a TUI. Read-only over the research side; places no orders.

- `app.py` is the menu-bar app; `tui.py` the terminal UI; `signals.py`, `status.py`,
  `roster.py`, `paper.py` the display model.
- `menubar_launcher.py` exists because py2app runs its target as a top-level script, which
  breaks relative imports — and because a Finder or launchd launch starts at `/`, so it
  `chdir`s to the repo before `data_dir="data"` is resolved.
- `setup_app.py` is an **alias** build, so the bundle references this checkout and must be
  rebuilt if the repo moves. Never install a bundle built from a worktree — the worktree
  gets deleted and login startup breaks silently.
- `commands.py` is the one registry of every console action (46 commands); `tui.py`, `cli.py`
  (`soltui call|list`), `api.py` (`soltui api`, loopback + bearer token) and `native_host.py` (Chrome
  native messaging, installed by `native_host_install.py`) all call `dispatch()` and return the same
  envelope. `liquidity.resume` is `requires_confirm`; no command moves funds. `presets.py` turns the Top 5 into
  one-click presets (`top5.presets`), `netpct.py` is the one net % definition and `pnl.py` the pure P&L maths
  behind `pnl.summary|series|breakdown`; `wallet.py` is the read-only wallet
  scan (`portfolio.scan`, `wallet.key_sources`): public endpoints only, no key, no signing; `hdwallet.py` (BIP32
  public derivation, address encoders, private-key refusal), `utxo_scan.py` (xpub scans of BTC, LTC, DOGE),
  `eth_scan.py` (Ethereum mainnet), `spot_prices.py` and `portfolio.py` (snapshots, `portfolio.changes`, the
  notice line) extend it; `portfolio_agent.py` installs the hourly `com.mitchhudson.soltui.portfolio` LaunchAgent.
- `soltui-service` is the operational surface: `status`, `start`, `stop`, `build`,
  `install`.

---

## `liquidity/`

An Aero (aero.xyz) Slipstream liquidity manager on Base. Full detail in `liquidity/README.md`.

```python
metrics.evaluate_pool(chain, market, pool, deposit_usd) -> PoolMetrics   # income, LVR, edge, model + backtest APR
scout.run_scout(chain, market, deposit_usd, out=path) -> dict            # ranked scout.json
allocator.plan_allocation(pools, idle_usd, deployed_usd, cfg) -> AllocationPlan
Rebalancer.rebalance / withdraw / deploy / topup / claim / collect       # every on-chain sequence
Daemon(cfg, live, signer).run()                                          # the loop
```

Three constraints shape it:
- **Income is measured, never quoted.** Fees come from `feeGrowthGlobal` deltas and AERO from the gauge's
  reward share. A volume × fee estimate overstated fee income about 5× on the pool where it was checked.
- **A pool must clear the bar twice.** The forward model and a replay of the pool's actual price path must
  both beat `min_net_apr`. When candidates are close, the daemon runs a side-by-side experiment instead of
  guessing.
- **Every on-chain sequence goes through one `Rebalancer` with a `Runner`.** Dry-run therefore simulates with
  `eth_simulateV1` exactly what live mode would sign. soltui never imports any of it; it reads the state files.

## Documented inputs and source details

> The Hanging man is a single-candle bearish reversal pattern that appears after an uptrend. It has a small body near the top of the candle and a long lower shadow, at least twice the size of the body. The shape shows that sellers were able to push prices sharply lower during the session, which can be an early sign that the uptrend is weakening.

> Trend filter: In the indicator settings, choose how the prior trend is detected (based on SMA 50, or SMA 50 and SMA 200), or turn trend detection off.

> Like any candlestick pattern, the Hanging man describes what has happened, not what will happen. Many Hanging man candles appear during strong uptrends and are followed by further gains. Without a confirming candle, the pattern often fails. Traders often combine it with stop-loss levels, for example above the high of the Hanging man, to limit losses if the uptrend resumes.

> Length of the lower shadow: A longer lower shadow relative to the body shows stronger selling during the session.

> The warning lies in the lower shadow. In an uptrend, buyers have been in control, yet during this session sellers were able to drive prices sharply lower. That shows selling pressure is building. If the next session opens and closes lower, traders who bought during the Hanging man session are left with losses, which may add to the selling.
