# Session candles & reversals / Flowly Indicators

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Session Candles & Reversals rebuilds candles around trading sessions, detects wick/engulfing reversals relative to the previous corresponding session, and reports historical conditional outcomes. It aims to reveal session-specific directional changes obscured by ordinary daily bars. Its statistics measure next-corresponding-session behavior, not a complete executable strategy. The author recommends using reversals with support/resistance and broader context, while checking sample size. Overlapping sessions and differing market hours make careful session alignment central to the interpretation.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Session OHLC aggregation, four reversal inequalities, next-corresponding-session success and magnitude denominators are explicitly defined. Missing portfolio trade rules are irrelevant to this indicator/statistics specification.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Aggregate session OHLC and compare each session with its own prior occurrence.
- Compare extremes with the previous corresponding session, not the immediately preceding different session. Wick-up requires lower high and lower low, close at least 65% up the session low-to-high range and open at least 40%. Wick-down requires higher high and higher low, close at most 35% and open at most 60%. Engulfing-up requires higher high and lower low with close at least 65%; engulfing-down requires higher high and lower low with close at most 35%.
- A reversal succeeds only if the next corresponding session closes higher for an up reversal or lower for a down reversal than the reversal close. Win rate is successful count divided by all reversal count. For successful up/down events, measure favorable percentage excursion from reversal close to next corresponding high/low, sum those excursions and divide by total reversal count (including failures). An optional selected-session moving average is separate.

## Outputs and intended use

- Session candles, reversal labels, historical win-rate/magnitude table, optional validation drawings and session MA support analysis.

## Parameters and stated settings

- UTC defaults: London 08–17, New York 13–22, Sydney 21–06 and Tokyo 00–09.
- Up reversals require close at least 65% of range; down at most 35%. Wick opens require at least 40% or at most 60%, respectively.
- MA supports SMA/EMA/HMA/WMA/RMA and session selection. Recommended chart interval is at most 1H; clearer object drawings cover 500 bars.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Magnitude is accumulated for successful events but divided by total reversal count, so it is not simply average winner excursion.
- Session samples can be small, overlapping and regime-dependent; metrics omit execution costs.
- Misaligned intervals or nontrading session hours cause incorrect/absent candles.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Default MA length, statistic sample limits, exact missing-session handling, fill/stop rules and out-of-sample validation are absent.

## Data requirements

Required inputs: intraday ohlcv aligned with configured sessions, session/timezone definitions.

Repository input-class support: unavailable or unresolved. Exact session boundaries require compatible intraday history; chart-history depth and coverage are not established.

# Keltner Channel Breakout

## What it is
Breakout of an ATR-width channel around an EMA.

## What it looks for
The same thing as a Bollinger breakout, measured with a volatility estimate that
includes gaps.

## Equation
```
TR_t  = max(H_t - L_t, |H_t - c_{t-1}|, |L_t - c_{t-1}|)
ATR_t = Wilder smoothing of TR with period p:  ATR_t = (ATR_{t-1}*(p-1) + TR_t)/p
enter if c_t > EMA(s)_t + m*ATR_t ;  exit if c_t < EMA(s)_t
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/signals.py::KeltnerBreakout`.

## Parameters
- **ema_span / atr_period / mult** — `mult` at 2.0 is conventional; it is also the knob
  that trades entry frequency against false starts.

## Works when
Trending markets with expanding true range.

## Fails when
The same chop problem as any breakout. Its one genuine advantage over Bollinger is
**gap handling**: true range includes the gap, close-to-close stdev does not.

## Backtest notes
ATR is also the documented **sizing and stop** unit: stops at 1.5–2 ATR, position sized
so that 1 ATR of adverse move equals about 1% of the account. That risk-overlay use is
arguably more valuable than the entry signal, and **it is not tested here** — see
`atr_position_sizing.md`.

## Pairs with
Trend confirmation; volume.

## Measured on SOL
Medium: IS +880.7% (Sharpe 1.391) -> **OOS -26.4%** on 6 OOS trades (below the evidence
floor). Short: **OOS Sharpe -1.954** on 13 trades despite a positive in-sample result.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

OOS -26.4% on 6 trades (below the floor) and **-1.954 Sharpe** at the short horizon
on 13 trades. Its one genuine advantage over Bollinger — true range sees gaps —
was never isolated by an experiment, and both lost out-of-sample anyway.

## Caveats and limitations
- 6 out-of-sample trades at the medium horizon cannot support a ranking.
- The gap-handling advantage over Bollinger is real but was not isolated by any
  experiment here; both simply lost out-of-sample.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy keltner --interval 1d
```

## Documented inputs and source details

> Trend Regime: Dual-Phase Oscillator (Zeiierman) is a volatility-sensitive trend classification tool that dynamically switches between two oscillators, one optimized for low volatility, the other for high volatility.

> Calculates returns-based volatility using standard deviation of price change

# Bjorgum Double Tap

Version: 1.1.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: v1.0.0 to v1.1.0; explain the complete publication mechanism, objective and source gaps.

**Classification:** trading-strategy. Spec-only; no runnable repository implementation or measured performance.

## Idea and objective

Recognize a failed retest of a high or low, then trade the neckline breakout as a double-top or double-bottom reversal/breakout pattern.

## How it works

- An alternating swing-high/swing-low zig-zag list is updated as extrema change. Pattern recognition searches that sequence for an M or W shape with a failed second test and a break of the intervening neckline.
- The default target projects one pattern height beyond the neckline. The stop lies beyond the invalidation extreme: above a double top or below a double bottom.
- An optional ATR trail starts at the projected target instead of executing the fixed take-profit. In that mode, the target is an activation threshold and exits occur by stops.

## Documented rules and trade lifecycle

- Confirm the double formation and neckline breakout before entry; the described default waits for bar close.
- Place the invalidation stop and a pattern-height target. Both offsets can be adjusted as percentages of pattern height.
- If the ATR trail is enabled, exclude the limit target and start trailing when the projection is reached. Trail from a chosen lookback extreme with an ATR offset.
- Track whether a pivot has already been traded to avoid duplicate detection. Per-tick recalculation is an alternate realtime mode and should not be treated as equivalent historical behavior.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Default target projection is 100% of pattern height. Stop/target percentages, swing lookback, ATR lookback/multiplier and strategy/indicator mode are configurable.
- Sizing and commission come from strategy properties; numeric size/fee defaults are not established by the description.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Zig-zag extrema and pivots can be revised while forming; never backdate a signal to the eventual turning-point bar.
- A same-bar neckline break, target trigger and stop interaction needs conservative execution sequencing.
- The author warns that historical equity growth/shrinkage affects alert quantities; replay-derived account size can produce an unexpected order size.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Recover pivot confirmation, double-test tolerance, spacing requirements, entry timing, duplicate keys and ATR trail recurrence.
- The author intentionally omits backtest results. No independent profit claim is made here.

### E1: pattern

> Doubles are technical formations that are both reversal patterns and breakout patterns. These formations typically have a distinctive “M” or a “W” shape with price action breaking beyond the neckline formed by the center of the pattern. They can be recognized when a ​pivot fails to break when tested for a second time and the retracement that follows breaks beyond the key level opposite. This can trap entrants that were playing in the direction of the prior trend. Entries are made on the breakout with a target projected beyond the neckline equal to the height of the pattern.

### E2: recognition

> Patterns are recognized through the use of ​zig-zag; a method of filtering price action by connecting swing highs and lows in an alternating fashion to establish trend, ​support and resistance, or derive shapes from price action. The script looks for the highest or lowest point in a given number of bars and updates a list with the values as they form. If the levels are exceeded, the values are updated. If the direction changes and a new significant point is made, a new point is added to the list and the process starts again. Meanwhile, we scan the list of values looking for the distinctive shape to form as previously described.

### E3: exits

> By default, the strategy will place a stop loss at the invalidation point of the pattern. This point is beyond the pattern high in the case of Double Tops, or beneath the pattern low in the case of Double Bottoms. The target or take profit point is an equal-legs measurement, or 100% of the pattern height in the direction of the pattern bias. Both the stop and the limit level can be adjusted from the user menu as a percentage of the pattern height. 
> 
> Trailing Stops
> Optional from the menu is the implementation of an ATR based trailing stop. The trailing stop is designed to begin when the target projection is reached. From there, the script looks back a user-defined number of bars for the highest or lowest point +/- the ATR value. For tighter stops the user can look back a lesser number of bars, or decrease the ATR multiple. When using either Alertatron or Trading Connector, each change in the trail value will trigger an alert to update the stop order on the exchange to reflect the new trail price. This reduces latency and slippage that can occur when relying on alerts only as real exchange orders fill faster and remain in place in the event of a disruption in communication between your strategy and the exchange, which ensures a higher level of safety. 
> 
> 👉  It is important to note that in the case the trailing stop is enabled, limit orders are excluded from the exit criteria. Rather, the point in time that the limit value is exceeded is the point that the trail begins. As such, this method will exit by stop loss only.

### E4: history

> It is important to understand that the calculations on the account size take place from the beginning of the price history of the strategy. This means that if historical results have inflated or depleted the account size from the beginning of trade history until now, the values sent in alerts will reflect the calculated size based on the inputs in the "Properties" tab. To start fresh, the user must set the date in the "Inputs" tab to the current date as to remove trades from the trade history. # Smart Trader, Episode 06, Isotropic Trend Lines

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Isotropic Trend Lines measures structural trend slope in log-price units normalized by realized volatility, aiming to make steepness less dependent on display scaling. It reduces non-overlapping blocks to range midpoints, finds a monotonic sequence, fits boundary lines through selected extremes and compares multiple scales. A state machine describes channel exits, returns and failures. This is contextual channel analysis rather than buy/sell advice. Volatility normalization helps comparability but cannot make different sampling intervals economically identical or make correlated prime-length analyses independent.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

## How it works

- Estimate Yang-Zhang sigma; form each block’s geometric high/low midpoint.
- Find longest recent same-direction midpoint chain and compute arctangent(log displacement/sigma/elapsed bars).
- Fit log-linear upper/lower boundaries through extreme highs/lows, aggregate scale directions and track sigma-distance break/retest states.

## Outputs and intended use

- Channel/projection/fill, endpoint markers, trend-angle label and narrative dashboard support structural context.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Six stated scales 3,7,13,19,29,47, with primary user period; later defaults say period26/groups5/sigma20, conflicting with repeated scale19 wording.
- One-sigma excursion/rebound defines retest/confirmation context; consensus examples 5/6,6/6 and range≥4/6.
- Live default updates intrabar; Close mode shifts one bar and suppresses all nineteen alerts.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Primary-scale/default inconsistency affects reproduction.
- Live mode repaints intrabar; Close mode retains a deliberately live price header.
- Yang-Zhang assumptions and channel-extreme ordering can fail in unusual data.

**Classification:** drawing-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Points and Line Chart transforms regularly sampled prices into an irregular price-movement display. Its aim is to compress long histories and clarify support/resistance or classic chart patterns while retaining actual source closes instead of always snapping them to fixed point intervals. The resulting chart is a separate interpretation of regular candles; the source advises hiding the underlying series rather than reading both as though they share the same time layout. A companion histogram preserves information about accumulated volume or elapsed source bars between plotted points.

- Filter movements using point/figure-style scaling by default, with ATR and percentage alternatives, and require a reversal amount in steps.

# Fair Value Gap Profile + Rolling POC [BigBeluga]

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

FVG Profile + Rolling POC profiles where candle-gap formations concentrate, rather than simply where volume traded. It separates bullish and bearish gap counts and associated volume to describe directional imbalance by price region. A rolling peak/average and optional moving average add temporal context. The financial purpose is identifying repeated gap-formation zones for discretionary reaction analysis. Calling them inefficiencies does not prove an arbitrage opportunity or that price must revisit them. Several important mapping and rolling calculations remain conceptual rather than fully defined.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for raw bullish/bearish three-bar FVG events and their gap boundaries, supporting optional live boxes. Mitigation, profile mapping/volume, Rolling POC and Auto-MA equations remain outside this scope.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Independent three-bar FVG events: bullish when Low_t>High_(t−2), with raw gap boundaries [High_(t−2),Low_t]; bearish when High_t<Low_(t−2), with boundaries [High_t,Low_(t−2)]. These inequalities/boundaries define newly formed gaps independently of profile binning, volume assignment or later mitigation.
- Divide lookback price range into bins and assign each gap to its nearest bin; accumulate directional counts/volume.
- Normalize strength against the largest count and calculate an unspecified rolling peak-imbalance series with optional smoothing.

## Outputs and intended use

- Bull/bear profile segments, strength labels, delta/heatmap, live gap boxes and rolling POC/MA support zone analysis.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Strongest bin normalizes to 100%; lookback, bins, moving-average type/length and Auto scaling are configurable but defaults absent.
- Narrow raw-gap mode uses current and two-bars-back high/low with strict inequalities; live gap-box display is optional. The source supplies no additional raw-gap threshold or numeric defaults.

- Gap-count density is not traded-volume density or actual resting liquidity.
- Moving bins and unspecified event-volume assignment can change apparent dominance.

Version: 1.0.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: first source-reconciled card.

> **Spec-only — no strategy implementation or performance result is claimed.**

## Mechanism and equations

## Documented inputs and source details

> Rob Booker’s Average Directional Index (ADX) Breakout is a trend strength indicator that affirms the belief that trading in the direction of a trend and continuing to follow its pull is more profitable for traders, while simultaneously reducing risk.

> Calculations for the ADX Breakout indicator are based on a moving average of price range expansion over a specific period of time. By default, the setting rests at 14 bars, this however is not mandatory, as other periods are routinely used for analysis as well.

> Traditionally, the ADX is plotted on the chart as a single line that consists of values that range from 0-100. The line is non-directional, meaning that it always measures trend strength regardless of the position of a price’s trend (up or down). Essentially, ADX quantifies trend strength by presenting in both uptrends and downtrends of the line.

> The ADX line is used to measure and determine the strength of a trend, and so the direction of this line and its interpretation are crucial in a trader’s analysis. As the ADX line rises, a trend increases in strength and price moves in the trend’s direction. Similarly, if the ADX line is falling, a trend decreases in strength and price then enters a period of consolidation, or retracement.

> The values associated with the ADX line help traders determine the most profitable trades and where risk lies in the current trend. **Classification:** drawing-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Replace conventional candles with an electrocardiogram-style visualization that distinguishes candle direction, close-to-close movement and the order of intrabar extremes.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for the ordered-OHLC block transformation and its three explicit color rules when extrema ordering is supplied; acquiring that ordering and exact plotting coordinates remain outside scope.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Given OHLC and the observed order of the bar’s high and low, build five connected segments: open–open, open–first extreme, first–second extreme, second extreme–close and close–close. Each block occupies seven ordinary candle spaces.
- Color its body green when close > open and red otherwise. Color its border green when current close > previous close and red otherwise. Color signal lines green if the high occurs after the low, and red if the low occurs after the high.

## Outputs and intended use

- Use the different color layers to inspect distinct dimensions of price behavior. Background highlighting helps map the expanded blocks back to the original candles.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Each block uses five lines and one box and occupies seven candle spaces. The author states a five-hundred-line limit allows no more than one hundred bars in this implementation.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Ordinary OHLC does not reveal whether high or low happened first. If the script infers order rather than observing it, the displayed sentiment narrative may be wrong.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- How intrabar extreme order is acquired, tie treatment and live persistence are unspecified. Exact segment x positions/vertical scaling and complete rendering parity are not printed.

Required inputs: OHLCV, intrabar ordering of high and low.

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Range Oscillator expresses the distance of the closing price from an adaptive equilibrium as a percentage of a volatility-adjusted range. Its heatmap is intended to distinguish directional pressure, transition areas and excursions beyond an ordinary range. The author offers both breakout and mean-reversion interpretations, so an extreme does not carry a single unambiguous trading instruction. The normalizing equation is disclosed, but the adaptive inputs and color engine remain substantially descriptive.

**Partly disclosed computation.** Core computation remains underspecified.

- RangeATR construction, weighted mean and heatmap computations are missing.

## How it works

- Detect a range using a minimum confirmation length and ATR width multiplier.
- Weight the equilibrium mean by consecutive candle-movement size, then compute 100 times close minus mean divided by RangeATR.
- Assign adaptive heat colors according to interaction intensity, heat levels and minimum touches.

## Outputs and intended use

- Above-zero green readings suggest bullish pressure and below-zero red readings bearish pressure.
- Excursions beyond +100 or -100 prompt breakout/exhaustion assessment; movement back toward zero suggests a possible range reset.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Minimum range length, ATR width multiplier, number of heat levels and minimum touches are configurable; numeric defaults are absent.

## Failure modes and caveats

# Volume and Price Z-Score [Multi-Asset] - By Leviathan

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Volume and Price Z-Score screens assets by how unusual current price and activity are relative to their own histories and, optionally, relative to the group. It distinguishes a single-bar anomaly from persistent averaged deviations and cross-sectional outliers. Multiple displays let the reader compare price-volume alignment, divergence and unusual participation without imposing one trade interpretation. The source correctly notes that financial price and volume are generally not normally distributed, so standardized distances should not be converted into normal-theory probabilities. OBV mode changes the question from activity magnitude to a cumulative directional-volume proxy.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for ordinary Current/Average price and regular-volume z-scores and price-minus-volume delta with a chosen averaging length and default 20-bar normalization window. Relative-group normalization and exact variance convention remain caveats.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- For ordinary Current mode, calculate each selected price or regular-volume observation minus its rolling mean, divided by the corresponding rolling standard deviation, over the chosen lookback (default 20 bars). Average mode takes the custom-length average of that z-score series. Delta equals price z-score minus volume z-score. Dispersion sample convention and zero-dispersion handling remain caveats.
- Relative mode standardizes a symbol’s z-score against group z-score behavior, although its exact denominator is not given.
- Choose regular volume or OBV and optionally subtract volume z-score from price z-score.

## Outputs and intended use

- Scatterplot maps price z-score horizontally and volume vertically; squares guide standardized distance.
- Paired columns/circles, delta columns and history heatmaps expose cross-asset anomalies and alignment.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Advertised coverage is 200 symbols; current z-score mean lookback defaults to 20 bars.
- Current, Average and Relative modes, custom averaging length, volume/OBV, display type and heatmap gradient are selectable.
- Scatter guides use ±1/2/3 SD; column/circle display range is described as -4 to 4.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Cross-sectional outliers depend on universe selection and aligned timestamps.
- OBV is a candle-direction proxy; price-volume convergence is not causal proof or a guaranteed signal.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Symbol universe, dispersion conventions, relative-mode formula, zero-variance handling, OBV initialization and order rules are missing.

> This candlestick pattern is a variation of the Morning Star pattern. A three-day bullish reversal pattern, which consists of three candlesticks will look something like this: The first being a long-bodied red candle that extends the current downtrend. Next comes a Doji that gaps down on the open. After that comes a long-bodied green candle, which gaps up on the open and closes above the midpoint of the body of the first day. It is more bullish than the regular morning star pattern because of the existence of the Doji.

> Traditionally, this candlestick pattern is recognized in conjunction with a specific trend direction, i.e. it might be important for the pattern if the price has been generally going up or down. The ‘Detect Trend Based On’ option allows you to specify which of the following methods to use to detect the trend:

> SMA50 - the indicator compares the current price of the symbol to its Simple Moving Average (SMA) with the length of 50. If the current price is below the SMA, this price movement is considered a downtrend. If the price is above the SMA, it is an uptrend.

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Estimate where hidden stop pressure might concentrate and contextualize possible breakout cascades. The indicator explicitly models unobservable stops rather than measuring actual stop locations, quantities or live order-book depth.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

**Partly disclosed computation.** Swing eligibility/lifetime, ATR period/scaling, volume distribution weights, trigger/retirement conditions and historical move horizon are undisclosed.

- Swing eligibility/lifetime, ATR period/scaling, volume distribution weights, trigger/retirement conditions and historical move horizon are undisclosed.

## How it works

- The swing model assigns all classified buy volume to the closest active low and sell volume to the closest active high after formation, producing comparative potential-stop magnitudes. Direction derives from higher/lower close classification.
- The volatility-at-entry model distributes directional volume over multiple timeframe ATR distances. Triggered clusters receive size-classification graphics; nearby modeled buy/sell clusters populate a table.
- For typical-move context, log-transform current and historical cluster magnitudes and choose neighbors within a spacing-based tolerance or the closest match, then retrieve their associated historical moves. A ratio meter sums active and triggered buy/sell clusters.

## Outputs and intended use

- Cluster zones, trigger graphs, nearest-level data and directional ratios support situational awareness around breakout areas.
- Historical similar-size outcomes are explicitly descriptive, sometimes having very few neighbors; they are not forecasts or proof of latent positions.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Model choice and lower-timeframe granularity defaulting to one minute; finer seconds/ticks trade coverage for detail.
- Volatility distribution references1m,5m,15m,30m,1h,4h and ATR multiples1,1.5,2.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Assigning all volume to stops ignores exits, hedges, alternative stops and positions already closed. Exaggerated magnitudes are relative proxies.
- Resting liquidity can absorb triggered flow; modeled cluster size cannot guarantee breakout acceleration.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Swing eligibility/lifetime, ATR period/scaling, volume distribution weights, trigger/retirement conditions and historical move horizon are undisclosed.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Volume is one piece of information that is often neglected, however, learning to interpret volume brings many advantages and could be of tremendous help when it comes to analyzing the markets. In addition to technicians, fundamental investors also take notice of the numbers of shares traded for a given security.

> Within this study, Relative Volume, Volume Weighted Bars and Volume Moving Average are presented, where Relative Volume relates current trading volume to past trading volume over long period, Volume Weighted Bars presents price bars colored based on short period past trading volume average, and Volume Moving Average is average of volume over shot period

> Volume Weighted Bars, a study of Kıvanç Özbilgiç, aims to present if price movements are supported by Volume. Volume Weighted Bars are calculated based on shot period volume moving average which will reflect more recent changes in volume. Price actions with high volume will be displayed with darker colors, average volume values will remain as they are and low volume values will be indicated with lighter colors.

> Relative Volume is presented as color-coded bars similar to regular Volume indicator but uses four color codes instead two. Notable increases of volume are presented in green and red while average values with back and gray, hence adding ability to emphasis notable increases in the volume. It is kind of a like a radar for how "in-play" a security is. **Goal:** Build one persistent CLI application for the full research-to-paper-to-gated-live bot lifecycle, sharing existing evidence and owner controls.

# Initial Balance Auction Intelligence by DGT

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Initial Balance Auction Intelligence follows how price behaves after an opening range, separating tentative probes from completed-window acceptance or failure. It layers retest continuation/rejection, session character and cumulative directional pressure over the basic IB references. The goal is auction context, explicitly not standalone signals or actual order-flow measurement.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** IB references and basic acceptance/failure is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Establish opening-session high/low/midpoint, then evaluate each completed post-IB window against those boundaries.
- Classify outside closes as accepted and beyond-boundary extensions closing inside as failed; track subsequent retest holds/failures and two-sided rejection.
- Accumulate bounded session pressure and grade event quality/maturity with additional price-structure criteria.
- Over caller initial-balance window take H=max(high),L=min(low),R=H-L,M=(H+L)/2. Project H+kR and L-kR for k=0.5,1,1.5. After completed IB,close outside H/L indicates acceptance;an outside excursion/extension followed by close back inside indicates failure under the source rule. Caller defines observation window/boundaries;pressure,quality,retest and advanced states excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- Read dashboard regime/bias/phase/state/pressure/quality and invalidation together; confirmed state transitions support alerts, while live decision candles remain provisional.
- Usable scope: IB references and basic acceptance/failure. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Post-IB windows include 5/10/15/30 minutes; extension references use 0.5/1/1.5 times IB range. Pressure spans -100 to +100.
- Engine operates on intraday charts at most thirty minutes and uses one-minute data on larger intraday bars. Session/timezone are configurable.

- Analytical: acceptance is a configured completed-window rule, not proof of durable market acceptance; projected extensions are expressly not guaranteed targets.

# Time-Series Momentum

## What it is
Long when the trailing *n*-bar return is positive.

## What it looks for
The sign of past return predicting the next period. This is the **time-series** form
(Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen), distinct from **cross-sectional** momentum, which ranks a
universe and therefore needs peers this repo does not have — see
`xs_momentum.md`.

## Equation
```
ROC(n)_t = c_t / c_{t-n} - 1
target_t = 1 if ROC(n)_t > threshold else 0
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/signals.py::TsMomentum`.

## Parameters
- **window** — 24 hourly, 60 daily and 200 daily behave like three different
  strategies. This is the parameter most worth *not* tuning on the data you report.
- **threshold** — 0.0 by default; raising it demands stronger drift before committing.

## Works when
Momentum is the most-documented anomaly family in the literature (Jegadeesh & Titman
1993: 3–12 month formation, 1-month hold in equities).

## Fails when
**Momentum crashes** — the family's defining risk. Sharp reversals arrive exactly when
the signal is most crowded, and a single-asset version has no cross-sectional
diversification to soften the blow.

## Backtest notes
Highly sensitive to the formation window. Do not tune the window on the same data you
report; that is the fastest route to a beautiful number that does not survive.

## Pairs with
A breakout for entry timing; an oscillator to avoid adding at exhaustion.

## Measured on SOL
Long (200): **IS +506.2% (Sharpe 1.098) -> OOS -77.2% (Sharpe -1.976)** — the worst
rankable long-horizon row. Medium (60): IS +392.8% -> OOS -51.1%.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

**OOS Sharpe -1.976** at the long horizon — the worst rankable long-horizon row — and
-51.1% at the medium. The published momentum edge is largely *cross-sectional*, and
this single-asset form discards exactly that while keeping the momentum-crash risk
that the diversification was paying for. `dual_momentum_12_1.md`, now implemented,
did not repair it.

## Caveats and limitations
- Single-asset momentum is the weakest form of a strong anomaly. The published edge
  comes largely from cross-sectional ranking, which is unavailable here.
- A -1.976 out-of-sample Sharpe on the slowest parameter set is consistent with the
  split landing on the top: a 200-bar formation window commits hardest, latest.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy ts_momentum --interval 1d
```

# Dollar-Cost Averaging (instalment ramp)

## What it is
Invest `budget / instalments` every `interval` bars regardless of price. Source formula: amount per purchase = total budget / number of scheduled purchases.

## What it looks for
Nothing. It is a deployment schedule: no signal, no timing. The question it answers is whether averaging in beats being fully invested from the first bar.

## Equation
```
done_t   = floor((bars_seen_t - 1) / interval) + 1
target_t = min(1, done_t / instalments)
```
The engine takes exposure targets, not cash orders, so an instalment is a fixed fraction of equity. True DCA buys equal cash; the invested share here drifts with price between instalments. The difference is second order next to the ramp itself.

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/textbook.py::DollarCostAveraging`. Uses `len(history.closes)` only, so it cannot read a future bar.

## Parameters
- **instalments / interval** set how fast exposure ramps. 10x7 on daily bars is fully invested after 63 days; 10x24 on hourly bars after about 9 days.

## Works when
The asset rises after the first bar but with deep early drawdowns: averaging in buys the dips of the ramp window.

## Fails when
The asset rises steadily from the start (the ramp holds cash while it climbs, so it lags buy-and-hold), or falls for the whole ramp (the average cost is still above the exit).

## Backtest notes
After the ramp completes this is exactly `buy_and_hold`. All difference is confined to the first `instalments * interval` bars, so on a long series it is mostly the baseline with a delayed start. A sweep ranks it against that baseline, not against zero.

## Pairs with
Nothing: with no signal there is nothing to diversify.

## Measured on SOL
Smoke run only, not a sweep row: `python3 -m backtester.cli --split 0.7 --interval 1d`, SOL daily 2021-06-17..2026-08-04, default parameters, 8 bps round-trip costs, one 70/30 split. The split is structurally hostile to long-biased rules (see `research/RANKED_LISTS.md`), so read it as one regime transition, not an estimate. The queue (`soltui/bgqueue.py`) will produce the evaluated numbers; this card stays `implemented` until a sweep supplies them.

Full sample: +108.96% (Sharpe 0.590, 33 trades) vs buy-and-hold +87.61% (Sharpe 0.617). 70/30 split: IS +588.5% (Sharpe 1.049) -> OOS -53.95% (Sharpe -0.456); buy-and-hold OOS -70.76% (Sharpe -0.651). The full-sample gain is the start date, not skill: both lines lose most of their value in the OOS window.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: base-rate. A deployment schedule has no edge of its own. It changes the entry date distribution, not expected return, and after the ramp it is the baseline.*

## Caveats and limitations
- Named by the cited trading guides catalogued in `tradingstrategyresults.json` (repo root, untracked source list). The guides give a verbal rule or a formula, not tested parameters; every default here is a convention, not a finding.
- Rated from the sweep's overall hit rate (14% of 311 rankable configurations had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe), not from this card's own result.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy dca --interval 1d --split 0.7
```

# Polynomial Regression Bands + Channel [DW]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Fit rolling polynomial regressions and display their current endpoints as a polynomial LSMA with surrounding bands. The accompanying redrawn curve teaches the relationship between regression fitting and endpoint moving-average plots.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Unsmoothed rolling polynomial fit/endpoint is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Optionally prefilter the source with Ehlers’ two-pole Super Smoother. Use a local integer time axis over the sample window, form power-sum normal equations and solve coefficients by LU decomposition with forward/back substitution.
- Evaluate the polynomial across the window; offset coordinates within the same fitted equation if requested. Standard deviation above/below the curve forms channels, and current endpoints become LSMA/band time series.
- Approximate each fitted curve using line segments and show its equation; bar colors reflect source disparity from LSMA. Drawing updates can be limited to closes without changing calculation updates.
- Choose degree d and window N>d,with caller chronological x=1..N and supplied y. Solve A*a=b where A[j,k]=sum(x^(j+k)),b[j]=sum(x^j*y),j,k=0..d,using LU/forward/back substitution for nonsingular cases. Evaluate yhat(x)=sum(a[k]*x^k);endpoint=yhat(N). Source repeated-a1 typo remains documented;orientation is explicit study convention. Optional smoothing/bands and Pine numerical parity excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- LSMA and bands can inform the caller’s analysis; the author discourages trading from the repeatedly redrawn historical curve.
- Equation/debug labels help inspect coefficients and numerical problems; the prose’s non-repainting endpoint claim remains unverified without code.
- Usable scope: Unsmoothed rolling polynomial fit/endpoint. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Source, optional smoothing, sample length, polynomial degree, regression offset, segment step and display controls.
- Default sample is 100 and drawing step 10; each of three curves uses 10 segments.

## Failure modes and caveats

- High-degree normal equations can be ill-conditioned despite local coordinates; overfit and floating-point roundoff increase with degree/window.
- The written polynomial repeats coefficient a1 for the squared term, a typographical ambiguity inconsistent with its otherwise general coefficient construction.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Band standard-deviation definition/multiplier, Super Smoother settings, LU pivoting and exact time orientation are unspecified.

  exit_z: {default: 0.0, type: float, desc: "spread z-score at or above which to exit"}
  stop_z: {default: -3.0, type: float, desc: "spread z-score at which to stop out"}
  adf_max_p: {default: 0.05, type: float, desc: "maximum ADF p-value that permits a trade"}
  require_cointegration: {default: true, type: bool, desc: "gate entry on the ADF test"}

# Pairs Trading / Cointegration vs BTC or ETH

> **Unblocked and measured.** The data gap that made this spec-only was "no peer price
> series". Coinbase serves BTC-USD and ETH-USD keyless through the fetcher already in
> this repo, so both were fetched (1,875 daily bars each, exactly aligned with SOL) and
> the mechanism was measured.

## What it is
Fit `SOL = beta * peer + c` over a trailing window, ADF-test the residual, and trade the
residual's z-score **only while that test says it is plausibly stationary**.

## Equation
```
Engle-Granger two-step, refitted every bar on trailing data only:
  1. regress SOL = beta*peer + c            (closed-form OLS)
  2. ADF-test the residual for a unit root
if p > adf_max_p:  take NO position          # the relation is not established
spread_z = zscore(residual, fit_window)
enter if spread_z <= entry_z ; stop if <= stop_z ; exit if >= exit_z
```

## Why this is not `zscore` with extra steps
`zscore.md` applies a stationarity-dependent method to raw price, which is **not
stationary** — a known theoretical error its measured result does not repair. Here the
traded object is a residual constructed to be stationary, and the assumption is
*tested*. `require_cointegration` makes the strategy refuse to trade until the test
passes. That refusal turns out to be the whole story.

## Implementation
`core/cointegration.py` (ADF + Engle-Granger, MacKinnon critical values, no
`statsmodels`) and `core/pairs.py`. Run through `backtester.paircli` — **not** the
strategy registry, because it needs two series and a registered strategy that silently
does nothing when its peer is missing would be a footgun.

## Measured on SOL

| Peer | Full-sample beta | Full-sample ADF | Cointegrated at 5% | OOS return | OOS trades |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | 0.0018 | −2.648 (p≈0.087) | **No** | 0.00% | **0** |
| ETH | 0.0644 | −3.127 (p≈0.032) | **Yes** | 0.00% | **0** |

The rolling gate screened out 1,121 of 1,624 windows against BTC and 1,224 against ETH.

**The result that matters is the contrast.** Disabling the gate on the ETH pair
(`--no-cointegration-gate`) produces **2 out-of-sample trades and −24.70%**. With the
gate on: no trades, no loss. The ADF screen is not decoration — on this data it is the
difference between losing a quarter of the account and standing still.

The figures come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, whose in-sample window
ends within one bar of the highest close in the series. `research/RANKED_LISTS.md`
documents why that makes it hostile, and `core/cpcv.py` is now the repo's primary
evaluation for exactly that reason. Read these as evidence about **one regime
transition**.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

Two findings pull in opposite directions, and neither supports more than low.

**In favour:** the rigour works. SOL and ETH *are* cointegrated on the full sample at
5%, which is a real structural relationship rather than a fitted one, and the gate
demonstrably prevented a −24.7% loss. Compare `zscore.md`, which had no such test,
bought dips through the same window, and produced the previously top-ranked medium row
that `RANKED_LISTS.md` later found consistent with noise.

**Against:** it made no money either, because it took **zero out-of-sample trades**. A
mechanism that abstains has demonstrated a filter, not an edge. And the honest reading
of "cointegrated with ETH" is unflattering — SOL and ETH are both high-beta crypto, so a
stationary spread between them may be measuring the same market twice rather than
finding a relative-value opportunity.

## Caveats and limitations
- **This is not the dollar-neutral pairs trade the literature describes.** Exposure is
  single-asset long SOL; the peer is an input to the signal, not a shorted leg. A real
  pairs trade needs short exposure this harness cannot express. That gap is the largest
  single reason to discount the numbers above.
- Engle-Granger is **order-dependent**: regressing SOL on ETH and ETH on SOL can
  disagree. Johansen is preferred for three or more series.
- `adf_pvalue` interpolates a lookup table. Treat 0.04 and 0.06 as the same answer.
- The practitioner rule of requiring cointegration across 3-, 6- and 12-month windows is
  **not** implemented; a single window is checked.
- Scanning many windows for cointegration will find some by chance — a 5% test has a 5%
  false-positive rate, and `test_pairs.py` asserts that rate rather than pretending it
  is zero.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.core.fetch --asset BTC --interval 1d --start 2021-06-17
python3 -m backtester.paircli --asset SOL --peer BTC --interval 1d --split 0.7
python3 -m backtester.paircli --asset SOL --peer ETH --split 0.7 --no-cointegration-gate
```

# Relative Bandwidth Filter

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Relative Bandwidth Filter identifies volatility regimes that another strategy can use to permit or suppress trading. It compares a broad channel width with a shorter-horizon ATR, then evaluates that ratio relative to its own Bollinger bands. The author explicitly interprets a high ratio as comparatively low volatility and a low ratio as comparatively high volatility, which should be preserved rather than replaced with an intuitive but different bandwidth interpretation.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Parameterized relative bandwidth/Bollinger context is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Divide a selected channel bandwidth by ATR. Channel choices are Bollinger, Keltner or Donchian.
- Apply Bollinger bands to that relative-bandwidth series to determine whether its value is comparatively high or low.
- Choose a standard Bollinger, Keltner or Donchian channel and calculate bandwidth=upper-lower. Divide by built-in ATR of caller length. Apply standard Bollinger mean plus/minus caller-multiplier standard deviation to the ratio. Lengths/channel multipliers are caller parameters; directional Signal mapping is excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- An unplotted Signal series is available through the data window and as another script’s external input. Values encode long-only, short-only, no trades or both directions.
- Usable scope: Parameterized relative bandwidth/Bollinger context. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Bandwidth length should exceed ATR length; no numeric defaults are supplied.
- Signal 1 allows long, -1 short, 0 no trades and 2 both sides.

- Analytical: regime filtering cannot establish the profitability of the downstream strategy and may suppress useful trades.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Track unmitigated fair-value gaps from a selected timeframe and add approximate volume pressure and a smoothed directional context. The indicator organizes candidate reaction zones rather than proving that institutions caused the price move.

## How it works

- A gap is the wick separation between the first and third candles of a three-candle sequence. Selected-timeframe OHLCV supplies the pattern; wick size relative to a running average filters weak candidates.
- Extending boxes persist until midpoint touch or full closure, according to the mitigation setting. Close position within the high-low range apportions volume into estimated buying and selling effort.
- A two-pole Butterworth filter smooths average gap values into a trendline, used to distinguish aligned and countertrend zones.

## Outputs and intended use

- Gap boxes, proportional volume sub-bars and an active-gap table with formation timestamps support zone tracking.
- The author favors bullish gaps with rising trend and bearish gaps with falling trend, using volume overlays as discretionary confirmation.

## Parameters and stated settings

- FVG source timeframe, wick sensitivity, midpoint/full-fill mitigation, table placement and gap styling.
- Trend smoothing exposes passband ripple and cutoff frequency from 0 to 0.5.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Close-location volume is a proxy for actual aggressor flow. Institutional origin and predictive validity are unverified interpretations.
- Higher/lower timeframe sampling and unconfirmed source candles could change live behavior; confirmation policy is not disclosed.

# ATR Rope

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Separate movement beyond an ATR-sized tolerance from smaller noise and preserve reference zones formed while the filtered center stays flat.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for the excess-distance rope-center recurrence with caller-supplied ATR tolerance, source and starting rope; exact published initialization and consolidation-zone lifecycle remain outside scope.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- For selected source S, previous rope R and supplied ATR tolerance A, leave R fixed while S is within [R-A,R+A]. When S exceeds the upper boundary, shift R upward by S-(R+A); below the lower boundary, shift it down by (R-A)-S. Thus the rope moves only by the distance beyond its tolerance envelope.
- Color upward rope motion green and downward motion red; a source crossing of the rope turns it blue/flat. Optional channel bounds are rope plus/minus ATR. During flat areas the upper/lower observations are accumulated and averaged into consolidation zones, whose exact lifecycle is not fully specified.

## Outputs and intended use

- Use rope, optional ATR bounds and extending zones to interpret trends, consolidation and retests. The author explicitly says it supplies no complete signal system.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Source is caller-selected, illustrated by separate high/low instances. ATR channel is hidden by default. The narrow recurrence accepts a supplied ATR series and initial rope value; published ATR length/estimator and seed defaults are not specified.

- The source claims live-drawn zones do not repaint, but unavailable code prevents verification. ATR changes and developing bars can shift boundaries; visual retests do not define executable setups.

# EWMA / GARCH(1,1) Vol-Targeted Trend

> **Implemented in this session** from spec-only mechanism #29 of
> `research/STRATEGIES.md`. Its stated gap was "implementable now — needs code, not
> data", so the code was written and it was measured on the same 1,875 daily SOL bars
> and the same 70/30 split as every other measured card.
# EWMA / GARCH(1,1) Vol-Targeted Trend

## What it is
`voltarget.md` with a variance *forecast* in place of a trailing estimate.

## Equation
```
sigma2_t = (1-lam) * r2_{t-1} + lam * sigma2_{t-1}       # GARCH(1,1), omega=0
target_t = min(1, target_vol / sigma_t)   if c_t > SMA(trend_window) else 0
```

## Why fixed lambda rather than fitted GARCH
`lam = 0.94` is the RiskMetrics convention and corresponds to
`alpha = 0.06, beta = 0.94`. Fitted GARCH coefficients are unstable on short samples,
and refitting every bar is both slow and an invitation to look-ahead. The fitted
version stays open work; this is the special case that needs no optimiser.

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/advanced.py::GarchVolTarget`, using the new
`indicators.ewma_vol`.

## Measured on SOL

| Leg | Return | Sharpe | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-sample | +18.9% | 0.321 | — |
| **Out-of-sample** | **-30.8%** | **-0.551** | **50** |

For reference on the same split: buy-and-hold made **+565.2% (Sharpe 1.030)**
in-sample and **-70.8% (Sharpe -0.651)** out. That row reproduces the figure the
existing cards document exactly, which is how these new numbers are known to be
comparable to them.


The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos.*

The forecast did not help. **-30.8% out-of-sample against `voltarget.md`'s -31.1%** —
the two are the same result to within a third of a percentage point, on 50 trades
against 73. Anticipating volatility clustering rather than measuring it after the
fact changed the trade count and almost nothing else.

That is informative: it says the lag in the volatility estimate was **not** what made
vol-targeted trend-following lose on SOL. The direction call was, and both cards
share the same crude SMA trend gate. Replacing the variance model was the wrong
repair.

### The hourly run exposed a three-way degeneracy

On 8,823 hourly bars at short-horizon scaling, `voltarget`, `garch_voltarget` and
`sma_regime` produced **numerically identical** results — median path Sharpe −2.282,
median return −19.9%, 292 trades, all three. That is not a coincidence and it is not a
bug: at `target_vol` 0.8 on hourly SOL the volatility cap binds on essentially every
bar, so `min(1, target/sigma)` collapses to 1.0 and both vol-targeted rules degenerate
into the plain trend gate they share with the regime filter.

The caveat was written on these cards before it was observed. Seeing three separate
"strategies" return one identical row is the cleanest demonstration available that a
sweep's configuration count overstates how many distinct ideas are in it.

## Caveats and limitations
- A variance forecast is not a return forecast. This changes sizing, never direction.
- `lam` fixed at the RiskMetrics value, unswept. A fitted GARCH may behave
  differently, and this card does not speak to it.
- Shares the trend gate with `voltarget.md`, so the two are not independent evidence.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy garch_voltarget --interval 1d
```

# Auto Chart Patterns [Trendoscope®]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Automatically identify multiscale chart patterns as pairs of nonintersecting trendlines, then label their geometry, direction and expansion behavior.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for thirteen-case supplied-line classification with caller tolerances; automatic zigzag/line discovery remains outside scope.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- For supplied line pairs and caller flat/parallel tolerances, thirteen cases are: both rising/parallel = ascending channel; both falling/parallel = descending channel; both flat = ranging channel. Both rising and widening/narrowing = expanding/contracting rising wedge; both falling and widening/narrowing = expanding/contracting falling wedge. Upper rising/lower flat = expanding ascending triangle; upper flat/lower rising = contracting ascending triangle; upper flat/lower falling = expanding descending triangle; upper falling/lower flat = contracting descending triangle. Upper falling/lower rising = converging triangle; upper rising/lower falling = diverging triangle.
- Generate recursive zigzags from several length/depth combinations and inspect the latest five/six pivots. Require an upper line touching highs, a lower touching lows and no intervening candle outside them. Classify relative slopes as channels,wedges or triangles and converging,diverging or parallel.

## Outputs and intended use

- Draw the accepted pattern and alert on new detections. Rising/falling channels,wedge variants,ascending/descending triangles and bidirectional triangles are geometric descriptions, not complete trades or validated reversal probabilities.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Configure base zigzags,pivot count,error/flat thresholds,last-pivot direction,bar-ratio filtering,overlap policy and group/individual pattern toggles. Avoid Overlap ignores a candidate starting inside an existing pattern; numerical defaults are absent.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Multiple scales generate correlated structures and flexible tolerances can overfit visual history. Latest zigzag pivots may change before confirmation; a valid pattern is not a guaranteed breakout or prescribed direction.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Base/recursive swing algorithm, exact trendline fit/touch tolerance,error/flat units,bar-ratio limit and candle containment price definition are omitted.

## Data requirements

Required inputs: ohlcv.

Repository input-class support: available. OHLCV supports geometric pattern scanning; missing detection equations are algorithm gaps.

> Fractional EMA Kalman Filter [D7] is an experimental smoothing and state-estimation tool that combines a Kalman filter framework with a fractional EMA input. The objective is to create a filter that remains subdued during ranging conditions while retaining responsiveness when directional structure emerges. By integrating adaptive variance logic and residual-based state control, D7 aims to balance smoothness, reactivity, and structural awareness.

> The difference between the incoming measurement and the current state estimate; the correction signal the filter acts on. Innovation = EMA − X

> The adaptive weighting factor that balances trust between the new measurement and the prior prediction. K = P / (P + R)

> The current filtered estimate of price, updated using a fractional-length EMA measurement input. This is what the filter believes the true underlying value to be at each step.

> Applies a double sub‑integer EMA length (e.g., 0.5‑period) to generate a high‑resolution measurement signal that responds to structural volatility and regime transitions faster than conventional smoothing. The fractional EMA is not intended to estimate price, but to precondition the observation space so that regime changes manifest as large, legible innovations. By transforming the input prior to filtering, the measurement emphasizes moments of structural change rather than steady‑state behavior, improving the responsiveness of adaptive state estimation.

> This script is a research tool for market structure analysis and educational purposes only. It does not constitute financial advice. Trading involves risk.

# Swing Trade Breakout with Confluence

## What it is
The guides describe swing trading as holding multi-day moves, with a breakout above resistance confirmed by SMA, Fibonacci, volume, MACD or RSI. This is that rule with the confirmations made explicit and countable.

## What it looks for
A breakout that other indicators back, to filter breakouts that fail.

## Equation
```
resistance = max(high over the PRIOR `breakout` bars)       (current bar excluded)
confirms   = [close > SMA(ma_window)] + [MACD hist > 0] + [RSI(14) > 50] + [OBV > mean(OBV, 20)]
enter  if close > resistance and confirms >= min_confirms
exit   if close < min(low over the PRIOR `exit_lookback` bars)
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/textbook.py::SwingConfluence`. Fibonacci is not one of the four confirmations: it has its own card (`fib_retracement`) and a retracement level is not a state that confirms a breakout.

## Parameters
- **breakout / exit_lookback** are the Donchian entry and exit windows.
- **min_confirms** from 1 to 4. At 4 it almost never fires; at 1 it is a plain Donchian breakout.

## Works when
Breakouts that follow through, usually in a rising regime where the SMA, MACD and RSI are already positive.

## Fails when
False breakouts in a range, and any move where the confirmations are lagging (all four are derived from the same closes, so they are correlated, not independent evidence).

## Backtest notes
The four confirmations are not independent: SMA, MACD and RSI all read the same close history. `min_confirms` therefore counts agreement among near-duplicates and is a weaker filter than the number suggests. Counting four threshold tests multiplies the free choices (windows, 50 for RSI, 20 for the OBV mean), so the multiple-testing denominator grows with each one.

## Pairs with
A volatility filter (`vol_regime`), which none of the four confirmations measures.

## Measured on SOL
Smoke run only, not a sweep row: `python3 -m backtester.cli --split 0.7 --interval 1d`, SOL daily 2021-06-17..2026-08-04, default parameters, 8 bps round-trip costs, one 70/30 split. The split is structurally hostile to long-biased rules (see `research/RANKED_LISTS.md`), so read it as one regime transition, not an estimate. The queue (`soltui/bgqueue.py`) will produce the evaluated numbers; this card stays `implemented` until a sweep supplies them.

Full sample: +571.09% (Sharpe 0.913, 27 trades) vs buy-and-hold +87.61%. 70/30 split: IS +794.1% (Sharpe 1.238) -> OOS -7.54% (Sharpe 0.019), maxdd -33.77%. The best OOS row of the five new cards but flat, not positive; OOS trade count was not captured in this run, so it may sit under the 10-trade floor.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: base-rate. A multi-indicator filter over correlated inputs, in the breakout family, which measured poorly out of sample.*

## Caveats and limitations
- Named by the cited trading guides catalogued in `tradingstrategyresults.json` (repo root, untracked source list). The guides give a verbal rule or a formula, not tested parameters; every default here is a convention, not a finding.
- Rated from the sweep's overall hit rate (14% of 311 rankable configurations had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe), not from this card's own result.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy swing_confluence --interval 1d --split 0.7
```

## How it works

- From the two-year price-high anchor, sum daily short-sale volume S and total volume V and calculate S/V. Color the connecting line red when S/V >= 20% and green otherwise. The numerator measures transaction flow, not outstanding short positions.
- For a new one-year short-volume high, aggregate the five preceding sessions, event session and four following sessions. For a price pivot defined as the highest high over 51 sessions, aggregate three preceding sessions, the event and two following sessions. Calculate short/total-volume ratios over those retrospective windows and apply the same color threshold.
- Secondary dollar estimates use VWAP with short and non-short turnover, but the exact VWAP anchoring is not defined.

## Outputs and intended use

- Labels, boxes and lines compare short-volume ratios around events. The text calls one measure short interest ratio, but its described numerator is short-sale volume, not outstanding short positions.

## Parameters and stated settings

- The threshold is twenty percent. The price pivot spans 51 sessions. Short-volume-high windows contain five preceding, the event and four subsequent sessions; price-pivot windows contain three preceding, the event and two subsequent sessions.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Both event windows include future sessions, so finalized stamps are retrospective. VWAP times turnover estimates gross transaction value and cannot establish remaining short positions.

# Andean Oscillator

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Andean Oscillator separates directional price variation into bull and bear components using exponential envelopes of prices and squared prices. It aims to show both trend direction and variation amplitude, with an additional signal line to filter component crosses. The source’s descriptions of which envelope creates bull versus bear must be retained as written rather than silently corrected to an assumed implementation.

## How it works

- Build upper/lower exponential envelopes for ordinary and squared prices, subtract squared ordinary-envelope values from squared-price envelope values and take square roots.
- The prose assigns upper-envelope variation to bull and lower-envelope variation to bear; smooth a signal line for additional cross interpretation.

## Outputs and intended use

- Green bull over red bear is interpreted as uptrend and the reverse as downtrend; author suggests component/signal crosses as a stronger filter than component crosses alone.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Length controls variation significance and Signal Length the signal average; no defaults or average type are given.

- Analytical: naive second-moment subtraction can suffer cancellation/negative roundoff, and crossing signals can whipsaw; narrative envelope assignment needs code verification.
