# Testing

## Standalone bot manager

The `botmanager/` package has its own unittest suite and CI job. Install the four
regular local projects into an isolated Python 3.13 environment, then run from the
repository root:

```bash
python -m pip install ./backtester ./oracle ./soltui ./botmanager
python -m unittest discover -s botmanager/tests -t botmanager
```

The suite uses temporary `SOLBOT_HOME` directories. CLI reads must leave missing
storage absent; defaults, pinned configurations and separate bot identities must
survive a fresh process. Owner-integration fixtures exercise actual HTTP requests
without starting or changing production bots. Runtime tests also exercise separate
instances, crash-before/after commit, stale generations, stopped intent, dead/hung
workers, snapshot integrity and canonical simulator parity. launchctl fixture tests
do not establish installed service behavior; that remains an independent gate.
Current runtime and venue limits are listed in `botmanager/README.md`; tests do not
establish a profitable trading edge.

The targeted macOS CI job also installs the headless owners and runs the blind
judge tests on an actual supported operating-system sandbox. Linux refusal tests
do not establish macOS isolation. When changing the judge, run this focused suite
on macOS and independently verify its installed runtime/profile:

```bash
python -m unittest discover -s botmanager/tests -t botmanager -p test_blind.py
```

## Existing component suites

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s backtester/tests -t .   # 1002 tests
python3 -m unittest discover -s soltui/tests -t .       # 1435 tests (~840s, optional)
python3 -m unittest discover -s mongo/tests -t .        # 46 tests
cd extension && npm test                                # 408 tests
python3 scripts/check_docs.py                           # these counts, and the retrieval indexes
```

The full SolTUI suite is optional and is skipped by normal PR/push CI. Run it
locally with the command above, or manually dispatch CI with the boolean
`run_soltui_suite` enabled. The other CI jobs and test-discovery count check stay
enabled. This delivery skips the full suite at the owner's explicit request;
focused UI, accounting and installed acceptance checks are recorded separately.

2891 tests total across the unittest and `node:test` suites. `liquidity/` additionally has its own pytest suite in its own virtualenv; see `liquidity/README.md`.

Every count on this page is checked by `scripts/check_docs.py`, which counts the suites by
discovery and fails on a stale figure. That exists because these numbers were wrong for
several commits — the docs claimed 250 backtester tests while the suite had grown to 454, and
nothing caught it.

## Extension — what the 408 tests cover

| Area | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Live prediction score | Shared Python/browser vectors bind all five grades, accuracy/sample floors, freshness and equal strategy weighting. Headless TUI and Chrome checks prove aligned immutable tick scores, leftward motion, automatic ten-second prediction refresh, error recovery, non-overlapping reads, coin-switch reset and obsolete-response/error suppression |
| Charts | the vendored Lightweight Charts file is the pinned 5.2.1 build (sha256), ships LICENSE and NOTICE; equity points map to ascending second-resolution line data (`test/charts.test.js`); `npm run e2e` draws it under the real extension CSP with the attribution link |
| Grid math | Arithmetic and geometric ladders against hand-computed values; endpoint pinning; degenerate configs rejected |
| **Round-trip economics** | An exit rests one rung above its lot, never at the same level; `gross === notional × rungWidth` |
| Planning | Lot aggregation (two lots on one rung produce **one** order, not a duplicate key); venue minimum; deadband; already-resting suppression |
| Risk rails | Each rail fires on its own breach; a batch cannot collectively breach a cap each member passes; rails **fail closed** on missing or NaN state; unusable orders blocked |
| P&L | FIFO across lots; partial closes realizing a proportional share of entry fees; carry subtracted; fees turning a gross win into a net loss; unmatched sells surfaced |
| Reconciliation | A venue echoing fewer decimals is matched, **not duplicated**; a missing order is orphaned and never auto-retried; unknown live orders adopted; two near-identical orders do not bind to one intent |
| Tick guards | Unusable price aborts before P&L; the daily counter measures today, not lifetime; a short grid on a spot venue says so |
| Wallet | base58 against real mints and the all-zero pubkey; shortvec boundaries; signature insertion into the correct slot; non-signer refused |
| Crypto | Sealed-seed round trip; wrong passphrase fails closed; fresh salt and IV per seal; Ed25519 signing |
| **Surface parity** | Every command routable over the API; `GET` restricted to read-only; CLI help lists all commands and every argument; UI messages all map to real commands |
| **Signal Desk** | Real installed module/style identity, four routes, saved comparison compatibility, exact snapshot handoff without starting, pending/accuracy/return units, archived mutators, local search/dialog focus, mobile/compact layouts and light/dark contrast samples. The new workflow regression uses memory-only native writes |
| **Dashboard workspace** | All installed TUI commands are reachable through workflow groups; explicit false/clear values, structured tables, sortable/filterable results, CSV/JSON, sparse heatmaps, editor guards and confirmation resets have dedicated coverage. The real-browser gate uses a memory-only transport for write regressions; no real order or document write is sent |
| **soltui bridge** | `soltuiCall` returns the identical envelope through the extension message, the CLI and the API; a refusal, an unknown command and a missing host are the same clean envelope everywhere; the confirm flag is forwarded untouched; a running soltui command does not hold the engine lock; transports (port and child process) time out, ignore other ids and reject junk frames |
| **Market reads** | ABI decoding against the live `tickSpacings()` answer; non-read RPC methods refused; endpoint fallback; wrong-chain endpoint refused; low-confidence prices unused; unpriced unknown mints listed but not counted; Jupiter holdings first, RPC fallback; exact CL output inside the active range and refusal past it; Jupiter replies that do not match the request refused |
| **Alerts** | Only fresh, backtest-positive, medium/high-confidence, unflagged, gauged scout pools above break-even may say "act"; a stale or undated scout cannot; an active strategy with no Top 5 record has no baseline; today's all-negative scout raises nothing; idle capital counts Base stablecoins only; quoted leads are info and do not notify by default; first scan records leads silently, and an empty read still counts as the baseline; acks survive re-scans; scans and acks run one at a time |
| **Auto-reload gate** | First observation only stores the hash; no reload while a tick is queued or running (the change is retried, not forgotten); the reload runs inside the engine lock and holds it; an unreachable host never reloads and is logged once; a failed `reload()` restores the old hash |

The parity suite probes all 35 commands with a deliberately invalid argument, which proves the route
resolved **without executing the handler** — no side effects, no network calls.

## What is NOT covered

Read this before trusting anything with money.

1. **No live order has ever been placed.** The write path (auth → vault → deposit craft → sign →
   create) matches the documented shapes but has never executed. It needs an API key and a funded
   wallet. Test with one rung at the $10 minimum.
2. **The Trigger contract has offline fixtures, not live acceptance.** History pagination and
   cancellation were checked against current public documentation. Wallet-specific responses,
   execution USD valuation and semantic transaction verification still need verified fixtures.
3. **Fee attribution is unconfirmed.** Unknown costs remain flagged for inspection and hold new
   admission. Uncertain execution price, quantity or timing also holds planning.
4. **Signature insertion is tested against synthetic transactions**, not a real Jupiter deposit.
5. **The e2e covers loading and dry-run only.** `npm run e2e` loads the unpacked extension in
   Chrome for Testing and checks install state, service worker, popup, dashboard, a dry-run plan
   and tick, rails and secrets. It never arms or signs and stubs the network, so it says nothing
   about live orders. Needs Chrome for Testing; it is not part of `npm test`.
6. **The Chrome alarm floor is assumed to be 30s.** The engine logs the real wake delta — watch it
   before trusting a sub-minute tick.

## Extension — real-browser e2e

`npm run e2e` (`extension/tools/e2e.mjs`, helpers in `extension/e2e/`) launches Chrome for Testing
headless, loads `extension/` with `Extensions.loadUnpacked` over the DevTools pipe, and drives the
real service worker, popup and dashboard. It uses Node built-ins only. 24 checks (25 with the production soltui host):

| Check | What it proves |
| --- | --- |
| Service worker starts | The manifest entry point loads as an MV3 worker |
| Installs disarmed in dry-run | `runtime.armed` and `killSwitch` are false and `config.mode` equals `DEFAULT_CONFIG.mode` after a real `onInstalled` |
| Install event and alarm | The journal holds the `installed` event; the tick alarm is scheduled |
| Popup and dashboard | Both render from the worker's `status`; dry-run and disarmed are shown |
| Registry parity | The worker's command list equals `COMMAND_NAMES`; unknown messages are refused |
| Plan and tick | `plan` is priced by the stubbed read and returns intents; a disarmed `tick` is skipped as `not-armed` and journals nothing |
| Rails fail closed | Missing, NaN or malformed state and limits block, run in the browser |
| Secrets | A canary API key appears in no DOM, no response and no `chrome.storage.sync` |
| Network audit | Chrome-level interception saw only keyless GET price reads; every other request was blocked |
| soltui bridge | The real extension talks to the soltui native messaging host (a host manifest is written into the throwaway profile's `NativeMessagingHosts`). `soltuiCommands` and a read-only `soltuiCall` return the same envelope as the extension CLI, and with the production host as `soltui list` / `soltui call`, byte for byte. An unknown command and a missing host are clean failed envelopes. The dashboard SolTUI panel lists the registry and shows the result as text. The 1-minute build probe alarm exists. The run says which host it used: the production host when soltui is installed, a protocol-identical fixture (`e2e/fixtures/`) where it is not, for example the Linux CI runner. `SOLTUI_E2E_HOST=real` fails the run if the production host cannot start |
| Disarmed at the end | The run never changed `armed` or the kill switch |

Safety is structural: `e2e/lib/guard.mjs` allowlists the messages the harness may send and
`test/e2e-harness.test.js` (part of `npm test`) fails when a new registry command is not classified.
Install a browser with `npx @puppeteer/browsers install chrome@stable` (branded Chrome ignores
command-line extension loading); set `CHROME` for another build and `E2E_NO_SANDBOX=1` in containers.

## Verification commands

```bash
cd extension

npm test                                              # unit + parity
node tools/dryrun.js --ticks 8 --osc 6 --offline 100  # a round trip must close positive
npm run e2e                                           # real-browser load + dry-run checks (needs Chrome for Testing)
node tools/dryrun.js --ticks 4 --walk 5 --offline 100 # trending case: bids fill, no exits
node tools/verify-endpoints.js                        # live Jupiter reachability
find src tools test -name '*.js' -print0 | xargs -0 -n1 node --check
```

The oscillating dry run is the meaningful one: it is the only check that closes a round trip and so
the only one that can detect a zero-spread regression.

## Backtester — 1002 tests

Correctness of the simulation is the priority, so the suite concentrates on the things that silently
inflate a result: **lookahead leaks**, cost application, and metric arithmetic. Any change touching
signal generation or fill timing needs a test that would catch a one-bar leak. See
`backtester/README.md`.

`test_scorecard.py` holds that test for the compound five-minute scorecard: every historical
component, the composite, the regime label and the target path must give the same value at bar t
whether or not the bars after t exist (prefix invariance), and a deliberately leaky component is
shown to fail the check. `test_compound_backtest.py` covers the 5m loader (traded-minute
aggregation, gaps split into segments, stale funding refused), the engine fill at bar t+1's open,
and that fees reach the P&L. The same prefix-invariance check runs with adaptive weighting on and with tuning forced to move, so a learned weight or an adopted setting at bar t never uses the outcome of bar t.
`test_fetch_minutes_alt.py` runs the other-venue minute fetcher against canned replies: KuCoin and
WhiteBIT's `[t, open, close, high, low]` rows land in OHLC order, OKX's unconfirmed candle is
dropped, a page with swapped columns stops the fetch before anything is written, and a resumed
fetch neither repeats nor skips minutes.

32 of those cover the ladder-grid simulator (`core/gridsim.py`), and they exist because that module
has to agree with `extension/src/core/grid.js` about what a round trip earns. Three groups matter
most: the **round-trip invariant** (gross `== notional × rung width`, plus rung width asserted
against the JavaScript implementation's own figures), the **no-lookahead group** (nothing fills on
bar 0; a bar spanning both legs books only the entry), and the **failure modes** (a one-way
downtrend fills every bid and loses; an unfundable rung is skipped rather than overdrawn; a forced
end-of-run exit is never counted as a captured rung).

36 of them cover the **strategy cards** (`core/strategy_cards.py`). Those tests exist because a card's
frontmatter supplies numbers to a backtest, so the machine-readable half is checked against the code
rather than trusted: registry drift is asserted in **both** directions (every registered strategy has
a card, every card's `registry_key` still exists), every declared default is compared against its
constructor's actual default, `warmup_bars` and `family` against the code, and every card's presets
against `research/sweep.py` so a card documents the same experiment the sweep runs. Every buildable
card is also constructed and run through a full backtest. Prose in a card can still be wrong — no
test catches that — but a number cannot.

31 more cover the **nine strategies implemented from spec-only cards**
(`core/strategies/advanced.py`). Each test targets what that mechanism could get
*wrong* rather than that it runs: the excluded window in dual momentum, the strength
gate in ADX, and above all the **displacement trap in Ichimoku** — the cloud sitting
at the current bar was computed 26 bars ago, so reading it as current reads 26 bars of
future data. That test asserts the value used equals the cloud computed from the
truncated slice *and* differs from the full-history cloud, so the distinction is
verified rather than assumed.

63 cover the **per-bar rule readout** (`research/decide.py`), and the one that matters
asserts *engine parity*: a recording wrapper captures every `on_bar` return
`run_backtest` asks for, and the readout's replay must reproduce that index sequence and
those values exactly for all 25 strategies. The rest guard the two ways the readout can
lie — a truncated-history test that fails if the replay is ever "optimised" into a single
call on the last bar, and a constructed series where that shortcut gives the *opposite*
answer, so the first test is known to be load-bearing rather than vacuously true.

## soltui — 1435 tests

The suite includes real Textual render cycles, subprocess lifecycle checks and offline strategy integration.
Run all tests with
`python3 -m unittest discover -s soltui/tests -t .`.

soltui keeps research simulations separate from explicitly confirmed manual Coinbase orders. Its tests cover
display correctness, not money. `test_compound.py` covers the Compound 5m tab end to end
(toggle, edit, refused values, a stubbed live signal) plus the forward ledger with stub venues:
the still-forming bar is dropped, a call is recorded once per bar and resolved by the next close,
and an enabled news gate blocks when its feeds are unreachable. `test_launcher.py` drives the `soltui` shell command
(`soltui/bin/soltui`) through a symlink with a fake interpreter, so it checks the repo
lookup, the module choice and argument pass-through without starting Textual. The
packaging paths — the py2app alias bundle and the launchd agent — are **not** covered by
any test; see `soltui/README.md` for the manual checks that stand in for them.

The optimization workbench has dedicated foundation, native runner and interface suites:
`test_experiments.py`, `test_experiment_runner.py` and `test_experiment_interface.py`.
They cover immutable cells, typed budgets, observed sparse maps, CSV units/provenance,
spent/explored temporal reservations, legacy fences, historical mutation, cooperative controls,
process termination/recovery, baseline comparison, adoption crash receipts and the headless UI.
Fixtures isolate configuration/data; tests stub the live order path and do not submit real orders.

## mongo — 46 tests

Split between pure helpers that need nothing and integration tests that **skip cleanly
when no mongod is listening**, so a checkout without a database runs the suite green
rather than red.

The one that earns its keep asserts *idempotency*. `load.py` drops before it writes, and
two consecutive loads must leave identical counts — a time series collection accepts no
unique index, so nothing else would catch a second load silently doubling all 18,381
bars. It runs over a three-collection subset to stay fast; the mechanism is the same for
every collection.

The rest guard the store's honesty: every document carries provenance, the server refuses
one that does not (strict validation, proven by an insert that must raise), NaN never
reaches the store, and the card counts track the registry — 49 cards with `registry_key`
set on exactly 25, every key real.

## Adding tests

- Extension: `extension/test/*.test.js`, `node:test` + `node:assert/strict`. Assert behaviour and
  observable effects, not line execution.
- Backtester and research: `backtester/tests/`, `unittest`. `research/` has no test directory of
  its own; its modules are tested from there (`test_decide.py`, `test_cpcv.py`, `test_interpret.py`).
- soltui: `soltui/tests/`, `unittest`.
- mongo: `mongo/tests/`, `unittest`. Guard anything server-dependent with the module's
  `needs_server` decorator so a checkout without mongod still passes.
- A new command needs no new parity test — the registry-driven suite picks it up automatically. If it
  takes an argument that changes money, add a behavioural test for that argument.


## Coverage target and CI gates

The coverage target is meaningful assertions on important and changed paths, including
failure modes, state transitions and emitted logs. This repository does not configure a
numeric line-coverage threshold. A blanket 100% line target is not an existing CI gate.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs extension unit/parity/syntax/manifest/offline-dry-run
checks, backtester tests/imports, soltui tests on macOS, MongoDB integration tests with
a service container, documentation/index drift checks, and liquidity Ruff/format/pytest.
The default liquidity pytest selection excludes the `network` marker. Public Jupiter
reachability is informational and runs on workflow dispatch, not on each PR.

A green suite does not prove that the installed Chrome extension, macOS bundle, live
liquidity daemon, or venue envelope matches the tested source. Record those acceptance
gaps separately. Installed-service tests must not be replaced by process-liveness alone.

Normal PR and push CI runs a bounded SolTUI bridge smoke gate plus modules mapped to changed areas. Unknown paths retain the smoke gate. This is not full-suite coverage. The four-shard full suite requires manual dispatch with `run_soltui_suite=true`.

Version: 1.0.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: first source-reconciled card.

## Mechanism and equations

## Documented inputs and source details

> VWAP Price Channel cuts the crust off of a traditional price channel (Donchian Channel) by anchoring VWAPs at the highs and lows. By doing this, the flat levels, characteristic of traditional Donchian Channels, are no more!

> While the DC upper or lower values are staying flat, the VWAPs improvise based on price and volume to project a level that may be a better representation of where future highs or lows may settle.

# Oscillator Evaluator (Analysis tool)

Version: 1.0.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: initial source-grounded companion card for a strategy-labelled tool.

**Classification:** evaluation-tool. Companion research-tool card; excluded from the executable strategy roster.

## Idea and objective

Compare how different oscillators behave under several common signal interpretations, holding the evaluation framework conceptually constant.

## How it works

- One selected oscillator is compared with two alternatives. Six test modes probe trend correlation, crossover behavior, zero crossings, extremes, short-horizon mean reversion, and trend profit-taking.
- The tool asks what information an oscillator provides; it is explicitly not presented as a complete strategy. Its modes are alternative experiments, not six confirmations to combine into one entry.

## Documented rules and trade lifecycle

- Mode 1 uses moving-average increase/decrease; mode 2 uses a two-moving-average crossover.
- Mode 3 enters long on a zero crossover and short on a zero crossunder.
- Mode 4 buys/sells at oscillator extremes. Modes 5 and 6 evaluate mean-reversion filtering/small changes and profit-taking within trends, respectively.
- The description does not give the exact thresholds, lengths, position handling or exit conditions for most modes.

- Oscillator selection, two comparison oscillators and one of six evaluation modes are described. Complete defaults are not provided.

# RedK Slow_Smooth Average (RSS_WMA)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

RSS_WMA deliberately favors a slow, smooth trend baseline over rapid response. It seeks to suppress small fluctuations so the trader can see broader price behavior and compare a stable reference with a faster moving average. The author also suggests considering direction changes as exit context, because the line is intended to respond only after a sustained move. This is a conscious lag tradeoff rather than a claim that smoothing removes trading risk.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Apply weighted-moving-average smoothing repeatedly; the combined smoothness value is distributed across consecutive WMA passes.
- Allocate increments first to the first pass, then the second, then the third, cycling through the passes.

## Outputs and intended use

- Use the line for macro trend inspection, noise filtering or comparison with a fast average; a sustained change in direction can inform discretionary exits.

- There are three WMA passes; initial first-pass length is one third of the Smoothness setting. Settings below 3 simply track the source.
- The control is Smoothness rather than a conventional single-window length; no default value or source-price default is supplied.

# Donchian Channel Breakout

## What it is
Long on a new *n*-bar high; flat on an *m*-bar low. The Turtle mechanism.

## What it looks for
Range expansion — the start of a new trend leg.

## Equation
```
Upper_t = max(H_{t-n} .. H_{t-1})     # EXCLUDES the current bar
Lower_t = min(L_{t-m} .. L_{t-1})
enter if c_t > Upper_t ;  exit if c_t < Lower_t
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/breakout.py`.

## Parameters
- **entry_lookback / exit_lookback** — asymmetric on purpose: enter on a longer
  channel, leave on a shorter one, so exits are faster than entries.

## Works when
Volatility expands out of contraction and the resulting trend runs far enough to pay
for the false starts.

## Fails when
False breakouts dominate. The Turtles' documented win rate was **30–35%** — the profile
depends entirely on a few large winners, so **missing a handful of big moves ruins the
year**. That makes short backtest windows especially unreliable for this family.

## Backtest notes
**The channel must exclude the current bar.** Including the current high makes the
comparison nearly always false and silently guts the strategy — a bug that looks like
a working strategy with poor results. Documented false-breakout filters worth testing:
require two consecutive closes beyond the level; require the breakout candle's body to
exceed 70% of its range; require above-average volume.

## Pairs with
Volume (a genuine breakout shows participation); a volatility-squeeze filter; a
reversion rule for the exit, which a pure breakout rule handles poorly.

## Measured on SOL
Full-sample medium: +620.7%, Sharpe 0.935. Walk-forward: **IS +860.2% (Sharpe 1.265)
-> OOS -7.5%** on only 7 OOS trades — **below the evidence floor**, which is exactly the
low-trade-count problem the Turtle profile predicts.
`any(breakout + zscore)` was the **best measured medium pair: OOS Sharpe +0.584, +30.8%**.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

OOS -7.5% on **7 trades** cannot be ranked, and a documented 30-35% win rate means any
window short enough to contain few large winners misrepresents this family in either
direction. The reason it is not very-low is `any(breakout+zscore)`, the **best measured
medium pair** (+0.584 Sharpe, +30.8%). The mechanism is documented and durable; this
sample cannot show it.

## Caveats and limitations
- With a 30–35% win rate, any window short enough to contain few large winners will
  misrepresent this strategy in either direction.
- 7 out-of-sample trades cannot rank. This card's headline is the *pair*, not the
  single.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy breakout --interval 1d
```

## Documented inputs and source details

> Reflex and Trendflex are zero-lag oscillators that decompose price into independent cycle and trend components using SuperSmoother filtering. These indicators isolate each component separately, providing clearer identification of cyclical reversals (Reflex) versus trending movements (Trendflex).

> Based on Dr. John F. Ehlers' "Reflex: A New Zero-Lag Indicator" article (February 2020, TASC), both oscillators use normalized slope deviation analysis to minimize lag while maintaining signal clarity. The SuperSmoother filter removes high-frequency noise, then deviations from linear regression (Reflex) or current value (Trendflex) are measured and normalized by RMS for consistent amplitude across instruments and timeframes.

> Both oscillators begin with a two-pole Butterworth low-pass filter that smooths price data without the excessive lag of simple moving averages. The filter uses exponential decay coefficients and cosine modulation based on the cutoff period, providing aggressive smoothing while preserving signal timing.

> • Reflex reversal with Trendflex agreement: Cyclical turn within established trend (entry/exit timing)

> Reflex isolates cyclical price behavior by measuring deviation from a linear regression line fitted through the SuperSmoother output. For each bar, the filter calculates a linear slope over the lookback period, then sums how much the smoothed price deviates from this trendline. These deviations represent pure cyclical movement - price oscillations around the dominant trend. The result is normalized by RMS (root mean square) to produce consistent amplitude regardless of volatility or timeframe.

> Trendflex extracts trending behavior by measuring cumulative deviation from the current SuperSmoother value. Instead of comparing to a regression line, it simply sums the differences between the current smoothed value and all past values in the period. This captures sustained directional movement rather than oscillations. Like Reflex, normalization by RMS ensures comparable readings across different instruments.

# VIX Curve Pro - Real-Time Term Structure with Statistics

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

VIX Curve Pro displays volatility-index values across maturities as a spatial curve and summarizes their historical relationships. Its aim is to identify upward- versus downward-sloping volatility structures and whether current ratios sit near historical extremes. Traders can use that context for volatility or options research, but the curve is a comparison of maturity-specific volatility indexes, not a directly specified tradable futures portfolio. The author’s example contradicts the earlier regime definitions by calling short-term volatility below long-term volatility backwardation; this inconsistency must be resolved before relying on its labels.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable narrowly for the raw maturity-ordered VIX curve, given external maturity series. Derived ratios/percentiles, regime labels and full feed-symbol mapping remain limitations; the contradictory backwardation example is preserved.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Independent raw curve: obtain contemporaneous values for the supplied 9-day, 30-day, 3-month, 6-month and 1-year VIX maturity series, order those observations from shortest to longest maturity and connect their untransformed values as a curve. This does not require the optional ratio, percentile or regime predicates.
- Collect VIX values at several horizons and connect them as a maturity curve.
- Calculate historical ratio percentiles and lookback minimum, maximum, average and median statistics.
- Flag curve inversions and regime changes; flips can drive alerts.

## Outputs and intended use

- Curve, statistical tables, regime/inversion indicators and optional explanatory guide support volatility-context inspection.

- Lookback and alert configuration are mentioned without numeric defaults.
- Raw curve maturity order is 9D, 30D, 3M, 6M, 1Y. Exact spatial spacing and the full feed-symbol mapping are not supplied.

> A bearish Tri Star pattern can form when three doji candlesticks appear in immediate succession at the end of an extended uptrend. The first doji candle marks indecision between bull and bear. Each doji candle has a shadow, all comparatively shallow, which signify an interim cutback in volatility.

> Traditionally, this candlestick pattern is recognized in conjunction with a specific trend direction, i.e. it might be important for the pattern if the price has been generally going up or down. The ‘Detect Trend Based On’ option allows you to specify which of the following methods to use to detect the trend:

> SMA50 - the indicator compares the current price of the symbol to its Simple Moving Average (SMA) with the length of 50. If the current price is below the SMA, this price movement is considered a downtrend. If the price is above the SMA, it is an uptrend.

# SOL Crypto Strategy Backtester

An offline, event-driven backtesting harness for crypto trading strategies,
built around SOL. Supports unlevered **spot** and **Jupiter-Perps-style
leveraged perpetuals** with a correctly-modelled borrow fee.

> **Historical simulation for research and education only. NOT investment
> advice, and not a recommendation to trade anything.** Simulated past
> performance does not predict future results. Leveraged perpetuals can lose
> your entire collateral. There is no live-trading capability in this codebase
> and none should be added — see [Scope](#scope).

## Why this exists

The ask was "backtest different crypto trading strategies, primarily SOL." The
hard part of that is not running strategies; it is running them *honestly*. A
backtester that is 20 lines shorter and silently leaks one future bar will
report a beautiful Sharpe ratio and lose money in production. So the design
priority here is: **correctness of the simulation outranks the number of
strategies shipped.** A tool that honestly reports a losing strategy is a
success; one that reports an inflated Sharpe because of a leaked bar is a
failure even if it runs.

## Install

```bash
cd /Users/mitch.hudson/dev/solmargintrader
pip install -r backtester/requirements.txt   # pandas, numpy, matplotlib
```

Python 3.13. `matplotlib` is optional (charts degrade to "skipped"); `pyarrow`,
`requests`, and `pytest` are deliberately **not** required.

## Usage

Fetch data once, then backtest from the local cache. The engine never touches
the network.

```bash
# 1. Populate the local CSV cache from the Coinbase public API (no key needed)
python3 -m backtester.core.fetch --asset SOL --interval 1d --start 2021-01-01

# 2. Compare all strategies, with a 70/30 walk-forward split
python3 -m backtester.cli --asset SOL --strategy all --split 0.7 --out results/

# 3. Leveraged perpetual run
python3 -m backtester.cli --asset SOL --mode perp --leverage 10 \
    --strategy breakout --start 2024-01-01

# Offline demo with no data file at all
python3 -m backtester.cli --synthetic 800 --strategy all
```

Run with no arguments to print usage. `python3 -m backtester.cli --help` lists
every flag.

### Key flags

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--mode {spot,perp}` | Unlevered spot, or Jupiter-style perpetual |
| `--leverage N` | Perp leverage. Spot rejects anything but 1 |

## Verified local history and result archives (experimental)

For the complete acquisition history, architectural decisions, operating procedures, backup recovery, and remaining work, see [the historical backtester handoff](../docs/backtester-history-handoff.md).

The history store imports a contiguous CSV as an immutable content-addressed
snapshot. It records the operator-supplied instrument, venue, source label,
interval and bar-open timestamp convention. The source label is an assertion,
not independent proof of provenance. A correction creates a new snapshot.
Import does not alter the original CSV. The database is private (mode 0600),
but its directory, filesystem encryption and off-machine backup remain the

so reading a large snapshot may be slow and use substantial memory.

For a verified SOL-USDC snapshot, pass `--quote USDC`; the spot engine records

Result archives store the exact manifest and its listed artifacts in one SQLite

charts created after the manifest are not included. `read_run()` returns the
original bytes and rejects a missing or altered artifact. `backup_archive()`
creates a new SQLite backup and checks stored run and history hashes; copy the
backup to an independent location and periodically test restoration. Hashes
detect changes but do not make an untrusted model or data source correct.

This is a foundation, not a completed multi-asset backtesting system. It does
not discover sources, fill missing histories, model chain-specific transactions
or infer execution costs; the 14-asset coverage, comprehensive simulator
validation, stress scenarios and representative performance benchmarks remain
open in the implementation plan.

## Minute-history collection and gap-safe queries

`backtester.core.kucoin_history` collects a named spot market into a private
SQLite database. Each fixed UTC window stores the exchange's exact response,
a SHA-256 digest and the normalized OHLCV rows in the same transaction. A
completed window is rechecked on resume. The documented KuCoin candle API
may omit intervals without ticks and may be incomplete; an omitted minute is
not silently replaced with a synthetic price. An `endAt` equal to the next
window boundary is exclusive for the tested market; version-1 databases made
with the older `endAt=boundary-60` request are refused. When multiple collectors
run at once, set `KUCOIN_HTTP_LOCK` to the same private lock-file path. They
then serialize HTTP calls and hold the lock through 429 backoff; processes that
do not use the same lock are outside that coordination.

`collect(database, symbol, start, end)` uses UTC epoch seconds and a half-open
`[start,end)` range. Keep the same start and end when resuming an interrupted
run, especially for the partial last window. `audit_store(...)` replays stored
responses and writes a gap ledger distinguishing `UNFETCHED` windows from
`UNOBSERVED` provider intervals. The distinction does not establish whether
an unobserved interval had trades. `read_range(...)` verifies every touched
source response and normalized row and refuses ranges with even one missing
minute. The database is indexed by timestamp and window.

`backtester.core.segmented_history` copies an existing ordered CSV into an
immutable private data file and indexes gap-free segments with byte hashes.
`read_range(directory,start,end)` uses **inclusive** UTC endpoints and refuses
a range crossing a gap. Unlike the source-preserving KuCoin store, these
legacy copies cannot prove the originating venue or quote unless an external
source provides binding evidence. A matching pair on a different venue is a
different market and must not silently replace missing candles.

Source data and local backups are not a guarantee of historical completeness,
point-in-time availability, trading liquidity, or independent disaster recovery.
For example, a venue may omit trades from a candle or omit a minute entirely;
the repository's candle-gap audit documents this failure.

## How look-ahead bias is prevented

Structurally, not by convention. The per-bar ordering is:

1. accrue borrow fees for the elapsed bar (perp only)
2. execute any fill scheduled for this bar, **at this bar's open**
3. liquidation check against this bar's low/high (perp only)
4. ask the strategy for a target, **given data ≤ *i* only**
5. schedule that target for bar *i + fill_delay*
6. mark to market at this bar's close

A strategy receives a `BarWindow`, whose every accessor returns `arr[:i+1]`.
There is no unguarded path to the underlying arrays, so a strategy reaching for
`closes[i+1]` gets an `IndexError` rather than tomorrow's price. `tests/`
includes a deliberately-cheating strategy and asserts that it raises — a guard
that cannot fail is not a guard.

Also enforced: rolling statistics use trailing windows only (never full-sample
normalization, the most common form of this bug); indicator warm-up produces no
trades; and fees/slippage are charged on the fill, never netted at the end.

Both public simulators validate finite, equal-length OHLCV arrays and require the
timestamp cadence to equal the configured interval. A loader's `--allow-gaps` flag
does not waive that simulation requirement. Missing bars refuse rather than producing
unsupported borrowing costs or annualization. Public history arrays own only the visible
prefix and cannot mutate future/caller data; this is not a sandbox for hostile Python.
Metrics include initial entry costs against explicit starting capital. The ladder limits
planning to 10,000 rungs, rejects key collisions and never exits below the actual lot entry.
Triple construction in `research/sweep.py` uses in-sample scores/trade counts only.

## The leverage cost model — a borrow fee, *not* a funding rate

This is the single most important thing to get right about Jupiter Perps, and
it is where a generic perp backtester goes wrong.

```
utilization      = custody.assets.locked / custody.assets.owned
hourlyBorrowRate = max_hourly_rate * utilization
hourlyBorrowFee  = hourlyBorrowRate * positionSizeUsd     # notional
```

* **Both sides always pay.** Longs and shorts both owe fees to the liquidity
  pool. There is no long-pays-short transfer, and no position is ever *paid* to
  stay open. The rate is a product of two non-negative quantities, so it is
  floor-bounded at zero. Porting funding-rate intuition here understates
  holding cost in one direction: always too low.
* The fee accrues on **notional**, not collateral and not units.
* Accrual is an index difference × notional — **additive, not fee-on-fee**.
  What feels like compounding is second-order: fees erode collateral,
  effective leverage rises, and the liquidation price drifts toward spot.
* Longs borrow volatile custody, shorts borrow stable custody, so the two sides
  take **separate rates** (`1.6` vs `0.3` bps/hr by default).

Rates are configured in **bps per hour** to sidestep the deci-bps ambiguity in
the venue docs: `1.6 bps/hr == 0.016%/hr == ~140% APR`, the documented SOL
reference point.

### Liquidation

Maintenance margin is `size / max_lev` where `max_lev` is a **protocol constant
of 500** — i.e. **0.2% of notional** — which is *not* the user-facing leverage
cap. The buffer as a fraction of entry price is:

```
buffer = 1/L - f_close - 0.002 - borrow_fee/size
```

| Leverage | Buffer at t=0 |
|---|---|
| 10× | 9.74% |
| 100× | 0.74% |
| 250× | 0.14% |

Because accrued borrow fees appear in that expression, **the liquidation price
drifts toward spot the longer you hold** — it is recomputed every bar, not
fixed at entry. Liquidation fills at the liquidation price and checks the
intrabar wick, so a bar that spikes through your level and recovers still
liquidates you.

The published formula's `abs()` bars are only valid while the bracketed term is
positive; past that the sign flips and the formula leaves its domain. That case
is flagged (`in_domain=False`) rather than propagated as a plausible price.

### One open question, not papered over

The published borrow formula is flat-linear in utilization, so the rate → 0 as
utilization → 0. But protocol governance separately proposed a **dual-slope
("jump rate") model with a kink near 80% utilization and a minimum floor around
10% APR**, which is mathematically *incompatible* with `utilization × max`.
Which is live cannot be settled from documentation.

So: flat-linear is the default, and `--min-borrow-bps` / `--kink-utilization`
let you model the proposed alternative. **If you are modelling low-utilization
periods, set the floor rather than trusting the flat-linear result, and read
the live value from the on-chain custody account.** All rate constants here are
governance-set configuration defaults, not constants of nature.

## Metric definitions

Ambiguous annualization is the most common source of a wrong Sharpe ratio, so:

* **Sharpe** = `mean(excess) / stdev(excess, ddof=1) × sqrt(periods_per_year)`.
  `periods_per_year` derives from the bar interval using a **365-day crypto
  year** (crypto trades every day — not 252). `stdev` is the **sample**
  standard deviation. The risk-free rate is an explicit parameter defaulting
  to 0. This convention is printed in every report, not just documented here.
* **Sortino** — same, against downside deviation.
* **Max drawdown** — peak-to-trough on the equity curve, reported with start
  date, end date, and duration in bars. Negative fraction (`-0.42` = −42%).
* **Calmar** = CAGR / |max drawdown|.
* **Profit factor** — gross wins / gross losses. Reported as `inf` when there
  are no losing trades; that is information, not an error.
* **Win rate / trade count** — over *closing* fills only. An opening fill has
  no outcome yet, so counting it would dilute the rate.
* **Exposure fraction** — mean |signed notional / equity|.
* Every run reports **gross** (zero-cost) alongside **net**, from a parallel
  book that mirrors each decision, so cost drag can't drift out of sync.

## Honest reporting

The comparison report is where a tool like this most easily misleads, so it
carries its own caveats:

* **Buy-and-hold is always included** as the baseline, and is added
  automatically if you leave it out. Underperformance against it is stated
  plainly, not buried in a sorted table.
* **Walk-forward** reports in-sample and out-of-sample as separate columns. The
  out-of-sample slice starts `warmup_bars` early so indicators warm from
  trailing in-sample bars — reading earlier history is not look-ahead, and
  starting cold would silently discard real out-of-sample data.
* **The multiple-comparisons warning is printed with the ranking.** The best of
  N backtests is upward-biased by selection, and the bias grows with N.
  Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016) argue the significance bar should rise from t ≈ 2.0
  to **t ≈ 3.0+** once multiple testing is accounted for. McLean & Pontiff
  (2016) measured **26% in-sample and 58% out-of-sample decay** across 97
  published factors. The report prints how many configurations were evaluated.

### What the real data actually showed

On 1,875 real SOL daily bars (2021-06-17 → 2026-08-04), spot, 6bps fee + 2bps
slippage, 70/30 walk-forward:

| Strategy | Full-sample return | In-sample | **Out-of-sample** |
|---|---|---|---|
| buy_and_hold | +87.6% | +565.2% | **−70.8%** |
| ma_crossover_20_50 | +298.3% | +735.6% | **−52.3%** |
| rsi_14_30_50 | −15.7% | −9.6% | **−21.9%** |
| breakout_20_10 | +620.7% | +860.2% | **−7.5%** |

Read that table before trusting any full-sample number, here or anywhere. Every
strategy looked excellent in-sample and lost money out-of-sample. The
full-sample column is dominated by one enormous bull run inside the in-sample
window. This is the tool working correctly — it is *supposed* to make that
visible rather than hide it behind a ranked Sharpe leaderboard.

**Leveraged runs are worse, and the reason is the borrow fee.** A 10× long from
2024-01-01 goes to −100% with 26 liquidations, and the cost breakdown is
\$722 of borrow fees against only \$211 of trading fees — carry, not churn, is
what kills it. At 3× with a 15% rebalance deadband, borrow fees reach **\$10,023
on \$10,000 of starting capital** over ~580 days. That is the documented venue
behaviour, not a modelling artifact: this is a venue built for short holding
periods, and its fee structure actively penalises carrying a position.

## Adding a strategy

Implement the Protocol and add one registry entry. No engine changes.

```python
# core/strategies/my_strategy.py
from ..types import BarWindow

class MyStrategy:
    def __init__(self, lookback: int = 30) -> None:
        self.name = f"my_strategy_{lookback}"
        self.params = {"lookback": lookback}
        self.lookback = lookback

    def warmup_bars(self) -> int:
        return self.lookback

    def on_bar(self, history: BarWindow) -> float:
        """Target exposure for the NEXT bar, in [-1, 1]."""
        closes = history.closes          # only bars <= now
        return 1.0 if closes[-1] > closes[-self.lookback:].mean() else 0.0
```

Then in `core/strategies/__init__.py`:

```python
REGISTRY["my_strategy"] = MyStrategy
```

**Then add its card.** `backtester/strategy_cards/my_strategy.md` carries the equations,
the reasoning, the failure modes and the parameter defaults — and
`tests/test_strategy_cards.py` fails if a registry entry has no card, or if a card's
declared defaults, `warmup_bars` or `family` drift from the code. That check runs in both
directions on purpose: a strategy nobody documented and a card for a strategy nobody
kept are both silent failures. See `strategy_cards/README.md` for the schema, and
`python3 -m backtester.core.strategy_cards` for the current inventory.

The engine — not the strategy — owns position sizing, fee application, and fill
timing. A strategy that can only emit a target exposure for the next bar cannot
leak the future.

**Sizing rule:** target exposure `e` means notional of
`|e| × current_equity × leverage`, marked at the fill price. Current equity,
not initial capital — so strategies compound.

## The ladder grid — backtesting what the extension actually trades

There are two different things called "grid" in this repo, and conflating them
would put a wrong number under the strategy that runs live:

| | What it is | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `grid` (`GridLong`) | An **exposure staircase**: exposure rises one rung per `step` below a rolling SMA anchor. A `Strategy` like any other, filled at a bar boundary. | `core/strategies/signals.py`, run via `backtester.cli` |
| **ladder grid** | A **ladder of resting limit orders** with paired exits one rung above each lot — the extension's strategy. Fills intrabar at known prices. | `core/gridsim.py`, run via `backtester.gridcli` |
| **DCA bot** | A **deal-based safety-order bot**: market base order, deeper (optionally larger) resting safety buys, one take-profit above the average entry; restarts after each exit. | `core/dcasim.py`, run via `backtester.botcli dca` |
| **triangle replay** | Three-leg USD cycles through a cross pair at the touch, executed at the quotes `latency_s` after detection; an L1 screening replay over snapshots recorded by `soltui/pricefeed.py`. | `core/trianglesim.py`, run via `backtester.botcli triangle` |

`GridLong` can imitate a grid's *position profile*, but it can never capture a
rung width, because it never has an order sitting at a level waiting to be hit.
That capture is the entire economic engine of a real grid, so it needs its own
simulator rather than a `Strategy` returning one target exposure per bar.

```bash
# The ladder and what it costs to fund, without running anything
python3 -m backtester.gridcli --lower 60 --upper 90 --rungs 7 \
    --notional-per-rung 12 --levels

# A run on cached bars, or offline on synthetic ones
python3 -m backtester.gridcli --lower 60 --upper 90 --rungs 7 \
    --notional-per-rung 12 --interval 1h
python3 -m backtester.gridcli --lower 60 --upper 90 --rungs 7 \
    --notional-per-rung 12 --synthetic 400 --capital 500 --json
```

`core/gridsim.py` ports `extension/src/core/grid.js` function for function —
geometric/arithmetic spacing with pinned endpoints, top-rung extrapolation,
paired exits, the deadband, the $10 venue minimum, paired-lot realization with FIFO fallback. Divergence
between the two would be worse than having no grid backtest at all, so
`rung_width_bps` is asserted against figures read off the JavaScript
implementation (699.1319 bps for a 60–90/7 ladder; 516.7 bps for the 0.85×–1.15×
ladder `tools/dryrun.js` builds).

**Three conventions keep it pessimistic**, because an optimistic grid simulator
makes a losing grid look profitable:

1. **An order cannot fill on the bar that planned it.** Planning happens at a
   bar's close, so the earliest fill is the next bar. This is the no-lookahead
   guard and it also makes a same-bar round trip impossible — "price dipped to
   the bid then rallied to the offer" is an assumption about the intrabar path,
   not an observation of it.
2. **Fills are adverse.** A buy fills at its level moved up by the full slippage
   allowance, a sell at its level moved down by it.
3. **Buys settle before sells**, so cash freed by a sell cannot fund a buy in the
   same bar.

Lot matching is additionally bounded to lots opened *before* the current bar. Without
that bound, two exits filling in one bar let the second reach inventory bought
that same bar — an indirect same-bar round trip. It fired on synthetic data
during development, so the bound is load-bearing rather than theoretical; when
old inventory runs short the exit fills partially and the remainder is re-planned.

**Realization is paired, as in the extension.** Each resting exit carries the lots it
was planned to close (`RestingOrder.closes`) and a fill closes those first, then falls
back to FIFO for the rest (`TASK-348`). Strict FIFO let an exit paired to a cheap lot
consume an older, dearer one, leaving a residual whose re-planned exit sat at the level
the held inventory was bought at: a zero-spread sell. `test_the_residual_after_an_exit_is_the_inventory_actually_held`
pins it; the end-of-run forced exit has no pairing and is FIFO.

Carry defaults to **0 bps/hr** because Trigger V2 is a spot venue with no borrow
leg — not because carry is free. `--carry-bps-per-hour` models a borrowed-margin
ladder, and the rate is echoed in the output so a run can never quietly claim a
cost structure it did not use.

Every run prints a buy-and-hold baseline on the same bars, paying entry costs
once. A grid that underperforms holding the asset has not earned its complexity.

## Peer-relative value: the rigorous version of a z-score

`zscore` assumes the series it measures is stationary, and raw price is not. A
cointegrated spread is *constructed* to be stationary and the assumption is **tested**:

```bash
python3 -m backtester.core.fetch --asset BTC --interval 1d --start 2021-06-17
python3 -m backtester.paircli --asset SOL --peer BTC --interval 1d --split 0.7
```

`core/cointegration.py` implements an Augmented Dickey-Fuller test and the
Engle-Granger two-step with MacKinnon critical values — no `statsmodels`, since
`requirements.txt` stays minimal. `core/pairs.py` refits beta every bar on trailing data
only and **refuses to trade** while the ADF test fails.

That refusal is the measured result. SOL and ETH are cointegrated on the full daily
sample (ADF −3.127, p≈0.032); SOL and BTC are not (p≈0.087). Either way the strategy took
**zero out-of-sample trades** — and with the gate disabled it took two and lost
**24.7%**. The screen, not the z-score, is what the mechanism contributes.

It runs through its own entry point rather than the strategy registry because it needs
two price series, and a registered strategy that silently does nothing when its peer is
absent would be a footgun.

## Archiving a series nobody publishes

Some data cannot be fetched retroactively at all. JLP is the example: Coinbase does not
list it, and Jupiter serves its spot price but no history.

```bash
python3 -m backtester.core.archive_price --mint JLP    # append one observation
```

Append-only, refuses a non-positive price rather than writing a zero, and warns while

```bash

```

| Test | Known answer |
|---|---|
| Buy-and-hold identity | Total return `== last_close/first_close − 1` at zero cost, to 12 dp |
| Look-ahead guard | A cheating strategy **raises** |
| Fill timing | Signal at bar *t* fills at bar *t+1*'s open |

| Data validation | Duplicate/gap/negative/NaN/millisecond input is rejected |
| Determinism | Two runs produce identical output |
| Ladder round trip | Gross `== notional × rung width`, to 9 dp — the same contract the extension asserts |
| Ladder rung width | Matches the JavaScript `rungWidthBps` to 3 dp |
| Ladder same-bar guard | A bar spanning entry and exit books the entry only |
| Ladder first bar | A bar-0 sweep of the whole ladder fills nothing |
| Ladder downtrend | Every bid fills, no round trips, final equity below capital |
| Ladder cash limit | An unfundable rung is skipped, equity never negative |
| Ladder book identity | At zero cost, final equity `== capital + realized P&L` |

## Scope

**Out of scope, deliberately.** No live or paper order execution, no exchange
API keys, no wallet or private-key handling, and no code path that can place,
sign, or transmit a real trade. No automated parameter search — the tool
evaluates the configurations it is given and reports their metrics; sweeping
for a winner is exactly the overfitting this harness exists to expose. (You can
still run it repeatedly by hand, which is why the report counts configurations
evaluated. Counting is not searching.)

## Known limitations

* **Single asset per run.** No cross-sectional universe, so no survivorship
  bias — but also no portfolio-level analysis.
* **Bar-resolution fills.** No order book, no partial fills, no queue position.
  Slippage is a flat bps assumption, which understates cost in a crash.
* **Utilization is an input, not a history.** Real Jupiter utilization varies;
  a constant is a modelling simplification. Governance has documented SOL
  utilization sitting at 100% for sustained periods, which more than doubles
  the borrow cost versus the 0.5 default.
* **Oracle execution is not modelled.** Jupiter is oracle-priced peer-to-pool
  with keeper fulfilment and no FIFO guarantee; a stop can lose the race to a
  liquidation. This harness assumes your stop/target logic executes.
* **Liquidation ignores the price-impact fee** a real liquidation would incur,
  so it is still mildly optimistic — but it does fill at `min(level, bar_open)`
  for longs, so a bar that *gaps* through your level fills at the open rather
  than at a price that never traded.
* **Resize costs assume the venue's merge semantics** — a same-side size change
  pays the base fee on `|Δnotional|` and blends the entry price, rather than
  paying a synthetic round trip. If you point this at a venue that really does
  charge a full round trip per adjustment, leveraged costs here are too low.
* **No funding-rate mode.** By design — this models Jupiter's borrow fee. Do
  not repurpose it for a CEX perp without adding a signed funding model.

# 120x ticker screener (composite tickers)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

This screener demonstrates packing multiple market prices into a synthetic composite ticker and decoding them after a shared data request. Its financial purpose is to display a wider set of ticker metrics under the request constraints discussed in the publication. The central contribution is a fragile encoding technique, not an independent trading strategy or a current guarantee about platform limits. Manually chosen decimal spacing preserves distinguishable price components only while the selected symbols remain within anticipated ranges.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** The worked scaling, rounding and subtraction example defines reproducible composite-close encoding/decoding with caller-selected symbols and scales; RMA/RSI extras are explicitly unreliable.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Scale component ticker prices by selected powers of ten, add them into a composite expression, request that expression and split it through rounding and subtraction.
- Use reconstructed close histories to calculate percentage change, SMA, RMA and RSI for a sorted table; debugging can compare components against ordinary ticker prices.

## Outputs and intended use

- Inspect multi-ticker metrics and use unsorted debug output to check price decoding; tickers and their scaling/rounding settings must be edited in source.

## Parameters and stated settings

- The method composes three tickers per composite; higher timeframe defaults to Daily. Metric length, table sorting, exchange labels and colors are configurable.
- The author identifies roughly 15–16 significant digits as a practical encoding limit and recommends one or two zero separators.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Mixed market hours can break composites; large price changes require rescaling. The author reports RMA/RSI differences on lower chart timeframes.
- Analytical: composite highs/lows and finite precision cannot be assumed to preserve independent asset observations. Historical platform-limit wording is not a current API fact.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- The full symbol universe, exact safe scaling bounds, missing-feed behavior and resolution-correct RMA/RSI reconstruction are unresolved.

Required inputs: selected multi-symbol price histories, composite ticker calculation support.

> MACD employs two Moving Averages of varying lengths (which are lagging indicators) to identify trend direction and duration. Then, MACD takes the difference in values between those two Moving Averages (MACD Line) and an EMA of those Moving Averages (Signal Line) and plots that difference between the two lines as a histogram which oscillates above and below a center Zero Line. The histogram is used as a good indication of a security's momentum.

> 1- Plotting of the Oscillator presented on top of the price chart (main chart) and applicable on both log and linear scale. Maximum plotting length is limited to 250 bars

> The MACD-Histogram measures the distance between MACD and its signal line (the 9-day EMA of MACD ). Aspray developed the MACD-Histogram to anticipate signal line crossovers in MACD . Because MACD uses moving averages and moving averages lag price, signal line crossovers can come late and affect the reward-to-risk ratio of a trade. Bullish or bearish divergences in the MACD-Histogram can alert chartists to an imminent signal line crossover in MACD

# Delta Volume Columns Pro [LucF]

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Inspect estimated directional volume through five balance models, with configurable columns, signal lines, divergence context and alerts. Crucially, the publication uses different historical and realtime methods and explicitly warns that refreshed elapsed realtime bars change.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Historical directional-volume raw/EMA balances is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Historically, classify lower-timeframe bars into buy/sell bins by direction, carrying the last polarity when unchanged. Realtime mode instead accumulates price/volume feed updates; initial existing bar volume is assigned by current polarity.
- On-bar balance is buy minus sell; average balance subtracts their EMAs. Momentum balance contrasts each EMA with a double-length SMA and applies centered RSI to the directional difference. Relative balance takes positive excesses above separate EMAs, subtracts them and ALMA-smooths; percent balance smooths delta divided by total volume.
- Combined balances sum directional states. Marker bias accumulates signed events; divergence levels retain and expand signal levels on disagreement with bar polarity, leaving subsequent movement to establish direction.
- For supplied historical LTF bars sign volume by candle direction,carrying last polarity when unchanged. U,D are summed directional volumes;OnBar=U-D;Average=EMA(U,n)-EMA(D,n) with caller n/LTF. This historical branch is reproducible independently of live update/reset behavior,ALMA/marker settings and initial-polarity policy;retain data_available=false for full realtime parity and all repaint warnings.

## Outputs and intended use

- Stacked buy/sell columns or a selected balance/bias line, independent coloring/fills, divergence channels and chart-bar colors support discretionary context.
- Markers cover balance agreement, consecutive directional bumps, divergence confirmation and state/bias shifts. The author stresses uncertainty rather than predicting reversals from divergences alone.
- Usable scope: Historical directional-volume raw/EMA balances. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Separate smoothing periods, historical intrabar auto/fixed choices, signal/display/marker selection and volume-discrepancy threshold. Default historical targeting uses at least50 intrabars per chart bar.
- Combined state range is -5 to+5; momentum RSI is centered on -50/+50.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Refresh/re-execution repaints elapsed realtime bars and confirmed alerts because they recalculate through the coarser historical model. Live update history cannot be reconstructed from generic candles.
- Volume feeds differ across resolutions and instruments. Legacy platform restrictions in the description are historical claims, not current API guarantees.

```text
Historical bars on TradingView charts contain OHLCV data only, which is insufficient to calculate volume​ delta on them with any level of precision. If your chart Is running at 1D on a 24x7 market for example, most 1D chart bars will contain 24 underlying 1H bars in their dilation. On historical bars, this indicator looks at those intrabars to amass volume​ delta information. If the intrabar is up, its volume​ goes in the Buy bin, and inversely for the Sell bin. When price does not move on an intrabar, the polarity of the last known movement is used to determine in which bin its volume​ goes.
```

> The bearish Abandoned baby is a three-candle reversal pattern that appears after an uptrend. A strong bullish candle is followed by a Doji that gaps above it, and then by a bearish candle that gaps below the Doji. The isolated Doji in the middle, "abandoned" by gaps on both sides, shows that buying momentum has stalled and sellers have taken over.

> Trend filter: In the indicator settings, choose how the prior trend is detected (based on SMA 50, or SMA 50 and SMA 200), or turn trend detection off.

> Like any candlestick pattern, the bearish Abandoned baby describes what has happened, not what will happen. The uptrend can resume after the pattern completes, especially in a strong market. Because the pattern is rare, there is also a risk of reading too much into a near-match, such as a Doji with a small overlap that does not meet the definition. Traders often combine it with stop-loss levels, for example above the high of the Doji, to limit losses if the reversal fails.

> The Abandoned baby is considered one of the strongest reversal signals among candlestick patterns, but it is also rare. Full gaps on both sides of the Doji are uncommon in markets that trade around the clock, such as crypto and forex, where one session's close is usually the next session's open. The pattern appears more often in stocks and futures, where overnight gaps are common.

# TTrades Daily Bias [TFO]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

TTrades Daily Bias assigns a next-period target toward a previous high or low from the latest completed period’s relationship to its own prior range. It then measures how often those target levels are reached and closed through. Daily and weekly modes share the same scenario logic, making the tool a directional-target heuristic plus historical reporting rather than a complete entry/stop strategy.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- A close above/below prior high/low favors continuation toward the corresponding next period’s prior extreme; a one-sided sweep closing back inside favors the opposite extreme.
- An inside period uses prior-candle bullish/bearish polarity; an outside period sweeping both sides and closing inside receives no bias.
- Draw reference levels, mark touches and count target-hit and subsequent close-through outcomes by scenario.

- Inspect current daily/weekly bias, reasoning labels, target status and sample-size statistics; configure new-bias or high/low-hit alerts.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Volume profile is an advanced charting indicator that displays trading activity over a specified time period at specified price levels. These indicators take into account user-defined parameters such as number of rows and time period and plots a histogram on the chart to reveal dominant and/or significant price levels based on volume.

> They take the total volume traded at a defined price during the given time period and divides the total volume into either up volume (trades that moved the price up) or down volume (trades that moved the price down) and then make that information easily visible.

> Volume profile indicators are calculated using data from lower timeframes for the same symbol.

> This backward-looking approach is actually valuable because it helps you understand why certain price levels matter. When you see a price level where significant buying activity occurred previously, that spot often becomes a support zone — a place where price tends to bounce back up. The same logic works in reverse — if you notice heavy selling activity at a higher price level, that area typically acts as resistance, pushing price back down when it tries to break through.

> Point of control (POC): The price level for the time period with the highest traded volume.

> Profile high: The highest reached price level during the specified time period.

> You can use volume profile to spot key support and resistance levels. This approach differs from others in that volume profile is a reactive tool, meaning it shows you what already happened rather than predicting what's coming next. Unlike proactive indicators like trend lines or moving averages that try to forecast future moves, volume profile reveals where significant trading activity took place in the past.

# Adaptive Candlestick Pattern Recognition System

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Recognize configurable candlestick formations and summarize their subsequent returns by market-range location. Adaptive label colors communicate historical pattern behavior rather than assigning textbook bullish/bearish labels unconditionally.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Elementary candle predicates/classic event returns is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Classic mode measures next-open to a selected future close after pattern detection. Breakout mode waits for a close at/beyond pattern high or low within a configurable confirmation window; nonconfirming patterns lose labels and are excluded.
- Prior trend comes from price relative to a chosen average or shorter versus longer averages, sampled before the pattern. Returns partition by higher-timeframe price-range location and update arrays of mean, median, deviation and positive/neutral/negative counts.
- Nested patterns can be overridden by larger formations and stop contributing returns. Target mode deliberately changes that behavior. Adaptive coloring compares pattern statistics across the matrix, optionally clipping at fixed tolerance limits.
- Range engulfing:second.high>=first.high AND second.low<=first.low;body engulfing:second body interval contains first body interval. Caller inclusive toggle chooses equality versus strict endpoints. Doji:abs(close-open)<=caller_tolerance*(high-low). On fixed supplied detections,classic forward return=100*(selected_future_close/next_open-1),measured only after future close matures. Full85-pattern detection,trend variants,confidence and override timing remain excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- Pattern labels/tooltips show names, range partition and historical statistics; switches/target mode limit visible formations while enabled patterns can continue accumulating observations.
- The author encourages parameter experimentation, while warning historical conditional returns and confidence displays do not guarantee future behavior.
- Usable scope: Elementary candle predicates/classic event returns. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Recognizes85 patterns spanning one to five candles. Breakout confirmation allows one to five candles; detection has a one-candle offset.
- Default range partitions use yearly high/low: top20%, middle80%–33%, bottom33%. Extensive body/range/wick, engulfing, gap and equality tolerances, two averages and sample/return horizons control detection.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Selection, overlapping returns and adaptive color comparisons create multiple-testing and sample-dependence risks. Labels require future outcome maturity and must not be mistaken for contemporaneously known performance.
- Target mode can retain otherwise overridden patterns and duplicate returns; disabling component dojis affects composite patterns. Equal average lengths force MA1 even with different types.

## Idea and objective

Zahorchak Measure supplies a broad-market trend bias to inform stock or ETF decisions. Positive values broadly indicate an uptrend and negative values a downtrend. This adaptation smooths a discrete composite into an oscillator, aiming to reduce whipsaws while accepting additional lag. Volume Delta Compare contrasts live-update and lower-timeframe estimates of directional volume. Its purpose is to show why the same chart candle can yield different delta values depending on observation granularity. - Assign incremental live volume to up, down or neutral according to the direction of the observed price change.
- For the lower-timeframe path assign each sub-bar volume by its price movement, which can disagree with the intrabar sequence.
- Subtract down from up volume for delta and sum delta for cumulative delta; compare candle direction with delta sign for divergence colors.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Directional Volume Shapes (Zeiierman) is a regime-classification oscillator that reframes volume analysis around a different question: not simply “how much volume traded,” but “what statistical shape has directional pressure been forming, and which way is it leaning?”

> Most volume tools show exactly what happened: green bar up, red bar down, and taller bar equals more volume. This indicator uses a two-stage process: classify, then synthesize.

> Instead of using a simple “close above open equals bullish” rule, the indicator models the candle’s high-low range as a triangular probability distribution centered at the close.

> When the EMA is above or equal to zero, polarity is Bull. When it is below zero, polarity is Bear.

> Instead of plotting raw buy and sell volume bar by bar, the indicator scores each candle for directional pressure using a triangular intrabar distribution model. It collects those scores in a rolling window, classifies the pattern into one of seven distribution shapes, and displays a smooth synthetic template of the detected shape.

> This gives high-volume bars more influence over the rolling shape-classification window. When disabled, the classifier uses directional pressure alone.

## Idea and objective

Machine Learning Neural Network Engine reduces daily market context to LONG, WATCH and CASH. It combines an online neural classifier with a structural trend baseline, adjusts neural influence according to matured prediction errors, and separately checks downside stress. The design attempts to avoid trusting the learned component when it adds little information and allows crisis conditions to override it. Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Adaptive Hull Moving Average+ varies its smoothing period with either volume or volatility and colors the resulting curve according to trend direction and slope. Its purpose is to distinguish relatively inactive conditions from stronger movement while preserving a moving-average support/resistance reference. The author positions it as a companion to other analysis and offers discretionary entries combining price location, curve color and RSI. These examples do not establish measured profitability or a fully defined execution policy.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for the named fixed-period WMA HMA curve with integer component lengths, obtained by equal period bounds. Adaptive volume/volatility lengths, colors and alerts remain incomplete.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Narrow fixed HMA mode sets Minimum Period=Maximum Period=N. Expand the named WMA-based Hull construction as HMA_N(X)=WMA_(int(sqrt(N)))(2×WMA_(int(N/2))(X)−WMA_N(X)); integer conversion replaces rounding of component lengths as disclosed. This is the fixed curve only, not the opaque adaptive charger or color logic.
- Construct the HMA from weighted averages with integer conversion rather than rounding of component lengths.
- Lengthen the adaptive period when the chosen activity measure is weak and shorten it when activity strengthens.
- Combine slope with activity state: yellow denotes flat conditions, light directional colors weakness and darker colors stronger movement.

## Outputs and intended use

- Use the colored average and optional background for market-condition assessment.
- A suggested long has price above the average, dark green color and RSI above 50; short is the inverse. Equal minimum and maximum lengths recover a fixed-period curve.

- The author example spans 172 to 233 around HMA 200, particularly on 15-minute charts.
- Charger type, period bounds, consolidation threshold and background are configurable.
- Choose a source series and period N with positive integer component lengths; set both period bounds to N. The source gives no source/default fixed-N contract beyond its examples.
