# Retrieval before exploration

Use the configured global AI hub semantic search first when it is available. If the
connector is unreachable or returns no relevant hit, use the existing local keyword
index (`python3 index/search.py --text "<query>"`) and targeted source reads. See
`index/README.md`. Do not start an indexer, watcher, inference runtime or embeddings
merely to begin a repository task. Semantic regeneration is a separate explicit action.

# CLAUDE.md — solmargintrader

Instructions for agents working in this repository. Read before changing code.

## Workflow records

Save each user request verbatim in `prompts.md` before implementation. Keep `memory.md`
current with the target, completed work, verification, and remaining steps. Increment the
record version and its delta fields on each update. These workflow versions are separate
from component package versions. Commit only the files owned by the current task.

## What this is

Ten components with different risk profiles. Know which one you are in:

| Component | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `ecosystem/` (Python) | Paper-only setup, durable F5 coordination, external bot registrations, sanitized manager telemetry and a local paper control room with authenticated, durable owner actions. Reuses existing workers and recorder. Never arms or submits orders. |
| `oracle/` (Python) | Source-labelled shadow forecasts and a historical event archive with read-only MCP subscriptions. Never signs or submits orders. Reference agreement is not profit probability; unavailable inputs fail closed. |
| `botmanager/` (Python) | Standalone `solbot` lifecycle and evidence application. Default paper/disarmed. Legacy adapters preserve the existing owner; missing data, credentials or execution capability fail closed. Never silently seize a bot or create a duplicate recorder/optimizer. |
| `backtester/` (Python) | Simulation only. **Never add live-trading capability here** — see its README's Scope section. The danger is a dishonest backtest, not a lost trade. |
| `research/` (Python) | Analysis built on the backtester. The danger is overstating a result. |
| `extension/` (JavaScript) | **Can place real orders and move real money.** Treat every change as production software. |
| `soltui/` (Python) | macOS research console with a separately armed manual Coinbase spot-order path and optional no-confirmation mode. |
| `mongo/` (Python) | Derived local datastore. Rebuildable from the repo; nothing else imports it. |
| `executor/` (Python) | **Moves real money** on Solana: guarded spot swaps through Jupiter. It signs and sends. Its own venv and pytest. Read `executor/CLAUDE.md` first: rails, verifier, journal, and what is not built yet. |
| `liquidity/` (Python) | **Moves real money** on Aero (Base). It manages, compounds and allocates LP positions. Its own venv and pytest. Read `liquidity/CLAUDE.md` first: it records the owner's live-operation authorization and its limits. |

## Live on-chain actions (owner's standing authorization)

**Liquidity archive, 2026-11-08:** The owner discontinued the liquidity manager and scout as unprofitable. Keep the Aero LP service disabled and the kill switch set unless the owner later requests reactivation. See `liquidity/CLAUDE.md`.

The owner has given this instruction three times (last on 2026-11-06). Do not ask for it again.

For the owner's own wallets, agents may act live without a further confirmation:
- Base `0x901a89cEC0608eB5435A915f006b45bD46405314` (key file `~/.ssh/wallet.private`);
- Solana `EMTK62aecgScjEuZqbqeGquk8cBoQF9Z4DnxQZxn8myV` (key file `~/.ssh/solana.private`).

To read the Base wallet (balances, the tokens the owner really uses, history), use the CDP MCP exactly as
`docs/BASE-WALLET-QUERIES.md` says: paginated token balances, time-bounded SQL, spam filtered by the owner's
own transactions.

Agents may:
- send live blockchain requests (reads, simulations and transactions) when the result gives useful information;
- buy, sell, swap, deposit and withdraw tokens when there is a clear and provable reason.

Conditions:
1. Validate the hypothesis first, as far as possible: model, backtest, quote, and simulate the exact
   transaction (`eth_simulateV1` on Base, `simulateTransaction` on Solana). Real money tests what survived that.
2. Record the reason and the evidence before sending, and report every transaction hash to the owner.
3. Keep each test as small as the test allows.
4. Agents have the key files: run the programs that load them to sign and move money (the owner asked for
   this explicitly on 2026-11-07; `liquidity`'s `load_signer` checks owner, mode 600 and the address). Never
   print, paste or copy key material into chat, logs, commits or other files, and keep both files mode 600.
5. The liquidity daemon still obeys its kill switch and the caps in `~/.aero-lp/config.toml`. Never raise a
   cap or lower `min_net_apr` without the owner asking (`liquidity/CLAUDE.md`).
6. Never visit or call the contracts or sites of unsolicited airdrop tokens. Burning them and closing their
   accounts through the standard token program is allowed.

Component boundaries still hold: `backtester/` stays simulation-only, and code defaults stay dry-run.
The executor's own rails (`executor/CLAUDE.md`) are the live path for swaps: use `executor swap` rather than ad hoc scripts.

## Non-negotiables — extension

1. **Dry-run stays the default.** `DEFAULT_CONFIG.mode` is `dry-run` and the extension installs
   disarmed. Never change a default so a fresh install can place an order.
2. **Risk rails live in code.** Every rail is a gate in `src/core/risk.js` that an order must pass. A
   rail documented but not enforced is not a rail. Rails must **fail closed** — a missing or NaN
   state field must not silently disable one (see `normaliseState`).
3. **Never guess a number that becomes an order.** If a price, quantity or fee is missing or
   unusable, refuse and surface it. Do not fall back to config, and do not fall back to zero.
4. **Reconcile before plan.** The venue's live order list is the source of truth at the top of every
   tick; local state is a cache. An intent that was submitted but is not live becomes `unknown` and
   is **never auto-retried** — that is how a rung double-fires after a crash.
5. **No secret material in logs, `chrome.storage.sync`, the DOM, or a response body.** The API key
   and the session-key vault are `chrome.storage.local` / mode-0600 file only. `setApiKey` returns a
   length, never the key.
6. **Three surfaces, one registry.** Every action belongs in `src/core/commands.js`. Do not add a
   message handler, CLI branch or HTTP route carrying its own logic — `test/surfaces.test.js` will
   fail, and correctly so.
7. **The exit is one rung above the entry.** A sell placed at the level it was bought at captures
   zero and pays two fees. `expectedRoundTripUsd` and its test exist because this bug shipped once.
8. **Market reads stay reads, and swaps stay quotes.** `src/market/net.js` refuses any JSON-RPC
   method that is not a read; `src/market/quote.js` returns a quote and a hand-off URL, never a
   transaction. A quoted APY (DefiLlama) may raise only an "info" lead; only the Aero scout's modelled figures (fresh, backtest-positive,
   medium or high confidence, unflagged) may raise an "act" alert (`src/core/alerts.js`, Stele KNOW-837, KNOW-838).

## Non-negotiables — backtester

1. **Correctness of the simulation outranks the number of strategies.** A tool that honestly reports
   a losing strategy is a success; one that reports an inflated Sharpe from a leaked bar is a
   failure even if it runs.
2. **No lookahead.** A signal at bar *t* may only use data through bar *t*. Any change touching
   signal generation or fill timing needs a test that would catch a one-bar leak.
3. **Costs are never optional.** Fees, slippage and the perp borrow fee stay in the P&L path.
4. **The engine does not touch the network.** Fetching is a separate, explicit step
   (`backtester.core.fetch`) writing a local cache.
5. **Every registered strategy has a card.** `backtester/strategy_cards/<id>.md` carries its
   equations, reasoning, limitations and parameter defaults, and `tests/test_strategy_cards.py`
   checks the machine-readable half against the code in both directions — a registry entry with no
   card fails, and so does a card whose defaults have drifted. Add the card in the same commit as
   the strategy.
6. **The ladder grid must agree with the extension.** `core/gridsim.py` is a port of
   `extension/src/core/grid.js`; a change to either one's economics needs the matching change in the
   other, or the backtest becomes a confident wrong number about the live strategy. Do not confuse it
   with the `grid` strategy in `core/strategies/signals.py`, which is an exposure staircase, not a
   ladder of resting orders.

## Before you claim a change works

Oracle uses its own installed environment: `python -m pip install ./backtester ./oracle ./botmanager ./soltui`, then `python -m unittest discover -s oracle/tests -t . -v` and `ruff check oracle`. Live feed availability and executor enforcement are separate gates; no unit test proves them.

Ecosystem setup and control room use `python -m pip install ./backtester ./oracle ./botmanager ./soltui ./ecosystem`, then `python -m unittest discover -s ecosystem/tests -t . -v` and `ruff check ecosystem oracle scripts/bootstrap_ecosystem.py`. Verify the installed environment and actual loopback UI separately. See `docs/ECOSYSTEM-BOOTSTRAP.md`.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s backtester/tests -t .   # 1002 tests
python3 -m unittest discover -s soltui/tests -t .       # 1435 tests (~840s, optional)
python3 -m unittest discover -s mongo/tests -t .        # 46 tests
cd extension && npm test                                # 408 tests
node tools/dryrun.js --ticks 8 --osc 6 --offline 100    # a round trip must still close positive
cd extension && npm run e2e                             # real Chrome for Testing: load, dry-run, rails (needs one; see below)
node tools/verify-endpoints.js                          # live Jupiter reachability
python3 scripts/check_docs.py                           # doc counts and retrieval indexes
cd liquidity && .venv/bin/pytest -q                     # liquidity (own venv; -m network for live reads)
cd executor && .venv/bin/pytest -q                      # executor (own venv; -m network for live read-only quotes and simulations)
```

`npm run e2e` (`extension/tools/e2e.mjs`) loads the unpacked extension into Chrome for Testing over the
DevTools pipe and checks loading and dry-run behaviour in a real browser (needs Chrome for Testing:
`npx @puppeteer/browsers install chrome@stable`, or set `CHROME`; exit 2 means no usable browser).
It never arms, signs or changes mode, limits or keys (`extension/e2e/lib/guard.mjs` enforces that),
and it blocks all network but a stubbed price read. It does not verify live orders. Do not describe
it as live verification; the headless dry run stays the economics gate.

## House style

**JavaScript** — ESM, no build step, **no npm runtime dependencies**. The one sanctioned runtime
library is TradingView Lightweight Charts 5.2.1, vendored and pinned in `extension/vendor/lightweight-charts/`
(owner's choice 2026-11-07; read its README before touching it). Do not add a package to solve
something the ~150 lines of `src/wallet/solana.js` already solve. Tests are `node:test` +
`node:assert/strict`. Keep `src/core/grid.js`, `risk.js` and `pnl.js` free of I/O and `chrome.*`.

**Python** — 3.13, stdlib-first. Backtester dependencies live in
`backtester/requirements.txt`; its tests use `unittest` and deliberately exclude
`pyarrow`, `requests`, and `pytest`. `mongo/` and `soltui/` declare their own requirements.
`liquidity/` and `executor/` use their own `pyproject.toml`, locked virtualenv, `pytest`, and Ruff; follow
`liquidity/CLAUDE.md` and `executor/CLAUDE.md` there. Use `from __future__ import annotations` and type hints.

**Both** — comments explain *why*, especially where the obvious implementation is wrong (MV3 timers,
base58 zero bytes, FIFO vs paired-lot attribution, one-bar leaks). Do not narrate *what*.

## Known-unverified areas

Read "Verification status" in `extension/README.md` before extending it. In short: **no live order
has ever been placed**. The unpacked extension is now loaded and exercised in a real browser (`npm run e2e`,
dry-run only), so the MV3 load path, service worker, popup, dashboard and message routing are
covered; live trading is not. Trigger history/cancellation have public-contract fixtures, but authenticated
wallet responses, execution USD valuation and fee attribution remain unverified. The bundled signer
has no semantic transaction verifier, so Trigger live signing stays blocked. `executor/src/executor/txverify.py` is a semantic verifier for Jupiter Swap v1 transactions (not for Trigger). Do not present live
execution as working.

SolTUI's manual Jupiter V2 path provides unsigned, structurally checked previews only. Submit and
quick-submit refuse before key loading, signing or sending until independent V2 economic verification
exists. Keep uncertain historical submissions blocking until chain evidence resolves them. A timeout
alone never proves absence. Manual Coinbase orders remain a separately armed path.

# Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index (Proxy)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

This Financial Conditions Index is explicitly a simplified proxy rather than a reproduction of Bloomberg’s proprietary series. It combines market-price proxies into a standardized reading intended to distinguish tighter from easier financial conditions. Negative territory is interpreted as deterioration and positive territory as accommodation, with a color gradient reinforcing that convention. The author cites broader financial-conditions literature, but those references do not validate this particular construction. Its financial purpose is macro/regime context; no exact asset-allocation or entry rule is supplied.

## How it works

- Use SPY for equities, TLT for bond conditions, LQD/HYG for credit, VIX for volatility and SHY relative to equities for liquidity.
- Transform component log returns into z-scores, apply approximate weights and aggregate a composite.

## Outputs and intended use

- Zero-centered colored index uses blue for neutral, green for accommodation and red for tightening.
- Read broad direction and unusual conditions rather than exact Bloomberg-equivalent values.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Source says six components but lists five conceptual categories; the category/symbol count is ambiguous.
- No numeric weights, normalization lookback or default settings are given.

## Failure modes and caveats

- TLT is a bond-price ETF, not a direct yield series, and LQD/HYG is not a pure credit-spread measure.
- The missing signs/weights make directional interpretation impossible to verify.
- Literature claims about other indexes do not establish predictive validity of this proxy.

# Cross-Sectional Momentum

> **Spec-only — never implemented, never run.** No performance figures appear on this
> card, deliberately. `research/STRATEGIES.md` mechanism #17.

## Equation
```
R_i = c_{i,t}/c_{i,t-n} - 1     for each asset i
long the top-k by rank, rebalance each period
```

## Why it might work
The most-documented anomaly family there is (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993: 3–12 month
formation, 1-month hold). Critically, **the cross-sectional form is the one the
literature supports**; `ts_momentum.md` is the weaker single-asset cousin.

## What implementing it would take
A multi-asset engine. This harness is single-asset by design — `run_backtest` takes one
`arrays` dict — so this is not a strategy addition, it is an engine change.

## Caveats
Survivorship bias inflates long-only equity backtest returns by an estimated
**1.5–2.0% annually**, and a crypto universe is far worse: the dead tokens are most of
the sample. A universe assembled today from surviving tokens would produce a
spectacular, entirely fictional result.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: a-priori — never run here, so this is a judgement about the mechanism and
the literature, not a measurement. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme: across
311 rankable configurations measured in this repo, 14% had a positive out-of-sample
Sharpe and 9% made money.*

The **cross-sectional** form is the one the momentum literature actually supports,
which is a real point in its favour — but it needs a multi-asset engine this harness
does not have, and a survivorship-free crypto universe, where the dead tokens are
most of the sample. A universe assembled today from survivors would produce a
spectacular fiction. Rated low rather than moderate because the implementation risk
*is* the main risk: the most likely outcome of building this carelessly is a wrong
number, not a losing one.

## Data gap
**No peer universe fetched. Would also require survivorship-free constituent history.**

> The Aroon Oscillator, created by Tushar Chande in 1995, is a trend indicator that measures the recency of the highest highs versus the lowest lows in market prices over a lookback period. It calculates the difference between the Aroon Up and Aroon Down values from the Aroon indicator to produce a single, bounded metric that oscillates between -100 and +100.

> The Aroon Oscillator's calculation relies on the values of Aroon Up and Aroon Down, which respectively measure the recency of the highest high and lowest low prices for a given lookback period. Both values range between 0 and 100, where:

> The indicator transforms these two readings into a single oscillator by calculating their difference:

> Aroon Up is 100 on bars where the market price reaches the highest high for the current period. The value decreases for each successive bar whose high price is less than the highest value.

> Aroon Down is 100 on bars where the market price reaches the lowest low for the current period. The value decreases for each successive bar whose low price is greater than the lowest value.

## Documented inputs and source details

> The bullish Abandoned baby is a three-candle reversal pattern that appears after a downtrend. A strong bearish candle is followed by a Doji that gaps below it, and then by a bullish candle that gaps above the Doji. The isolated Doji in the middle, "abandoned" by gaps on both sides, shows that selling momentum has stalled and buyers have taken over.

> Trend filter: In the indicator settings, choose how the prior trend is detected (based on SMA 50, or SMA 50 and SMA 200), or turn trend detection off.

> Like any candlestick pattern, the bullish Abandoned baby describes what has happened, not what will happen. The downtrend can resume after the pattern completes, especially in a weak market. Because the pattern is rare, there is also a risk of reading too much into a near-match, such as a Doji with a small overlap that does not meet the definition. Traders often combine it with stop-loss levels, for example below the low of the Doji, to limit losses if the reversal fails.

> The Abandoned baby is considered one of the stronger reversal signals among candlestick patterns, but it is also rare. Full gaps on both sides of the Doji are uncommon in markets that trade around the clock, such as crypto and forex, where one session's close is usually the next session's open. The pattern appears more often in stocks and futures, where overnight gaps are common.

## Idea and objective

Expected Value Monte Carlo contrasts historical holding-period returns with a forward GBM projection fitted to recent behavior. It expresses both in return and dollar terms, with win-rate and Sharpe summaries, so the user can inspect assumptions about horizon and recent trend. # DEX-vs-CEX Price Dislocation

> **Spec-only — never implemented, never run.** No performance figures appear on this
> card, deliberately. `research/STRATEGIES.md` mechanism #36.

## Equation
```
basis_t = (P_dex - P_cex) / P_cex
act when |basis_t| exceeds threshold plus round-trip cost
```

## Why it might work — and why that claim has been withdrawn

This card used to say it was "one of the few edges here that is a genuine arbitrage rather
than a forecast." **That is false in the DEX-CEX form and has been struck.**

The dividing line between an arbitrage and a spread trade is whether some contractual event
forces the spread to zero. A dated future has an expiry. A DEX-CEX pair has nothing: the two
legs do not settle atomically, the on-chain leg can be dropped, reverted or sandwiched, and
a one-sided fill leaves naked directional risk. It is a spread trade wearing the name.

The same test disposes of perpetual funding carry, which is the variant people reach for
next: perps never expire, so there is no convergence date, and funding flips sign and stays
flipped. Only intra-venue triangular (see `triangular_arbitrage.md`) and dated
cash-and-carry survive it — and even those are riskless only while inventory is already
sitting on both venues.

## What implementing it would take
Synchronised quote history from both venue types, and — critically — **MEV-aware
execution modelling**. `docs/trading-signals-concept-family.md` covers the relevant
machinery: private RPC, Jito bundles, and the sandwich exposure a naive public-mempool
arb walks into.

## Caveats
This is a latency business. A bar-resolution backtest of an arbitrage that lives in
milliseconds would be a fiction, and this harness is bar-resolution by design.

Two hazards specific to any future attempt:

- **Timestamp alignment is a lookahead vector.** Different close conventions, timezones or
  oracle publish-lag silently embed future information. It is worse on an oracle-priced
  venue, where the signal series and the fill series are *the same series* — a naive
  backtest then trades on the print it also fills at, a zero-cost round trip that will look
  spectacular and be fiction. `BarWindow` guards index leakage, not cross-series
  misalignment.
- **`core/perps.py` takes utilization as a constant (default 0.5)**, while
  `funding_utilization_extremes.md` documents sustained 100%. Any Jupiter-leg cost inherits
  that and is understated by construction.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: a-priori — the mechanism was never run here. The basis series above was measured,
but measuring the input is not measuring the strategy, so this stays `a-priori` rather than
claiming `measured-oos`.*

**Lowered from `low`.** The old rating rested entirely on the claim that this is a genuine
arbitrage rather than a forecast, and that claim is struck above: the legs do not settle
atomically, so it is a spread trade. Once it is a spread trade it is competing with the
literature in the section above, which is four-for-four negative on the bar-testable
version, and with three searchers who capture 75% of the executable version.

The measurement supplies the rest. On the oracle basis the threshold this card itself
proposes was never reached in 4,310 hours. On pool prints it is reached 3.11% of the time in
single-hour bursts that look like print artifacts.

## Data gap — restated, because the old wording was wrong

This card previously said "no DEX quote history". **Price history is in fact retrievable**:
Pyth Benchmarks serves complete 1h OHLC for `Crypto.SOL/USD` back to 2022-02-03, and
GeckoTerminal serves Solana pool 1h OHLCV. (Pyth requires an API key from 2026-08-18.)

What is actually missing is narrower and harder: **synchronous quote mid with depth**, and
an MEV-aware execution model. Bars give a last print, and this mechanism is defined on the
executable side of a book at an instant.

## Measured: the basis you can retrieve is either zero or noise

Two series were pulled and compared against the repo's Coinbase SOL leg. The contrast
between them is the finding, and it is why `data_available` stays `false`.

| | Pyth oracle vs CEX | Orca pool print vs CEX |
|---|---|---|
| Aligned hours | 4,310 (2026-02-06 → 08-05) | 1,320 (2026-06-11 → 08-05) |
| Median abs basis | **0.7 bps** | **12.8 bps** |
| p99 abs basis | 4.6 bps | 37.2 bps |
| Hours above 8 bps (one leg of this repo's cost model) | 0.88% | 68.86% |
| Hours above 30 bps (**this card's own default threshold**) | **0.00%** | 3.11% |

**On the oracle basis the card's own 30 bps threshold was never reached, in 4,310 hours.**

The pool-print column looks tradeable, and probably is not. Two pieces of evidence point at
microstructure artifact rather than economics: the 39 episodes above 30 bps have a **mean
length of 1.05 hours** and a maximum of 2 — single-bar spikes, not dislocations arbitrageurs
failed to close — and the signed distribution is near-symmetric about zero. Candidate
mechanisms are asynchronous last-print timing inside the bar, swap prints embedding taker
impact so buys print above and sells below mid, and SOL/USDC-versus-SOL/USD depeg.

**This is a hypothesis, not a settled result.** The test that would settle it: compare
against a pool mid reconstructed from reserves at the bar boundary, or against a second
independent SOL/USDC pool. If two independent pools disagree with each other by ~13 bps, it
is microstructure.

The reason this matters more than a null result would: the retrievable series shows a gap
large enough to look tradeable and short-lived enough to be an artifact. A naive
implementation would find "signal", and the backtest would look excellent.

## Funding carry is not available on this venue at all

Worth stating because it is the obvious next idea. **Jupiter has no funding rate.** The
borrow rate is `(hourlyFundingDbps/1000) x utilization`, charged on notional to **both**
sides and structurally floored at zero — nobody is ever paid to hold. Long spot plus short
perp therefore pays borrow on the hedge as pure cost. Carry on this venue is harvestable
only by *becoming* JLP, which is a long crypto basket with a written short-vol overlay, not
a delta-neutral trade.

For scale on what the trade earns where it does exist: Ethena's sUSDe, the largest public
delta-neutral funding-carry vehicle, averaged 18% in 2024 and **3.50% in Mar/Apr 2026**
(Ethena governance disclosures). Aggregate perp funding averaged ~11% annualised in 2024 and
~5% in 2025 (Coin Metrics *State of the Network* #335, 2025-10-28).

## Basis as a *signal* rather than a trade: four negatives

The bar-testable version of this idea is "does a dislocation predict short-horizon returns".
The literature is against it:

1. The one paper claiming carry positively predicts returns — Franz & Schmeling, *Crypto
   Carry*, SSRN 3774118 — **has been withdrawn** (the SSRN page returns HTTP 410). It cannot
   be cited as support and its magnitudes are unrecoverable.
2. The peer-reviewed treatment predicts **liquidations, not returns**: Schmeling, Schrimpf &
   Todorov, *Crypto Carry*, Management Science (online 2026-05-06) — a 10% rise in
   standardised carry predicts a rise in short-futures liquidations of 22% of open interest
   over the next month. High carry forecasts unwind risk, arguably the opposite trading
   implication.
3. A direct test of funding to next-period price finds nothing: contemporaneous 7d funding
   vs 7d price R^2 = 12.5%, but predictive T→T+1 correlation near zero (Presto Research,
   2024-08-02; industry, not peer-reviewed).
4. Basis is **absent from the priced factors** in the broadest cross-section: Babiak &
   Bianchi, JFQA (online 2025-10-27), 600+ coins — liquidity, size, reversal, market and
   downside risk are priced; basis is not.

Cost sensitivity is the number that decides it: He, Manela, Ross & von Wachter,
arXiv:2212.06888, report a BTC perp ladder falling from Sharpe ~3.9 gross to ~1.9 at retail
costs, with annualised alpha 22.6% → 5.5% and **the t-statistic dropping to 1.38 — not
significant**.

A counterweight in fairness: Cao, Zhai & Luo, *Journal of Futures Markets* (in press), find
a two-factor model including log-basis explains a large set of perp predictors. That is
support for basis carrying systematic information as a priced factor — not for a
cost-surviving short-horizon directional forecast.

## What the arbitrage is worth to those who can execute it

Documented and large, and captured by very few. Wu, Sui, Thiery & Pai (AFT 2025,
peer-reviewed) measure **$233.8M** extracted across 7,203,560 CEX-DEX arbitrages by 19
searchers, Aug 2023 – Mar 2025, with **three searchers capturing roughly 75%**. Two of them
transfer ~90% of arbitrage revenue to their integrated builders. Heimbach, Pahari &
Schertenleib (IEEE S&P 2024) put non-atomic arbitrage at over 25% of volume on Ethereum's
five largest DEXes, **$132B**, with eleven searchers responsible for over 80%.

The historical spatial opportunity has decayed sharply. Makarov & Schoar (JFE 135(2), 2020)
recorded US-Korea daily average price ratios above 15% and reaching 40% in Dec 2017 – Feb
2018. Crépellière, Pelster & Zeisberger (Journal of Financial Markets 64, 2023) — the direct
follow-up — find the average maximum price difference falling from 2.8% (2017-18) to 1.1%
post-2019, and state plainly that "starting in 2019, the strategy does not provide
consistent profits any longer... net returns are negative due to trading costs." Makarov &
Schoar attribute the original persistence to **capital controls** rather than transaction
costs — their sharpest evidence being that when USD/BTC differed by more than 20% between
the US and Korea, ETH/BTC on the same exchanges differed by only about 3%.

# Intrabar Efficiency Ratio

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Gauge the directional efficiency of each chart bar relative to movement observed in its lower-timeframe components. Unlike unsigned Kaufman efficiency, this variant retains direction and smooths the result into a momentum-style display.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Partly disclosed computation.** Chart/intrabar change boundary conventions, zero-denominator handling, precise weighting formula and default lengths are not given.

- Chart/intrabar change boundary conventions, zero-denominator handling, precise weighting formula and default lengths are not given.

## How it works

- Divide signed chart-bar change by the sum of absolute intrabar changes, then apply moving-average smoothing. Optional percent-rank weighting reduces contributions from relatively small chart-price changes.
- The line view shows the middle-length average. Synthetic candles use long/short averages as open/close and extrema across those plus raw efficiency as high/low. Circles show three averages colored by their rolling ranks.
- Lower-timeframe selection trades intrabar precision against historical coverage, using stepped, fixed-minute or approximate target-count modes. An information box reports actual coverage.

## Outputs and intended use

- Line, candles or circle displays expose directional efficiency; the author also suggests absolute efficiency as an adaptive-average input, without supplying that downstream system.
- Coverage statistics help distinguish a recent high-resolution sample from a longer coarser history.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Seven average families; ALMA offset 0.85 and sigma 6. Circle ranks use 100 bars with thresholds 10%, 50% and 90%.
- Target intrabar options 12,24,50,100,250; relative-change weighting period and MA lengths are configurable.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Intrabar bars still omit within-bar tick paths. The historical platform intrabar limit in the prose should not be assumed current.
- Different session coverage and selected precision can change apparent efficiency; absent/flat intrabars require defined handling.

> Traditionally, this candlestick pattern is recognized in conjunction with a specific trend direction, i.e. it might be important for the pattern if the price has been generally going up or down. The ‘Detect Trend Based On’ option allows you to specify which of the following methods to use to detect the trend:

> SMA50 - the indicator compares the current price of the symbol to its Simple Moving Average (SMA) with the length of 50. If the current price is below the SMA, this price movement is considered a downtrend. If the price is above the SMA, it is an uptrend.

Divergence Screener compares oscillator and price pivot directions and can expose its outputs to a watchlist screener. - Calculate a built-in oscillator or accept an external plot, then detect oscillator zigzag pivots and compare corresponding price direction.

- Filter by zigzag structure, moving-average change between pivots or an external signed trend; reject lines violated by intermediate bars.

> This indicator displays a ​Volume-Weighted Average Price anchored to the leftmost visible bar of the chart. It dynamically recalculates when the chart's visible bars change because you scroll or zoom your chart.

> Load the indicator on an active chart (see the Help Center if you don't know how). By default, it displays the chart's ​VWAP in orange and a simple average of the chart's visible close values in gray. This average can be used as a companion to the ​VWAP, since both are calculated from the same set of bars. The script's settings allow you to hide it.

> You may also use the script's settings to enable the display of the chart's OHLC (open, high, low, close) levels and the values of the high and low. These are also calculated from the range of visible bars. You can complement the high and low lines with their price and their distance in percent from the chart's latest visible close. You can use the levels to quickly identify the distances from extreme points in the visible price range, as well as observe the visible chart's beginning and end prices.

> If you are not already familiar with ​VWAP, our Help Center will get you started. The typical ​VWAP is designed to be used on intraday charts, as it resets at the beginning of the day. Our Rolling ​VWAP, instead, resets on a rolling time window. You may also find the VWAP Auto Anchored built-in indicator worth a try.

# RedK Compound Ratio Moving Average (CoRa_Wave)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

CoRa Wave gives more recent observations geometrically increasing weights to create a responsive moving average. Its aim is to reduce the influence of the oldest observations while retaining a finite-window average that can be used for trend and swing tracking. An accelerator changes how aggressively weights favor recent prices, and optional smoothing moderates the response. The author proposes crossover use, including equal-length lines on open and close, but provides no full trading system. Low-lag language describes intent and examples rather than a measured guarantee.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for a parameterized geometric-weight moving average using disclosed compound-ratio equations with caller-chosen endpoints/window. Actual endpoint defaults, accelerator and automatic/manual smoothing remain outside the usable scope.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Independent unaccelerated, unsmoothed geometric-weight MA: choose positive start weight P, endpoint A and t weight steps. Compute r=(A/P)^(1/t)−1; index the oldest sample as j=0 and set w_j=P×(1+r)^j. Return sum(w_j×source_j)/sum(w_j) over the selected window. This is a normalized weighted average using the disclosed weight sequence, not a reconstruction of undocumented accelerator/smoothing defaults.
- Apply an accelerator to emphasize recent observations and optional automatic/manual smoothing.

## Outputs and intended use

- A price-tracking MA supports trend observation or caller-defined crossovers.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Default resolution is chart timeframe and source hlc3.
- Multiplier zero produces SMA; source says effects are strongest around 1–5 then diminish.
- Example comparison length is 20; actual length/smoothing defaults are absent.
- Narrow geometric-weight scope requires chosen window, positive endpoint weights P and A, with t the number of weight steps; the source gives no endpoint defaults. Disable added acceleration and smoothing for this scope.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Greater recent-price weighting increases sensitivity to noise.
- The prose’s contrast with EMA should not be read as proof of uniquely geometric weighting or universal lag reduction.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Start/end weight choices, exact accelerator/smoothing formulas, confirmation timing and entry/exit rules are absent.

## Data requirements

Required inputs: ohlcv.

Repository input-class support: available. Weighted chart prices and smoothing are OHLCV-derived.

# Sol bot control room

Version: 1.0.1
Delta: v1.0.0 to v1.0.1; resolve instance identity and existing singleton worker limits after builder review.
Date: 2026-11-09
Status: proposed product design; prototype only. No production UI or trading behavior changed.

## Purpose and design call

Give the owner one place to create a bot, establish what it can actually do, and understand its current behavior. The main question is **“What is this bot doing with my capital, and why?”** Creation and monitoring must share the same configuration and evidence identity.

The requested outcome is an ideal management and creation UI. The responsive browser surface is the designer's choice, not a platform decision approved by the owner. It complements the existing terminal console and the separate CLI planning task, TASK-1092. It can become a bot workspace inside the existing extension dashboard. It is not a second trading engine.

The primary user is the technically experienced owner. They want rapid setup, automatic tuning with manual control, and immediate operational visibility. These needs are supported by existing request history, including persistent Council voting, bot P&L, wallet actions, per-coin settings and fewer workflow buttons. No interviews or participant research were performed for this proposal.

Success means the owner can find a bot's mode, health, exposure, net outcome and last decision without opening multiple screens. They can prepare a bot without confusing a saved draft with a running job. Losses, weak evidence and blocked capabilities remain easy to recognize.

## Scope and current capability boundary

All paths in this document refer to the canonical checkout. The proposal was authored in the isolated worktree /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader-wt-01a1c198 from commit `4d4c7a1`.

| Verified source | What exists | Design consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/bots.py:72 | DCA, Grid, Arbitrage, Trend and Council choices; workbench bots are simulations | Offer all five templates. Do not advertise unattended live support for them. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/bots.py:281 | Per-coin configuration retrieval | Show the active coin and effective configuration together. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/bots.py:323 | Atomic configuration save with mode checks | Keep manual mode and per-coin version ownership explicit. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/paper_workflow.py:86 | Paper coordinator reuses shared owners | A “Prepare paper fleet” action should reuse existing jobs and display real stage receipts. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/paper_workflow.py:122 | Stopping the coordinator leaves independent shared workers running | A stop receipt must say which owners stopped and which continue. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/extension/src/core/commands.js:560 | Shared native command bridge | Reuse this boundary for an integrated UI; preserve three-surface parity. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/extension/src/core/risk.js:212 | Authoritative fail-closed order gates | UI validation helps the owner; engine enforcement remains decisive. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/executor/CLAUDE.md:80 | Live strategy runner is not built | A design must show missing bot execution capability instead of a pretend Start live button. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/CLAUDE.md | Trigger signing and Jupiter V2 submission remain blocked; manual Coinbase is separately armed | Capability is specific to venue, product, action and verification state. No universal “live connected” badge. |
| /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/docs/design/chrome-workspace/proposal.md | Existing Signal Desk design and evidence boundary | Extend its bot-monitor workflow; keep its backtest/forward/live separation. |

The interactive prototype uses synthetic examples and imports none of these modules. Its apparent controls alter only page memory. No account, secret, job, market feed or execution path is connected. The discontinued Aero LP component stays archived.

### Bot identity and concurrent instances

Every saved draft has a stable UUID. Duplicate creates a new draft UUID and never takes over an active session. A runtime session is a separate identity, owned by the backend.

The first integrated release supports **one active paper session per existing backend strategy slot**, including across markets when the current owner is strategy-scoped. In /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/bots.py:1055, forward sessions are stored under the bot kind; per-coin saved settings do not establish concurrent per-coin workers. Council has its own owner. If an active slot exists, offer Open existing session or Save another draft; refuse a duplicate start. Do not overwrite it, silently reuse a different configuration, or reserve a second budget.

The ideal model can represent multiple named instances of the same strategy/market. Enabling them requires an explicit future backend `per_instance` capability with isolated worker locks, journals, configuration identity and aggregate risk accounting. That backend migration is outside the first integration plan. Until then, the studio and fleet disclose the slot limit. This is a designer's scope decision, not a claim that concurrent instances already work.

## Three directions considered

| Direction | Strength | Cost | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Trading desk: fleet roster plus selected-bot inspector | Fast comparison, persistent context, inspect a decision in place | Must reflow the inspector on narrow screens | Recommended and mocked up |
| Strategy canvas: drag connected entry, exit and risk nodes | Good for complex custom strategy composition | Harder keyboard interaction; easy to hide execution semantics in wires | Later advanced view, backed by the same rule model |
| Guided launchpad: full-screen setup and one bot at a time | Clear first-run learning | Poor fleet comparison and incident awareness | Use its guided flow in Bot studio |

The memorable feature is a persistent **What it’s doing** explanation beside a readable rule and the evidence that supports it. Decorative market tickers and celebration effects would compete with that job.

## Information architecture

1. **Bot fleet:** the working home. Capital, net P&L, health, roster, selected bot, incidents and event ledger.
2. **Bot studio:** create from a template, duplicate a configuration or later import a validated strategy specification. Always opens as a draft.
3. **Research & evidence:** historical runs, prospective observations, compatible comparisons and immutable evidence detail.
4. **Activity:** bot, owner, external-wallet and risk actions with actor and source attribution.
5. **Accounts & capabilities:** account aliases, public identifiers, permissions, network and supported action matrix. Secrets never enter the UI.

Settings are secondary. The command palette finds destinations and scoped actions, but critical actions also have visible controls. Product navigation stays under six primary destinations. Drafts and selected rows must survive ordinary navigation in production.

## Fleet composition

The top context bar identifies the workspace and mode. A real implementation also shows connection age, account alias and capability. Paper and live scopes have different labels, not just different colors. Changing mode never migrates funds or configuration implicitly.

The summary strip shows paper starting capital, net P&L, capital allocated and current fleet state. Every metric has its currency, period and scope. Do not combine paper P&L with wallet balances or live results. An unavailable metric reads “Unavailable” or an em dash with an explanation, never zero.

The equity chart labels starting capital and the portfolio line. The final plotted value agrees with the displayed figure. Production charts include a table alternative, sample provenance, gaps and tooltip values; do not interpolate across outages as if trades occurred. A benchmark is only comparable when dates, capital and costs match.

The roster compares name/market, state, net P&L and last decision. A production sortable header is a button with an announced sort direction. Refreshes preserve sorting, filters, selection and keyboard focus. At narrow widths the last decision moves to the inspector; it is not discarded from the user journey.

The inspector contains:

- Bot identity, mode, effective configuration version, account and venue.
- Process state, heartbeat age, last evaluated market time and last actual decision. Process liveness and market freshness are separate.
- Plain-language current action, reason, next trigger and active blocker.
- Allocated capital, current exposure, remaining budget, net realized and net unrealized results, and included cost attribution.
- Open positions/orders, resolved fills and unresolved submissions. A production expandable detail view provides these; the prototype samples the high-level inspector.
- Historical, prospective and live evidence with their own states and identifiers.
- Scoped actions that reflect capability and ownership.

Activity stays useful when the bot does nothing: “Kept current ladder: price remained inside the range” is better than a flashing Running label. Each event has event time, received time when relevant, actor, account alias, bot/config ID, reason and correlated intent/fill ID. Unattributed wallet actions remain “external / unattributed”; never assign them to a bot by guess.

## Bot studio: five stages

### 1. Strategy

Offer DCA, Grid, Arbitrage, Trend and Council. Each template explains its behavior and one material failure mode. Template selection is a native radio group, usable without dragging or hovering. An untested template has no profit badge.

Grid offers arithmetic and geometric spacing. Neither is labelled more profitable without a matched comparison. Trend starts with the existing long-only semantics. Council explains eligible voters and stale-signal exclusion. Arbitrage distinguishes recorded quotes from candle-close research proxies and requires all-leg fee/latency evidence for any future execution.

### 2. Market & budget

Choose market, data/cost venue, account alias where supported, simulated capital and observation interval. The design uses USD-denominated example markets because the current workbench reads Coinbase market data. A future SOL/USDC Jupiter path is a distinct instrument and cost model; renaming SOL/USD is insufficient.

The sidebar preview repeats scope and budget. Multiple markets create separate configuration/evidence identities, not one tuned configuration copied across all coins. The prototype permits a single market at a time. Arbitrage uses the fixed example USD/SOL/ETH triangle and labels that scope.

### 3. Rules & tuning

Use simple typed forms, then an always-visible readable rule: **when / action / exit / conditions that prevent action**. The compact prototype demonstrates template parameters; production must expose every actual parameter through a schema-driven form, including advanced fields, units, defaults, bounds and dependencies.

Automatic proposals are the default. Manual mode freezes the user's values. An automatic proposal shows current versus proposed configuration, the exact coin, matching evidence, expected behavior change and adoption status. “Tentative” is a separate evidence state and never means statistically confirmed. A losing valid run remains visible; a failed run is a different outcome.

Edits make a new immutable draft version. Editing a running bot cannot silently change active behavior. Production shows a diff and stages the change at an acknowledged decision boundary. Existing intents retain their original version.

### 4. Risk boundaries

Show maximum allocation/exposure, daily loss, slippage, input age, trade size/frequency and allowed assets/venues as applicable. The prototype samples exposure, loss, slippage and age. Numeric fields show exact units and an equivalent percentage where useful: `30 bps = 0.30%`. Refuse NaN, infinity, empty strings, impossible dependencies and unavailable execution prices/costs.

Inherited account/engine ceilings appear beside per-bot limits. The effective limit is the stricter value. The UI cannot weaken engine rails. Server-side validation repeats every money-related check. Missing risk state blocks action.

### 5. Review & test

Summarize strategy/version, market, account/mode, readable rules, capital, all effective limits, cost assumptions, optimization policy and evidence status. Keep Edit links in production. “Save paper draft” does exactly that: no worker, observation, reservation or order starts. The prototype adds a memory-only draft to show the resulting state.

In production, offer a separate **Prepare paper bot** action after valid configuration. It shows one transparent plan: validate data → historical assessment → prospective paper observation → evaluate tuning proposals. Reuse eligible existing jobs. Display queued/running/completed/partial/failed/canceled stages, owner, progress, cancel scope and retryable reason. A losing backtest may still justify an explicitly requested paper investigation; it does not become “passed” evidence.

Live activation is a separate capability review. Show supported venue/product/action, reconciled exposure, exact configuration/evidence identity, limits and authorization policy. Preserve the owner's existing explicit fast/no-confirmation preference where supported; do not insert a fresh confirmation per automatic tick. Unknown submissions, unavailable economics, unsupported capability and failed risk gates remain hard blockers regardless of confirmation preference.

## States and action semantics

Treat mode, lifecycle, data quality, evidence and execution certainty as independent dimensions. A single status string cannot represent them honestly.

| Dimension | States | Presentation / consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mode | paper, live | Persistent text; never mixed in result totals |
| Lifecycle | draft, queued, starting, running, paused, stopping, stopped, failed, interrupted | Receipt-backed state; process loss becomes interrupted |
| Inputs | fresh, stale, missing, gap, disconnected | Data age and reason; new intents held when policy fails |
| Evidence | untested, pending, valid loss, valid gain, failed measurement, tentative, confirmed under policy | Method, sample, scope and limitations remain inspectable |
| Submission | prepared, submitted, confirmed, rejected, unknown | Unknown requires venue/chain reconciliation; never auto-retry |

**Pause entries:** stop creating new entry intents for the specified bot. It does not promise to cancel existing orders, flatten exposure, stop a recorder or release shared workers. Resume requires current eligibility and an acknowledged backend receipt. The prototype deliberately cannot resume held Council signals.

**Stop bot:** request that bot's worker stop and show the terminal receipt; retain positions and journals. **Cancel orders:** a separate scoped venue operation with partial/unknown outcomes. **Close position:** a separate verified execution action with quote/economics and account scope. **Emergency stop:** use the actual engine kill/disarm semantics and show what remains exposed. Do not relabel an entry-pause button as a global kill switch.

Production bulk actions show eligible/skipped/failed counts for each bot and preserve item receipts. One unknown item must not produce “All stopped.” Browser closure cannot imply cancellation, disarm or successful job stop.

Empty fleet: explain the first useful action and offer Create bot. Loading: reserve layout and show which source is pending. Offline: retain last-known state with its timestamp and hold new actions. Permission denied: show the missing capability and supported remedy. Long-running work: progress and cancellation remain available. Error recovery preserves drafts and already-completed evidence. No repeated starts from a stale button or reconnect.

## Visual system

Use a quiet light work surface with a deep blue navigation rail. Blue means primary action/selection, green means a positive result or running state with text, amber means a held condition, and red means a negative result/error. Never make red mean both a sell instruction and an error without explicit labels.

| Token | Value / rule |
| --- | --- |
| Canvas / surface | `#f2f5f9` / `#ffffff` |
| Primary text / secondary text | `#172942` / `#53657b` |
| Primary action / navigation | `#2757c4` / `#142d50` |
| Positive / attention / negative | `#14654f` / `#805108` / `#ac354b` |
| Typography | Avenir Next/Avenir on macOS; Segoe UI fallback; no network font dependency |
| Scale | 32px page heading, 24–25px financial emphasis, 17px section title, 14px base; compact metadata is secondary |
| Spacing | 4/8px base; 16/24/32px group spacing |
| Corners | 6px controls; 10px panels; circle reserved for actor/state markers |
| Numbers | Tabular figures; explicit currency, sign, precision and period |
| Controls | 44px target design goal; visible 3px focus outline; native controls first |

Do not imply that small prototype metadata is a validated production readability choice. Validate legibility with the owner at actual display scale; production should support a comfortable density mode and text enlargement. Do not introduce decorative charts, fabricated confidence percentages or profit celebrations. Motion answers user actions and respects reduced motion.

At ≥1200px use the roster and inspector side by side. Between 720 and 1000px the inspector moves below the roster while retaining its content. At ≤720px navigation becomes a horizontal local destination strip, metrics use two columns, creation steps compress and forms stack. Table scrolling is local if needed; the page itself must reflow at 320px. The application cannot disable browser zoom. Mobile keeps mode, blockers and meaningful controls visible.

## Architecture proposal

Use the existing no-build ESM/HTML/CSS conventions. Keep presentation, view-state derivation and side-effect dispatch separate inside the current extension. Do not add a framework, a second backend, a signer or copied strategy logic to ship a new look. These are proposed components; the prototype files are not production modules.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Owner[Owner] --> UI[Bot workspace: fleet, studio, evidence]
  UI --> VM[Pure view models and draft validation]
  UI --> CMD[Existing commands registry and native bridge]
  CMD --> PAPER[Existing Python paper owners and evidence stores]
  CMD --> LIVE[Explicit supported venue adapters]
  LIVE --> RISK[Authoritative risk, verification and reconciliation]
  PAPER --> READ[Versioned status and result snapshots]
  RISK --> READ
  READ --> VM
  VM --> UI
```

This is a proposed responsibility diagram, not an implemented network contract. Existing authentication, command envelopes and local native boundaries govern integration. Designing new remote endpoints is outside this design task.

**UI view model:** identify bot, version, strategy kind, market, mode, capability, lifecycle, owner/heartbeat, input freshness, decision/reason, allocation/exposure, nullable result components, evidence references and unresolved intent count. Derive labels from explicit fields. Never infer “running” from a positive P&L or “flat” from missing positions.

**Draft model:** versioned configuration with typed parameter values/units, per-market tuning mode, effective risk limits, cost model and schema version. Save/restore drafts independently from running configuration. Persist only safe configuration; keys and bearer tokens never appear in a form, export, DOM or sync storage.

**Command boundary:** user gestures request existing registered commands; the backend validates ownership, current version and capability. Use idempotency at the existing owner/dispatch boundary. A delayed response cannot overwrite a newer market, selection, configuration or command receipt. Reconcile before new plans. Do not translate UI pause into an unrelated coordinator stop.

**Result identity:** strategy/config version, market, dataset/proof hash, dates, interval, engine version, cost model and result mode. Missing values remain unavailable. Compare only compatible evidence; show both when compatibility fails. Current summaries lack some desired path/equity/fee detail, so richer visualizations wait for typed measured fields.

### Proposed decisions and tradeoffs

- **ADR-UI-1, proposed:** integrate the bot workspace into the existing extension rather than creating a parallel execution application. Benefit: shared routing, defaults and safety boundary. Cost: extension lifecycle and native-host constraints remain.
- **ADR-UI-2, proposed:** table/inspector for fleet, guided form for creation, readable rule representation underneath both. Benefit: rapid monitoring and accessible setup. Cost: complex custom strategy graphs are deferred.
- **ADR-UI-3, proposed:** treat capability, input age and uncertain execution as first-class state. Benefit: honest operations under partial failure. Cost: more explicit view fields and refusal states.
- **ADR-UI-4, proposed:** reuse source schema and current per-market policy; draft edits create versions. Benefit: UI and engine do not drift. Cost: migration/version-conflict handling is required before integrated editing.
- **ADR-UI-5, proposed:** stable draft identity with separate runtime ownership; default to the backend's current strategy slot limit. Benefit: creation cannot clobber another running bot. Cost: concurrent duplicate instances wait for explicit backend support.

### Quality scenarios

| Trigger | Required response / acceptance target |
| --- | --- |
| Owner opens a 20-bot fleet | Mode, capital, held bot count and last decisions are visible; proposed usability target: identify a blocked bot within 10 seconds |
| Inputs become stale while the owner is reading | Update age and blocking reason without moving focus/selection or pretending the last value is current |
| A submit times out | Show unknown and reconciliation status; no automatic resend; keep exposure visible |
| A configuration changes in another client | Detect version mismatch; preserve the draft and show a resolvable diff |
| Owner closes browser during a test | Durable owner continues or stops under its documented policy; reconnect shows its real receipt, no duplicate start |
| A bulk pause partially fails | Show per-bot outcomes and remaining active exposure; no aggregate success lie |
| Owner uses keyboard at 320px/400% zoom | Reach all stages/actions and see field errors without page-wide horizontal scrolling |

These are design targets, not measured user-study results or current product guarantees.

## Validation and handoff

The interactive sample covers fleet selection/filtering, pause/resume semantics, stale Council hold, evidence and blocked-live explanation, action search, and draft creation for all five template choices. It does not implement jobs, sorting persistence, account connection, complete strategy schemas, real evidence, positions/orders, full wallet attribution, dark mode or actual arming. These are explicit implementation work.

Browser review receipts and captures live in /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/docs/design/bot-control-room/REVIEW.md and /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/docs/design/bot-control-room/screens/. Skill applicability is recorded in /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/docs/design/bot-control-room/SKILLS.md. The implementation plan is /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-09-bot-control-room.md.

Before product integration, test five realistic tasks with the owner: identify a stale bot, explain a loss after costs, create a manual Grid draft, compare incompatible runs, and stop entries while explaining remaining exposure. Record completion, errors, time and perceived difficulty. Include keyboard and screen-reader users for broader release. A design review or automated browser test cannot replace that evidence.

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Interactive Motive Wave Checklist tests a manually selected price structure against disclosed Elliott-wave-style conditions. It is an educational validation aid: the user supplies the candidate rather than an automatic market scanner discovering it. The checklist distinguishes general motive requirements from impulse and expanding/contracting diagonal constraints. Its results express consistency with the stated geometry and do not establish a price forecast.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for individual generic-motive and expanding/contracting diagonal checks on six supplied ordered pivots. The impulse extension rule and equality/boundary parity are not claimed.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Narrow generic-motive/diagonal checklist: take six chronologically increasing pivot points P0…P5 with alternating high/low direction, and wave lengths L_i=abs(P_i−P_(i−1)). With direction d=sign(P1−P0), require L2<L1, d×(P3−P1)>0 and (L3>L1 or L3>L5), following the source strict bigger-than wording. For diagonals additionally require L4<L3 and P4 strictly inside the P0-to-P1 price territory. Contracting requires L1>L3>L5 and L2>L4; expanding requires L1<L3<L5 and L2<L4.
- Require chronologically ordered alternating pivots, limit second-wave retracement and require the third wave to exceed the first endpoint without being the shortest action wave.
- For impulses prohibit overlap of the first and fourth waves and test extension constraints.
- For diagonals restrict fourth-wave retracement, require overlap with first-wave territory and compare sequential action/correction magnitudes for expansion or contraction.

## Outputs and intended use

- After selecting the points, inspect pass/fail checklist items on the chart.
- Use the result to learn how candidate impulse/diagonal structures differ.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Six pivots define the candidate. Retracement rules use 100% and extension is defined above 200%.
- User selects six timestamped price pivots; no automatic pivot detection is needed. Strict inequalities define the narrow checklist; complete impulse validity and extension>200% denominator remain outside scope.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Manual candidate selection introduces hindsight and interpretation bias.
- The phrase all not extended is ambiguous about whether every action wave is individually prohibited from extension.

# Kalman-Filtered Dynamic Hedge Ratio

> **Spec-only — never implemented, never run.** No performance figures appear on this
> card, deliberately. `research/STRATEGIES.md` mechanism #24.

## Equation
```
state:       beta_t = beta_{t-1} + w_t      w ~ N(0, process_var)
observation: X_t    = beta_t * Y_t + v_t    v ~ N(0, obs_var)
```

## Why it might work
Static hedge ratios are documented as unstable, and re-estimating per window produces
jumps at window boundaries. A filter makes the ratio a smoothly evolving estimate, which
is both more honest and less prone to boundary artifacts.

## What implementing it would take
A peer series plus a scalar Kalman filter — perhaps forty lines, no dependency.

## Caveats
Two variance parameters tune how fast beta moves, and they are usually chosen by
eyeballing the result, which is fitting by another name. A filter that adapts quickly
enough will track any relationship, including one that has genuinely broken.

the literature, not a measurement. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme: across
311 rankable configurations measured in this repo, 14% had a positive out-of-sample
Sharpe and 9% made money.*

## Documented inputs and source details

> The information in this guide is intended to get you started with your understanding of options, the terminology, and their basic characteristics. In addition to this guide, it is recommended that you study all information available under the education section of your broker’s website. Most brokers who cater to options traders provide good information that will help you learn.

> Buyers of calls have the right, without any obligation, to buy the underlying stock at the strike of the options contract. They retain their right until the option no longer exists, defined by the expiration date.

> Scenario 2: After closer review of the painting, it is discovered that the signature on the back is not of a famous artist, but is the brother of a famous artist. This actually drives the value of the painting down to $500. If the buyer exercised their option to purchase the painting it would cost $1,000. This would not make sense because the buyer could instead just buy it at “market price” for just $500. Since the buyer had no obligation to purchase based on the option contract, the agreement, or contract, would just expire and the buyer would lose the $50 premium paid.

> Call buyers anticipate the value of the underlying stock will rise. When it does, the value of the option will also increase at approximately the rate of the Delta. Buyers pay for the right to buy the stock in the future, sometime before expiration of the option. When buying the option, they pay the ask price. The premium they pay is less than buying the stock, yet they will still benefit from any appreciation in the value of the stock.

> Sellers of call options are selling to someone else the right to buy the underlying stock from them. When/if the buyer chooses to buy the stock from the seller, (remember, the buyer has no obligation to do so) it is referred to as an exercise…the buyer is exercising the right to buy the stock. The seller is obligated to deliver the stock to the buyer. A seller’s obligation ends when the stock is exercised, the option expires, or the option is bought to close (BTC).

> The example demonstrates two important points. When you buy an option, you have a right, but not an obligation, to do something. You can always let the expiration date pass, at which point the option becomes worthless. If this happens, you lose 100% of your investment, which is the money you paid for the option.

> Put buyers anticipate the value of the underlying stock will go down. When it does, the value of the option will increase at approximately the rate of the Delta. Buyers pay a premium for the right to be able to put (sell) the stock to someone else in the future, sometime before expiration of the option. When buying the option, they pay the ask price.

> Sellers of put options are selling to someone else the right to sell/put the underlying stock to them. When/if the buyer chooses to put their stock to the seller, this is referred to as being assigned……the buyer of the put option is assigning the stock to the seller. The seller is obligated to buy the stock based on the strike price of the contract. A seller’s obligation ends when the option expires or the option is bought to close (BTC).

> Say you wanted to buy XYZ stock because you think it is going to move up from its current price of $84. Remember, all the trader is doing is buying the right to buy the stock without any obligation to actually buy it. The option only costs $4.00 for the right to buy the stock at some future date. Buying 1,000 shares of the stock would require $84,000 but buying 10 options contracts would only cost $4,000.

Win rate tells us what are the odds (historically) of session reversal producing a clean supporting move that was persistent enough to close that way too.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Moving Regression is a generalization of moving average and polynomial regression.

> The procedure approximates a specified number of prior data points with a polynomial function of a user-defined degree. Then, polynomial interpolation of the last data point is used to construct a Moving Regression time series.

> The effects of the moving window Length and the Local Polynomial Degree are confounded. This allows for​ finding the optimal trade-off between noise (variance) and lag (bias). Higher Length and lower Polynomial Degree (such as 1, i.e. linear), will result in "smoother" time series but at the cost of greater lag. Increasing the Polynomial​ Degree to, for example, 2 (squared) while maintaining the Length will diminish the lag and thus compromise the noise-lag tradeoff.

> When the degree of the local polynomial is set to 0 (i.e., fitting data to a constant level), the Moving Regression time series exactly matches the Simple Moving Average of the same length.

# Sniffer

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Sniffer searches historical chart windows for formations resembling a user-selected candle sequence. It avoids a fixed named-pattern catalog by comparing feature vectors, so the same workflow can examine a single candle or a multi-candle structure. The resulting boxes provide historical analogues for further inspection; similarity is not a forecast or measured probability of a particular outcome. The user controls which features and distance definition matter, making the results dependent on the chosen representation.

## How it works

- Map bar range, signed body, volume, directional head/tail wicks and their ratios into features; optional momentum and directional indicators expand the vector.
- Compare candidate sequences with the chosen input using cosine, Euclidean, Lorentzian, Manhattan or Pearson methods, then sort and retain top matches.

## Outputs and intended use

- White marks the input; green, yellow and red divide matches into upper, middle and lower thirds.
- Optional box text shows similarity percentages; adjust the input time range after changing timeframe.

## Parameters and stated settings

- The processing discussion says maximum 5000 bars, while final notes restrict displayed matches to 4500 bars.
- Top-match count, lookback, feature set and distance method are user inputs.

- The author reports array-bound errors during input setup; the two historical limits should not be conflated.

## Documented inputs and source details

> The Channel BreakOut Strategy creates a channel with its bands based on the highest and lowest values for the last X bars (X is the value of the 'Length' setting). The strategy enters long if the high of the current bar is higher than the upper channel band of the previous bar. It enters short if the low of the current bar is lower than the lower channel band of the previous bar.

> length = input.int(title="Length", minval=1, maxval=1000, defval=5)

> The Channel Breakout Strategy attempts to create a strategy just like its name says - trades based on whether a symbol breaks out from a channel or not. The channel is dependent on the length, which is chosen in the strategy settings. The strategy then enters long if the high of the current bar is higher than the upper channel band of the previous bar. It enters short if the low of the current bar is lower than the lower channel band of the previous bar.

> strategy.entry("ChBrkLE", strategy.long, stop=upBound + syminfo.mintick, comment="ChBrkLE")

> strategy.entry("ChBrkSE", strategy.short, stop=downBound - syminfo.mintick, comment="ChBrkSE")

# MACD Crossover

## What it is
The gap between two EMAs, compared against an EMA of that gap.

## What it looks for
Acceleration in trend, earlier than a raw moving-average cross.

## Equation
```
EMA(s)_t = a*c_t + (1-a)*EMA(s)_{t-1},   a = 2/(s+1)
MACD_t   = EMA(fast)_t - EMA(slow)_t
Signal_t = EMA(sig) applied to the MACD SERIES
Hist_t   = MACD_t - Signal_t
target_t = 1 if MACD_t > Signal_t else 0
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/signals.py::MacdCross`. Note the signal line is an EMA
*of the MACD line*, so a history of MACD values is needed — see
`indicators.ema_series`.

## Parameters
- **fast / slow / signal** — the classic 12/26/9 is a daily-bar convention, not a law.
  At the short horizon 6/13/5 was used, and it behaved like a different strategy.

## Works when
Directional moves with steady acceleration.

## Fails when
Chop produces constant sign flips. **This is the worst measured row in the entire
sweep at the short horizon:** `macd_6_13_5` scored **OOS Sharpe -4.621 across 205
trades**. That number is what fast-parameter whipsaw plus 8 bps round-trip cost looks
like, and it is the single most useful row here for calibrating how much damage
turnover does.

## Backtest notes
Naively recomputing MACD history each bar is O(signal*cap * slow*cap) and once
dominated total sweep runtime. The single-pass `ema_series` reduces it to
O(cap*slow + count). Worth knowing before extending this.

## Pairs with
`stochastic` as an oscillator brake, to stop MACD adding into an exhausted move —
measured as one of only eight positive medium-horizon pairs.

## Measured on SOL
Medium (12/26/9): **IS +1,356.5% (Sharpe 1.347) -> OOS -52.8% (Sharpe -0.720)**,
21 OOS trades. One of the starkest decay rows in the sweep.
Short (6/13/5): **OOS Sharpe -4.621**, 205 trades.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

**OOS Sharpe -4.621 across 205 trades** at the short horizon is the worst row in the
entire sweep, and the medium horizon decayed from +1,356.5% in-sample to -52.8% out.
Fast parameters on hourly SOL bars pay more in fees than the signal earns. Nothing in
the measurement or the mechanism argues for a better rating.

## Caveats and limitations
- A four-figure in-sample return next to a negative out-of-sample Sharpe is the
  clearest illustration in this directory of why full-sample leaderboards are
  worthless.
- Turnover is the dominant term at fast parameters. Do not read the short-horizon
  result as "MACD does not work"; read it as "MACD at 6/13/5 on hourly SOL bars pays
  more in fees than it earns in signal".

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy macd --interval 1d
```
