Build a reusable, offline backtesting program for crypto trading strategies, primarily `{{ASSET}}` (default `SOL`), over `{{START_DATE}}`–`{{END_DATE}}` (defaults `2021-01-01` to today) starting from `{{INITIAL_CAPITAL}}` (default `10000` USD). Every one of those four slots has a working default: if a value is not supplied, use the default — never emit the literal `{{...}}` text into code or CLI help. The deliverable is research infrastructure a person can add new strategies to — not a single strategy, and not a recommendation to trade. Correctness of the simulation outranks the number of strategies shipped: a tool that honestly reports a losing strategy is a success; one that reports an inflated Sharpe because of a leaked future bar is a failure even if it runs.
</goal>

<scope>
In scope: historical simulation, strategy comparison, performance metrics, a CLI, equity-curve charts, tests, README.

Explicitly OUT of scope — do not build these, and do not add dependencies for them:
- Live or paper order execution, exchange API keys, wallet or private-key handling of any kind.
- Any code path that can place, sign, or transmit a real trade.
- **Automated** parameter search — no optimizer loop, no grid search, no "find the best settings" mode. The tool evaluates the configurations it is explicitly given and reports their metrics. (A user may still run it repeatedly by hand with different parameters; that is why the report counts configurations evaluated per run, so a reader can see how much searching produced the headline number. Counting is not searching.)
- Web UI, database, containerization, deployment.
</scope>

<environment>
Verified facts about the target machine — rely on these, do not re-derive:
- Python 3.13, `pandas` 2.2.3, `numpy` 2.2.6, `matplotlib` 3.10.8 available. **`pyarrow` is NOT installed, so Parquet is unavailable** — use CSV as the cache format, and treat Parquet as an optional path guarded by an import check. Prefer the standard library plus pandas/numpy/matplotlib; justify any other dependency in the README and do not add one that the test suite needs in order to pass.
- Code conventions: type hints on every public function, a one-line docstring on every module and public callable, 4-space indent, no formatter or linter dependency required.
- Outbound HTTPS works. **The Binance API is geo-blocked and returns `"Service unavailable from a restricted location"` — do not use it.**
- The **Coinbase Exchange** public REST API works with no API key: `GET https://api.exchange.coinbase.com/products/SOL-USD/candles?granularity=86400`. It returns rows ordered `[time, low, high, open, close, volume]` — note that this is **not** OHLCV order; mapping it positionally as OHLCV silently corrupts every backtest. It returns at most 300 candles per request, so long histories require paginating backwards with `start`/`end`.
- CoinGecko `/coins/{id}/ohlc` also works keyless and can serve as a fallback source.
</environment>

<data_layer>
Implement data access as a pluggable loader interface with three implementations, so the engine never depends on the network:
1. **CSV loader** (primary): reads a local cached file. This is the path the engine and all tests use. The on-disk schema is exactly these columns, in this order, with a header row: `timestamp,open,high,low,close,volume`. `timestamp` is **UTC epoch seconds** (integer); reject tz-naive local times and tz-aware non-UTC values rather than coercing them. One row per bar, sorted ascending. Parquet may be supported behind an `import pyarrow` guard, but CSV is the format every test uses.
2. **Fetch script** (separate module, invoked explicitly by the user): pulls from Coinbase with pagination, writes the local cache, and never runs implicitly during a backtest.
3. **Synthetic generator** (seeded, deterministic): produces a known price series so the full test suite passes with zero network access.

Validate every loaded series and fail loudly rather than silently proceeding: reject non-monotonic or duplicated timestamps, gaps larger than one bar interval, non-positive prices, and `high < low`. Report the count and location of any rows dropped. If a required series cannot be loaded, do not substitute a different asset or a shorter window — stop and say what was missing.
</data_layer>

<correctness_requirements>
These are the load-bearing requirements. Everything else is secondary.

**1. No look-ahead. Enforce it structurally, not by convention.**
- A signal computed on the bar closing at time *t* may read only data at or before *t*.
- The resulting order fills at the **next** bar (default: `t+1` open), never at bar *t*'s close. Make the fill delay an explicit configurable parameter with a default of 1 bar, so the assumption is visible rather than buried.
- Any rolling statistic (mean, stdev, z-score, normalization) is computed from a trailing window only. Never normalize using full-sample statistics — that is the most common form of this bug.
- Indicator warm-up periods produce no trades; the first tradeable bar is the first bar at which every indicator is fully defined.

**2. Fees and slippage are applied to the fill, never netted at the end.** Each fill pays: taker fee (bps of notional, configurable) plus slippage (bps of notional, configurable), charged at the executed price. Record per-trade cost so the README can show gross-vs-net.

**3. Determinism.** Same inputs plus same seed must produce byte-identical results. Seed every random draw, sort deterministically, and pin the data cache. Emit a run manifest (asset, date range, bar interval, strategy parameters, fee/slippage settings, data-file checksum, library versions) alongside every result set.

**4. Leverage cost model — read this carefully; the two models are not interchangeable.**

Support two execution modes:

- **Spot** (default): long-only or long/flat, no borrowing, no liquidation.
- **Leveraged perpetual**, modeled on **Jupiter Perps** (jup.ag) on Solana, which is the venue this project targets.

Jupiter charges a **borrow fee**, *not* a funding rate. Implementing a signed funding rate here understates leveraged holding cost in one direction, always. The differences you must honor:

```
utilization      = custody.assets.locked / custody.assets.owned
hourlyBorrowRate = (hourlyFundingDbps / 1000) * utilization
hourlyBorrowFee  = hourlyBorrowRate * positionSizeUsd        # notional, NOT collateral
```

- **Both sides always pay.** Longs and shorts both owe borrow fees to the liquidity pool. The rate is the product of two non-negative quantities, so it is **floor-bounded at zero and never negative** — no position is ever paid to stay open. Do not implement a long-pays-short transfer.
- The fee accrues on **notional**, not on collateral and not on the borrowed token amount.
- Accrual is a **cumulative-index difference times notional**, which is additive/linear — not fee-on-fee compounding. Settlement happens when the position is touched (close, liquidation, collateral change, size change).
- Longs and shorts draw on different collateral pools with different utilizations and different max rates, so make the rate configurable **per side** (a documented reference point: SOL ≈ 0.016%/hr max versus stablecoin ≈ 0.003%/hr max). Expose `max_hourly_rate_bps_long`, `max_hourly_rate_bps_short`, and a `utilization` input (constant or time series).
- Charge a base fee of 0.06% of notional on open and again on close (0.12% round trip) by default, configurable.

**Liquidation.** Maintenance margin is `size / max_lev` where `max_lev` is a protocol constant of **500** — i.e. **0.2% of notional** — which is distinct from the user-facing leverage cap. The published liquidation price is:

```
Liq Price (Long)  = entry - (|collateral - close_fee - borrow_fee - size/500| * entry) / size
Liq Price (Short) = entry + (|collateral - close_fee - borrow_fee - size/500| * entry) / size
```

Equivalently, the buffer as a fraction of entry price is `1/L - f_close - 0.002 - borrow_fee/size`. Because accrued borrow fees enter that expression, **the liquidation price drifts toward spot the longer a position is held** — recompute it every bar rather than fixing it at entry. Note in the code that the absolute-value bars in the published formula are only valid while the bracketed term is positive; once collateral falls below maintenance the sign flips and the formula leaves its valid domain. Handle that case explicitly instead of propagating a nonsensical price.

**One documented open question you must not paper over.** The published Jupiter formula is flat-linear in utilization, so the rate goes to zero as utilization goes to zero. But protocol governance has separately proposed a dual-slope ("jump rate") model with a kink around 80% utilization and a **minimum rate floor near 10% APR**, which is mathematically incompatible with `utilization × max`. Which one is live cannot be settled from documentation. Therefore: implement the flat-linear formula as the default, **plus a configurable `min_hourly_rate_bps` floor defaulting to 0**, and an optional `kink_utilization` / second-slope parameter. Document in the README that a user modeling low-utilization periods should set the floor rather than trusting the flat-linear result, and that the live value must be read from the on-chain custody account. Do not silently pick one model and present it as authoritative.

Treat these numbers as configuration defaults with a comment pointing at their source, not as constants of nature: they are governance-set and change. Do not fetch them at runtime.
</correctness_requirements>

<strategies>
Ship these four, each as a separate module implementing one interface: buy-and-hold (the mandatory baseline), moving-average crossover, RSI mean-reversion, and breakout (Donchian channel).

Every strategy implements exactly this interface, and the engine — not the strategy — owns position sizing, fee application, and fill timing. A strategy that can only emit a target exposure for the next bar cannot leak the future.

**Sizing rule (be explicit; this choice changes every equity curve).** Target exposure `e` means a position whose notional equals `e × current_equity × leverage`, where `current_equity` is mark-to-market equity at the fill bar — not initial capital. So `e = 1.0` in spot mode at `leverage = 1` is "fully invested," and the strategy compounds. Rebalance toward the target only when the gap exceeds a configurable `--rebalance-threshold` (default 0 = rebalance every bar), so that fee drag from trivial rebalances is a visible parameter rather than a hidden one. Fractional units are allowed; SOL is divisible.

```python
class Strategy(Protocol):
    name: str
    params: dict

    def warmup_bars(self) -> int:
        """Bars required before the first valid signal."""

    def on_bar(self, history: BarWindow) -> float:
        """Return target exposure for the NEXT bar, in [-1.0, 1.0]
        (or [0.0, 1.0] in spot long-only mode).

        `history` exposes only bars up to and including the current one;
        it raises IndexError on any attempt to read beyond it.
        """
```

Adding a strategy must require only a new module implementing this Protocol plus a registry entry — no changes to the engine.
</strategies>

<metrics>
Define each metric unambiguously in both code and README; ambiguous annualization is the most common source of a wrong Sharpe ratio.

- **Total return**, **CAGR**.
- **Sharpe ratio**: `(mean(excess_returns) / stdev(excess_returns)) * sqrt(periods_per_year)`, where `periods_per_year` is derived from the bar interval (365 for daily crypto, since crypto trades every day — state this choice explicitly), `stdev` uses the sample standard deviation (`ddof=1`), and the risk-free rate is an explicit parameter defaulting to 0. State the convention in the output, not just the docs.
- **Sortino ratio**, **max drawdown** (peak-to-trough on the equity curve, reported with its start/end dates and duration), **Calmar ratio**.
- **Win rate**, **profit factor**, **average win/loss**, **trade count**, **exposure fraction**, **total fees paid**.
- For leveraged runs: **liquidation count** and the bar at which each occurred.

Report both **gross** and **net-of-cost** figures so the cost drag is visible.
</metrics>

<honest_reporting>
The comparison report is where this kind of tool most often misleads, so it must carry its own caveats:

- Always include buy-and-hold as the baseline. A strategy that underperforms buy-and-hold on the same data must be shown as underperforming, prominently, not buried in a sorted table.
- Support **walk-forward / out-of-sample evaluation**: split the history, report in-sample and out-of-sample metrics as separate columns, and never present a single full-sample number as the headline result. Two rules at the boundary: (a) the out-of-sample segment's indicators **may** warm up from the trailing in-sample bars — reading earlier history is not look-ahead, and starting cold would silently discard the first `warmup_bars` of out-of-sample data; (b) the split index is computed once from the date range and never adjusted after seeing results.
- Because the tool compares N strategies and the reader will look at the best one, the report must state the multiple-comparisons problem in plain language: the best of N backtests is upward-biased by selection, and the bias grows with N. Print the count of strategy/parameter configurations evaluated in this run (this is bookkeeping on what the user asked for, not a search the tool performs). Ground it concretely — Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016) argue the significance bar should rise from t ≈ 2.0 to t ≈ 3.0+ once multiple testing is accounted for, and McLean & Pontiff (2016) measured 26% in-sample and 58% out-of-sample decay across 97 published factors.
- Every report and the README carry a one-line notice: results are a historical simulation for research and education only, not investment advice, and past simulated performance does not predict future results.
- Do not tune parameters to improve reported results and then present those results as out-of-sample.
</honest_reporting>

<deliverables>
Create this structure under `backtester/`:

```
backtester/
  README.md              # what it is, install, usage, metric definitions, limitations
  requirements.txt
  cli.py                 # argparse entry point
  core/
    types.py             # Bar, BarWindow, Trade, Position, RunManifest
    data.py              # loader Protocol + CSV and synthetic implementations
    fetch.py             # explicit Coinbase fetch + pagination -> local cache
    engine.py            # event loop, fill timing, fee application
    perps.py             # borrow-fee accrual, margin, liquidation
    metrics.py           # metric definitions
    report.py            # comparison table + caveats
    plotting.py          # equity curve, drawdown chart
    strategies/
      __init__.py        # registry
      buy_and_hold.py
      ma_crossover.py
      rsi.py
      breakout.py
  tests/
    ...
```

Build in this order, so that each step is testable before the next depends on it: `types.py` → `data.py` (+ synthetic generator) → `metrics.py` → `engine.py` (spot only) → tests for the buy-and-hold identity and fill timing → `strategies/` → `perps.py` + its liquidation tests → `report.py` → `plotting.py` → `fetch.py` → `cli.py` → README. Do not start the perpetual/leverage layer until the spot engine passes its known-answer test; a leverage bug on top of a broken accounting core is untraceable.

The CLI must support at minimum: `--asset` (default `{{ASSET}}`), `--start` / `--end` (defaults `{{START_DATE}}` / `{{END_DATE}}`), `--capital` (default `{{INITIAL_CAPITAL}}`), `--strategy` (repeatable, or `all`), `--interval`, `--mode {spot,perp}`, `--leverage`, `--fee-bps`, `--slippage-bps`, `--fill-delay`, `--split` for walk-forward, `--seed`, and `--out`. Running with no arguments must print usage rather than silently starting a long fetch.

`--out DIR` writes, deterministically: `comparison.csv` (one row per strategy, one column per metric), `run_manifest.json` (the manifest defined above), `trades_<strategy>.csv` (one row per fill: timestamp, side, price, units, notional, fee, slippage, borrow-fee-settled, realized PnL, equity after), `equity_<strategy>.csv`, and the PNG charts. The human-readable comparison table also prints to stdout. Machine-readable files must not contain the caveat prose; the caveats belong in stdout and in `report.md`.
</deliverables>

<verification>
You are not done when the code is written. You are done when you have **run** it and shown the output. Before reporting completion:

1. Run the test suite and paste the actual result. These tests must exist and pass:
   - **Buy-and-hold identity**: with zero fees and zero slippage, buy-and-hold total return equals `last_close / first_close - 1` to within floating-point tolerance. This is the engine's known-answer test — if it fails, the accounting is wrong and nothing else matters.
   - **Look-ahead guard**: a deliberately cheating strategy that tries to read beyond the current bar must raise, not succeed. A guard that cannot fail is not a guard, so assert the exception is raised.
   - **Fill timing**: a signal on bar *t* produces a fill at bar *t+1*'s open, verified on a hand-checked fixture.
   - **Fee arithmetic**: a single round-trip trade's cost equals the hand-computed expected value.
   - **Borrow-fee sign**: borrow fees are non-negative for both long and short positions, for every utilization in `[0, 1]`.
   - **Liquidation**: a position with a known entry, leverage, and adverse move liquidates at the hand-computed price; and a held position's liquidation price moves monotonically toward spot as borrow fees accrue.
   - **Data validation**: malformed input (duplicate timestamp, `high < low`, negative price) is rejected.
2. Run at least one real end-to-end backtest on actual fetched SOL data, comparing all four strategies, and paste the resulting comparison table.
3. Confirm two runs with the same seed produce identical output.
4. Re-read this specification and confirm each requirement is met or explicitly report it as not met. Do not report success for a partially finished component.

If a component cannot be completed, say plainly which one and why, rather than shipping a stub that appears to work.
</verification>

<failure_handling>
If a step fails and you cannot fix it, respond with: "I was unable to complete <component>. Here is my best partial attempt: <attempt>. The specific failure was: <error>. Please review." Retry a transient failure (network timeout, rate limit) at most 3 times with backoff, then stop and report — do not loop indefinitely and do not silently fall back to synthetic data for a run the user asked to run on real data.

If any requirement in this specification is ambiguous or conflicts with another, ask exactly one targeted question before proceeding. If nothing is ambiguous, proceed without asking.
</failure_handling>

<hard_constraints_restated>
Four constraints override any other consideration, including shipping on time. Re-read them before you report completion:

1. **No look-ahead.** A signal on bar *t* reads only data ≤ *t* and fills at *t+1*. Never normalize with full-sample statistics.
2. **No live trading capability.** No keys, no wallets, no signing, no order transmission — not even unreachable code.
3. **Borrow fees are never negative and are charged on notional to both sides.** This is not a funding rate.
4. **The buy-and-hold known-answer test must pass** (`last_close / first_close - 1` at zero cost). If it fails, the accounting is wrong and no other result is meaningful.
</hard_constraints_restated>

> While net volume is useful information, it can be a blunt data point. Volume composition breaks down the content of volume, allowing a more detailed look inside each volume node. Volume composition consists of the following information:

> Buy and sell volume is defined by volume associated with lower timeframe up/down moves. This classification is further broken down to passive/active, standing for decreasing/increasing volume, e.g. a move up with volume higher than previous bar volume = active buy volume, a move up with volume lower than previous bar volume = passive buy volume.

This could be replaced with OHLC4 for example, resulting in a volume direction based on OHLC average.

> Volume is arguably one of the most important data points as it directly relates to liquidity. High volume can be an indication of strength (price likely to continue moving) or absorption (price likely to halt/turn). Same applies to active volume, but with an element of aggression. High active volume serves as an indication of exuberance or otherwise forceful transacting, like stop losses triggering. With these principles in mind, the composition of volume allows distinguishing potentially important events.

> 2. Dominating volume threshold exceeded. Can be defined via input menu, 70% of total volume by default.

> 6. Dominating active volume threshold exceeded. Can be defined via input menu, 70% by default.

# Percent Rank Histogram

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Percent Rank Histogram compares where each selected instrument currently sits within its own historical distribution. It uses percentile position rather than directly comparing raw price levels across assets, then colors columns and adds arrows for rising/falling rank. The author suggests midpoint readings as trend context, but percentile rank is relative position within a window rather than a forecast probability or a cross-sectional capitalization rank.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** The source defines percentile ranking and its caller-selectable window; unspecified display defaults do not block that computation.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- For each selected series, calculate the share of historical observations less than or equal to its current value over the chosen rank window.
- Display ranked percentages as gradient columns and label whether the percentile increased or decreased.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Bollinger BandWidth (BBW) is a technical analysis indicator derived from the standard Bollinger Bands indicator. Bollinger Bands are a volatility indicator which creates a band of three lines which are plotted in relation to a security's price. The Middle Line is typically a 20 Day Simple Moving Average. The Upper and Lower Bands are typically 2 standard deviations above and below the SMA (Middle Line). Bollinger BandWidth serve as a way to quantitatively measure the width between the Upper and Lower Bands. BBW can be used to identify trading signals in some instances.

> Bollinger BandWidth = (Upper Band - Lower Band) / Middle Band * 100

> Bollinger BandWidth (BBW) uses the given calculation and outputs a Percentage Difference between the Upper Band and the Lower Band. This value is used to define the narrowness of the bands. What needs to be understood however is that a trader cannot simply look at the BBW value and determine if the Band is truly narrow or not. The significance of an instruments relative narrowness changes depending on the instrument or security in question. What is considered narrow for one security may not be for another. What is considered narrow for one security may even change within the scope of the same

> One of the most well-known theories in regards to Bollinger Bands is that volatility typically fluctuates between periods of expansion (Bands Widening) and contraction (Bands Narrowing). With this in mind, the major trading signal generated by Bollinger BandWidth is known as The Squeeze.

> There is a period of low volatility. The means that the bands are narrow and price is moving relatively sideways.

# AI Predictive Flow (Zeiierman)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Estimate forward movement by matching multibar price-feature patterns with historical analogues. A smoothed nearest-neighbor output becomes an oscillator and projected-price regime, offering model-based directional context rather than a validated prediction guarantee.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

## How it works

- Features comprise log one-bar return, lookback momentum, centered RSI and normalized fast/slow EMA spread. Separate matrices store sequences, and equal feature-weight squared differences across the pattern are summed before taking a square root.
- The nearest distances select outcome labels. Each outcome weight is one minus its distance divided by the selected distance sum, with a special single-neighbor/zero-distance branch. The shown function sums weighted labels without normalizing total weight.
- Prediction passes through EMA stages and a signal EMA. Projected price is base times exp(prediction); ATR-offset projected references set a state when their rolling extrema are reached, with the bearish assignment last if both tests fire.

## Outputs and intended use

- Oscillator zero side, signal crossovers, histogram and background regime provide directional alignment context.
- The author favors aligned oscillator/regime signals; no allocation, costs or empirical forecasting performance is supplied.

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Liquidity Void Detector emphasizes unusually large recent returns when volume is weak relative to its own baseline. It explicitly offers a practical OHLCV proxy, not measured order-book emptiness. The narrative associates upward low-volume moves with potential downside refill and downward moves with upside refill, but its settings section reverses those buy/sell labels, so consumers must preserve that contradiction rather than wire labels into orders.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Parameterized numerical void oscillator is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Compute log volume relative to its SMA and Z-score that shock; compute and Z-score one-bar log return.
- Multiply return Z-score by full weight in low-volume conditions or by a configurable fade otherwise.
- volTrend=SMA(volume,L);vs=log(volume)-log(volTrend) for positive inputs;vsZ=ZScore(vs,vzLen);lowVS=(vsZ<=vzThr). r1=log(close/close[1]);retZ=ZScore(r1,rLen);osc=retZ*(1 if lowVS else fadeNoLow). ZScore=(x-mean)/std under caller convention with nonzero std;fadeNoLow in[0,1]. Contradictory side labels and signal decisions remain excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- Inspect signed low-participation displacement alongside price zones and other tools; do not assume voids necessarily fill.
- Usable scope: Parameterized numerical void oscillator. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Low-volume threshold examples are -0.5 to -1.0. Fade ranges 0–1, with zero ignoring non-low-volume bars and one ignoring the volume condition. Lengths/oscillator thresholds are configurable without defaults.

- Analytical: weak reported volume is not actual depth, standardized returns can be unstable and the narrative/settings side labels contradict.

> The Clusters Volume Profile [LuxAlgo] indicator utilizes K-Means clustering to categorize historical price action into distinct groups and generates individual volume profiles for each detected cluster. This tool provides a unique perspective on volume distribution by isolating price behaviors based on proximity rather than strictly chronological order.

> The indicator identifies "clusters" of price activity within a user-defined lookback period. Each cluster is assigned a unique color and its own horizontal volume profile, allowing traders to see where liquidity is most concentrated within specific price regimes.

> Iteratively assigning each price bar to the nearest centroid based on the HLC2 (median) price.

> Cluster boundaries and POC lines provide concrete levels for trade management. An entry can be sought when price retests a high-volume cluster POC, while stops can be placed outside the total price range of that specific cluster (the area covered by its volume profile). Conversely, targets can be set at the POC of the next major cluster above or below current price action.

> Initializing "centroids" across the price range of the lookback period.

> Lookback Period: Determines the number of recent bars used for the clustering analysis.

> Traders can use the Point of Control (POC) of high-volume clusters to identify significant institutional interest. Because the K-Means algorithm groups price action by density rather than time, a cluster's POC often represents a "fair value" level where significant exchange occurred. These dashed POC lines frequently act as robust support or resistance levels when price returns to them in the future.

- Fit forming rails to swing structure using a perceptual score and one-pole slope adjustment. Lock after sufficient geometric stillness, touches and span without channel inversion; freeze locked/broken geometry. Bin intrabar volume by rail distance, smooth it with kernel density and render calibration ribbons, density-scaled reach and peak ghost lines.

- Dotted/solid/restyled rails expose forming/locked/broken state. Audit badges show wick-through, modeled survival and maturity. Forecast layers refresh at the live edge without history and are explicitly model estimates rather than price predictions.

- Mode sets fast/medium/slow evidence tempo; Precision controls fit window and intrabar sampling no finer than one minute. Wick-through target is ten percent. Layer/color/contrast and channel toggles are configurable.

# Buyers & Sellers Profile + Dynamic S/R (Zeiierman)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Buyers & Sellers Profile + Dynamic S/R refines confirmed swing levels using nearby volume-profile evidence. It aims to combine structural pivots with actual historical participation proxies instead of drawing every swing. Candle volume is distributed by price-range overlap and split by closing location, explicitly as an estimate rather than true footprint data. A nearby profile node can pull a pivot-derived level toward stronger participation, while a second score incorporates candle absorption/rejection. The result supports discretionary retest monitoring, not proof of institutional buying or guaranteed support.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Partly disclosed computation.** Proportional overlap and buyShare are disclosed, but no source rule defines the profile row-domain endpoints/boundaries. Adding caller-supplied row intervals would extend the source input contract; a complete rolling profile/POC is therefore still incomplete.

- The rolling profile price-domain endpoints and row-boundary construction are unspecified.
- Zero-range candle allocation is unspecified.

## How it works

- For a nonzero-range candle, buyShare=(Close−Low)/(High−Low), sellShare=1−buyShare. For a defined profile row interval [a,b], the stated proportional overlap allocation corresponds to Volume×max(0,min(High,b)−max(Low,a))/(High−Low), then multiply by the respective shares. Sum row volume over the lookback and choose the maximum-volume row as POC. The source does not define the actual row-domain endpoints, equal-spacing rule or zero-range allocation; this formula therefore describes allocation conditional on rows, not a fully specified published profile.
- Search around confirmed pivots in ATR distance and score node strength, local prominence, directional volume and proximity.
- Blend raw pivot toward chosen node, score profile/absorption/volume/wick evidence, merge nearby same-side levels and invalidate on buffered closes.

## Outputs and intended use

- Rolling split profile, POC and scored support/resistance lines show participation-confirmed structure.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Profile evidence weights 50/20/20/10%; final score weights 50/20/15/15%.
- Lookback/rows, swing length, search/min-node/evidence/pull/score, level cap, merge and break ATR are inputs; defaults absent.

- Closing-location allocation is an estimate and zero-range candles require handling.
- Confirmed pivots and historical profile reconstruction must use information available at evaluation time.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Volatility Qaulity Zero Line attempts to keep a trader out of ranging markets, but the original calculation on TradingView had to be adjusted for each instrument. To avoid this issue, I have applied a z-score calculation to the VQZL so the result is standardized for all instruments. A Z-Score is simply a value's relationship to the mean (average) of a group of values, measured in terms of standard deviations from the mean.

> This calculation allows us to compare current volatility to the mean (moving average) of the population (Z-Length). The closer the VQZL Z-Score is to the mean, the closer it will be to the Zero Line and therefore price is likely consolidating and choppy. The farther VQZL Z-Score is from the mean, the more likely price is trending.

> The MA Mode determines the Moving Average used to calculate VQZL itself. The Z-Score is ALWAYS calculated with a simple moving average (as that is the standard calculation for Z-Score).

> The Threshold Levels are the levels at which VQZL Z-Score will change from gray to yellow, orange, green (bullish), or red (bearish). These levels can be adjusted but you should adjust the Threshold Lines as well (in the style section), so they line up with your adjusted values.

> Statistically speaking, confidence levels in relation to Z-Score are noted below. The built in Threshold Levels are the positive and negative values for 90%, 95%, and 99%. This would indicate when volatility is greater than these values they are out of the ordinary from the standard range. You may wish to adjust these levels for VQZL Z-Score to be more responsive to your trading need

## Documented inputs and source details

> The Time Weighted Average Price (TWAP) is a trading indicator used to help traders manage their positions in the market. It is calculated by dividing the total value of a security traded over a specific period of time by the total number of shares traded during that period. The resulting value provides a simple and effective way to measure the average price at which a security is traded over a given timeframe.

> Indicator calculation period. This setting specifies the Anchor, i.e. how frequently the TWAP calculation will be reset. For TWAP to work properly, each TWAP period should include several bars inside of it, so e.g. setting both and timeframe to '1D' is not useful because the indicator will be reset on every bar.

> The source for the TWAP calculation. Traditionally, the bar's average value is used as the source. By default, the source is ohlc4.

> TWAP is most commonly used to facilitate execution of bigger orders without excessive impact on the market price. The order is split into separate smaller orders which are executed with a delay between them to ensure that the size of the orders does not affect the market negatively. The TWAP value represents the average price for the specified period and can be used to automatically specify a proper price for the order.

> Adding a new custom timeframe through the Interval menu above the chart will also add said timeframe to the Anchor Period dropdown in the indicator settings.

# Open Interest Footprint IQ [TradingIQ]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** analysis-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Visualize cryptocurrency open-interest changes by intrabar price level. The footprint labels opening/closing behavior inferred from price direction and OI change, making it a positioning proxy rather than direct observation of which participant initiated a trade.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Four nonzero price/OI sign labels is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Retrieve lower-timeframe price ranges, direction and OI changes. Rising price with rising OI is labeled longs opening; rising price/falling OI shorts closing; falling price/rising OI shorts opening; falling price/falling OI longs closing.
- Aggregate categories into footprint price levels, either resetting each bar or accumulating until a selected reset boundary. Delta and percentage overlays summarize net change.
- A value-area/POC view highlights concentration. Level delta exceeding a selected imbalance percentage produces markers; consecutive imbalanced levels trigger an alert.
- Given synchronized nonzero price/OI changes classify(+,+)=UU longs opening,(+,-)=UD shorts closing,(-,+)=DU shorts opening,(-,-)=DD longs closing. These reproduce heuristic labels,not true participant identification. Zero cases,footprint rows,delta percentages/value area remain outside scope;external OI is still required.

## Outputs and intended use

- Boxes display delta, delta percentage and inferred long/short opening/closing categories, with category or simple up/down colors.
- The author suggests absorption/exhaustion and entry-context use; chart data does not verify those causal interpretations.
- Usable scope: Four nonzero price/OI sign labels. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- One-minute, one-second or one-tick granularity; manual tick spacing or zero for ATR-based automatic spacing.
- Cumulative/reset timeframe, value-area percentage, imbalance threshold/count and visibility/colors.

## Failure modes and caveats

- An OI increase creates both a long and short contract; direction-based attribution cannot uniquely identify longs or shorts opening.
- Tick/second histories and OI timestamps may have different coverage. Signed changes also make a percentage-containing value area ambiguous.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Price-level allocation, ATR spacing formula, delta denominator, value-area/POC calculation and zero-price-change handling are absent.

## Data requirements

Required inputs: lower-timeframe crypto price bars or ticks, exchange-specific synchronized open interest history, instrument tick size.

Repository input-class support: unavailable or unresolved. Exchange-specific synchronized lower-timeframe open interest is required and is not established as available.

# Moving-Average Ribbon

> **Implemented in this session** from spec-only mechanism #19 of
> `research/STRATEGIES.md`. Its stated gap was "implementable now — needs code, not
> data", so the code was written and it was measured on the same 1,875 daily SOL bars
> and the same 70/30 split as every other measured card.
## What it is
Several SMAs at once; exposure is the fraction of adjacent pairs in the correct
order. A graded version of `ma_crossover.md`.

## Equation
```
spans    = [base, 2*base, ..., windows*base]
target_t = (# adjacent pairs where SMA(shorter) > SMA(longer)) / (windows - 1)
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/advanced.py::MaRibbon`.

## Measured on SOL

| Leg | Return | Sharpe | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-sample | +452.0% | 1.119 | — |
| **Out-of-sample** | **-54.0%** | **-1.242** | **160** |

For reference on the same split: buy-and-hold made **+565.2% (Sharpe 1.030)**
in-sample and **-70.8% (Sharpe -0.651)** out. That row reproduces the figure the
existing cards document exactly, which is how these new numbers are known to be
comparable to them.


The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos.*

The card written before implementation called this "the weakest candidate in this
tier — more knobs on a mechanism already measured as regime-dependent is not
progress." The measurement agrees: **-54.0% on 160 trades**, worse than
`ma_crossover` at the same horizon (-52.3%), with 23x the trade count.

Grading the exposure did smooth the whipsaw — 160 trades against a binary rule's 7
means it was rarely fully in or out — but smoothing the entry to a losing signal
produces a smoother loss. There is no mechanism here that `ma_crossover` lacks.

## Caveats and limitations
- 160 trades at 8 bps round trip is roughly 1.3% of notional in costs.
- Two parameters that jointly determine five windows, none of them swept.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy ma_ribbon --interval 1d
```

- Compute minimum and maximum risk from weighted annual stock-minus-benchmark returns divided by annual maximum and minimum ATR percentages respectively.
- Blend transformed minimum and maximum risks using exponent and scaling factors derived from trader win rate and profit ratio. Aggressive and conservative modes exchange which factor receives the larger value.
- Multiply the unadjusted risk score by a drawdown-tolerance adjustment, then combine capital, risk and a condition-dependent ATR multiplier to estimate size.

## Outputs and intended use

- Use the estimated risk percentage and size to plan exposure; by default an underperforming stock receives no position-size calculation.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Historical metrics use five-year weighted annual values; trader defaults are win factor 50% and profit ratio 1.5.
- Optional underperformer calculation substitutes minimum 1% and maximum 2%; the adaptive ATR multiplier ranges from 1 to 3.5.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Analytical: estimated risk depends on trader-supplied performance and tolerance; historical relative strength does not establish safe exposure.
- The written position-size expression is ambiguous about parentheses and ATR placement, so it must not be translated directly into an order quantity.

> A line break chart is a Japanese chart type that disregards time intervals and only focuses on price movements. It is similar to the Kagi and Renko charts by the calculation method but differs in its appearance.

> You can control the number of past lines used in the calculation via the "Number of lines" input in the chart settings. The typical "Number of lines" setting is 3, which means that the chart forms a new up line only when the closing price is above the high prices of the last three lines, and forms a new down line when the closing price is below the past three lines' low prices.

> The user defines the "Number of lines" value. The chart compares the current close to the high and low values from the "Number of lines" previous lines. If the input's value is 3, the calculation compares the current close to the highs and lows of the latest three confirmed lines, forming a new up or down line only when the close is above the highs or below the lows. The appropriate line is then drawn (or not drawn) based on the above guidelines.

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Rolling Z-Score Trend standardizes closing price around a rolling mean and displays the smoothed deviation together with its bar-to-bar change. It supports both momentum and mean-reversion interpretation: an extreme can indicate a strong ongoing move or a possible reversal context, so direction alone does not decide the trade. The source says signals use confirmed bars, which is an implementation claim rather than an independently verified live guarantee.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

- Compute closing-price Z-score from rolling mean/standard deviation, apply a short EMA and take successive differences for momentum columns.
- Show standardized level, momentum and directional information in a numerical table.

- EMA smoothing is three periods; threshold defaults +1.5/-1.5 and ±2 is an illustrated extreme. Rolling lookback is user-selected, with no default stated.

## Idea and objective

Asset Rotation System compares a user-selected set of assets against USD and against each other, seeking to hold the strongest relative candidate. It presents a trend matrix, hypothetical rotation equity and individual buy-and-hold comparisons. ## How it works

- Narrow RSI matrix: take six caller-selected USD asset source series X_i and aligned ratio sources X_i/X_j. Calculate RSI at the selected source/length for each USD and ratio series. Mark crossing up through 50 when current RSI>50 and previous≤50, crossing down when current<50 and previous≥50; above/below50 gives the corresponding directional state. - Classify each asset/USD and asset-ratio trend with RSI, CCI, SuperTrend, DMI or PSAR, individually or in an All mode.
- Identify an optimal asset and calculate a system equity curve assuming exclusive investment in that asset.
- Report return dispersion, Sharpe, Sortino, Omega and drawdown alongside individual asset equity.

- Use the matrix to compare relative trends and confirmed-optimal-asset alerts to notice a possible rotation.
- Calibrate settings cautiously; the author explicitly warns against maximizing historical performance.

- RSI uses a 50 crossover; indicator lengths/sources, SuperTrend factor and PSAR acceleration settings are configurable.

## How it works

- Filter prices with SuperSmoother, compare its history against a fitted/end-to-end slope for Reflex and against the current filtered value for Trendflex. Normalize raw deviations using an exponentially weighted squared-deviation state, then optionally form MAD, standard-deviation or percentile thresholds.

## Outputs and intended use

- Use zero/sign changes for cycle/trend context and disagreements for caution. Six alerts are described as bar-close only. The source later clarifies near-zero rather than literally zero lag and warns of normalization artifacts.

## Failure modes and caveats

# Trading Report Generator from CSV

Version: 1.0.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: initial source-grounded companion card for a strategy-labelled tool.

**Classification:** reporting-tool. Companion research-tool card; excluded from the executable strategy roster.

## Idea and objective

Reconstruct a strategy-tester performance report from an existing transaction log; it evaluates executed decisions rather than generate new ones.

## How it works

- Parse pasted CSV transactions once, build trade objects and sort them chronologically.
- For the chart instrument, map logged transactions to the next bar's time interval and submit limit orders at the recorded fill price.
- The broker emulator is used as a reporting container. Its replay orders encode history; they are not predictions or an autonomous trading policy.

## Documented rules and trade lifecycle

- Required documented columns are Symbol, Side, Qty, Fill Price and Closing Time.
- Changing the chart instrument selects the corresponding transactions when the CSV includes multiple instruments.
- The author assumes the real fill price lies inside the relevant historical bar range so the replay limit order can execute. That assumption must be checked.

## Parameters and stated settings

- A single text input holds the CSV. The chart symbol and timeframe affect the reconstructed report.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Timezone mistakes, bar mapping, mismatched instrument identifiers or fills outside the bar can distort or omit replayed transactions.
- Limit-order replay may fail to preserve real fill sequencing, partial fills, costs and realized accounting. Compare against the original log.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- The complete CSV parser, instrument matching, timezone conversion, position accounting and fee treatment are absent from the saved code field.

### E1: purpose

> This script is a special strategy that parses transactions in csv format from Paper Trading (and it will also work for other brokers) and “plays” them. As a result, we get a Performance Report for a specific instrument based on our real trades in Paper or another broker.

> leaving only: Side, Qty, Fill Price, Closing Time.

### E3: replay

> At the beginning of the calculation, we parse the csv once, create trade objects (Trade) and sort them in chronological order. Next, on each bar, we check whether we have trades for the time period of the next bar. If there are, we place a limit order for each trade, with limit price == Fill Price of the trade. Here, we assume that if the trade is real, its execution price will be within the bar range, and the Pine strategy engine will execute this order at the specified limit price.

## Idea and objective

Zeiierman Trend Pressure separates fast local pressure, persistent range-based trend and a candle-structure pressure core. It aims to distinguish a short pullback within an intact trend from broader deterioration, then track sustained extreme states through confirmation and release hysteresis. The author suggests trend-following alignment and treating pressure release as a possible reversal cue, explicitly warning that an active box alone is not an entry. ## How it works

- Normalize close within recent range and blend with a stochastic transformation to form EMA-smoothed Z-Pulse.
- Blend fast/trend/macro range readings and adapt persistence according to agreement/efficiency.
- Combine candle location, body, wick and impulse into reactive/regime Pressure Core; enter extreme states when pulse/trend align and release after separate confirmation rules.

## Outputs and intended use

- Three pressure views, core colors, dots, event triangles and active-state price boxes support trend/continuation/reversal context.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Scale 0 to -100. Pulse blend weights 0.72/0.28; trend weights 0.10/0.18/0.72.
- Core weights close/mean/body/wick/impulse 0.42/0.23/0.13/0.12/0.10; impulse spans five bars.
- Range/stochastic/smoothing lengths, persistence, exhaustion zone, sensitivity and regime weight are configurable.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Reversal release indicates weakening pressure, not a guaranteed price reversal.
- Sensitivity changes state stability and may create inconsistent behavior at low settings.

# Logarithmic Moving Average (LMA) [QuantAlgo]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Logarithmic Moving Average converts a logarithmically weighted price average into a trend-quality-adjusted slope oscillator. Its aim is to favor recent data while distinguishing cleaner directional movement from weaker drift. Optional log-return momentum further amplifies agreement; this is a designed weighting rule rather than evidence of statistical significance or higher continuation probability.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** LMA/ten-bar slope is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Weight closing prices by inverse squared log of age plus steepness, normalize into an average and measure its percentage slope over a fixed lag.
- Multiply slope by a half-base/half-R-squared trend-quality factor; optionally apply a same-direction momentum multiplier.
- For ages i=0..N-1,w_i=1/log(i+steepness)^2;LMA=sum(w_i*close[i])/sum(w_i). Require i+steepness>0 and not1. Slope=100*(LMA-LMA[10])/LMA[10] for nonzero lagged value. Final quality/momentum/smoothing excluded.

## Outputs and intended use

- Positive/negative values convey bullish/bearish momentum, zero crosses suggest regime transitions and threshold zones flag stronger readings; gradient/bar colors and latest classification aid inspection.
- Usable scope: LMA/ten-bar slope. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Slope uses a ten-bar lag. Long/short thresholds default +0.5/-0.5; source calls ±1 strong extremes. Period, steepness, smoothing and momentum controls lack full defaults.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Analytical: log weights need valid domain/normalization, trend-quality weighting is not calibrated predictive confidence, and optional amplification changes scale.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- R-squared calculation window, steepness bounds, momentum annualization/multiplier, smoothing and full defaults are not fully disclosed.

# Historical backtester: implementation and recovery handoff

**Evidence date:** 2026-11-09. **Status:** the historical-data and result-storage foundation is implemented and in use. The complete, production-qualified multi-asset and multi-bot backtester is **not finished**. This handoff describes the work performed in this session, how to operate what exists, the decisions behind it, and the remaining implementation. Existing UI, forward testing, signal generation, and orchestration are separate workstreams.

Start with the local [market-data catalog](/Users/mitch/.local/share/solmargintrader/historical-data-1128/CATALOG.md) and its per-dataset receipts for current paths and exact coverage. Those files and the datasets are not in the public source repository. The snapshot inventories are as-of records, not a live freshness service. This document records a point-in-time state and must be rechecked before use.

## Scope and decisions

The owner selected BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP, HYPE, DOGE, LINK, NEAR, SUI, AVAX, JitoSOL, KMNO, USDC and XMR; the primary market is SOL/USDC. The goal is reliable historical strategy and bot replay, with timestamped trades, balances, P&L, fees, realistic adverse conditions and recoverable results. Backtesting remains offline and simulation-only. Its output describes a model of past data, not proof of future returns.

The design separates **network collection**, **validation and storage**, **simulation**, and **result archival**. This keeps a replay from fetching mutable data mid-run, lets inputs be checked independently, and avoids interfering with the active forward-testing and UI owners. SQLite was selected for this local workload: it supplies indexed timestamp keys, transactions, and a consistent backup API without running a server. The trade-off is that the current full-snapshot verification and result loading can be expensive; a multi-gigabyte performance and memory qualification remains open.

The records use UTC bar-open timestamps and a declared interval, instrument, quote and venue. `SOL-USDC`, `SOL-USD`, and `SOL-USDT` are distinct instruments; prices from different venues are also distinct. A source label supplied at import is an operator assertion, not proof that a source is authentic. Stablecoins are not converted at a presumed peg, and a centralized-exchange candle is not evidence of an on-chain trade. Missing observations are recorded, never silently forward-filled. Checksums detect byte changes but do not prove that an exchange's data was complete, historically available at decision time, or economically representative.

## Work performed and delivery

1. Ran the explicitly requested prompt optimization and wrote the [integrity implementation plan](superpowers/plans/2026-11-09-backtester-integrity.md). The [prompt review](superpowers/plans/2026-11-09-backtester-prompt-review.md) records the actual scope: structural reviews were performed, but the full optimizer manifest, mechanical acceptance gate, behavioral comparison and telemetry were not produced. The subsequent SOL/USDC clarification was not independently re-audited. Do not call the full optimizer protocol formally clean.
2. Added and tested immutable, content-addressed OHLCV snapshots; an adapter to the existing loader; an atomic run-artifact archive; and SQLite backup/verification. Added explicit USDC and USDT accounting for matching snapshot-backed **spot** runs. The main foundation merged in [PR 174](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/pull/174), with its continuation record in [PR 176](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/pull/176).
3. Measured existing history, retained raw source pages and original files, and created source-labelled daily snapshots for all 14 assets where a contiguous series was available. Existing daily files with unknown venue or quote remain distinct; the snapshot loader refuses an unknown venue. Early BTC/ETH daily attempts that failed continuity were retained separately, not promoted as complete.
4. Added the resumable KuCoin minute collector and gap-aware indexed CSV segments in [PR 177](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/pull/177). Recorded a verified recent snapshot per asset, deeper SOL/USDC and KMNO/USDT data, gap ledgers and quarantined suspect inputs.
5. Used Firecrawl to locate primary Jito and OKX documentation and Kraken's downloadable historical archive. Retrieved selected Kraken archive members by HTTP range, normalized and indexed 14 markets, and backed up the acquired datasets to a private GitHub repository. The research and backup record merged in [PR 178](https://github.com/mithudso/solmargintrader/pull/178).
6. Executed real-data simulations as **smoke tests**, not profitability claims. One four-strategy daily SOL/USDC run covered 1,631 bars with a 70/30 split; one minute snapshot smoke covered 43,200 bars; a later one-day SOL/USDC buy-and-hold smoke used the deep snapshot. The one-day run covered 1,440 bars, used assumed 6 bps fee and 2 bps slippage, and was archived as run `d37b58aea6dffecf1fa744127ce1cb67b7a3a7503dae68e0fd9668a0ea659137`. These assumptions are not a verified historical fee schedule.

## Components and data flow

| Component | Role and boundary |

| `backtester/core/kucoin_history.py` | Explicit 1-minute spot collector. Each fixed window stores the raw response bytes, SHA-256, normalized candles and page metadata in a single SQLite transaction. The engine itself does not fetch. |

## Time and simulation semantics

`kucoin_history.collect` and `kucoin_history.read_range` accept **half-open** `[start, end)` epoch-second bounds. Its `audit_store` ledger also reports exclusive ends. In contrast, `segmented_history.read_range` and `history_store.read_history` use **inclusive** start and end bar-open timestamps. The CLI accepts dates as inclusive calendar dates; an intraday end only includes bars that have fully closed. Do not interchange these interfaces without converting and testing the boundary.

In `engine.py`, an existing perpetual position is checked for a liquidation at the current open first; scheduled open-price fills run next; borrow accrual and the bar's liquidation check follow; the strategy receives a `BarWindow` through the current bar; the engine schedules a later fill or, if explicitly configured with `fill_delay=0`, fills at this bar's close; then it marks equity. The default delay is one bar. A zero-delay close fill is a distinct modeling assumption and must not be described as a next-bar fill. `BarWindow` limits a strategy's exposed history, and tests include a deliberately cheating strategy, but broader cross-asset joins, feature availability, training labels and every bot adapter still require independent prefix-invariance tests.

The snapshot-backed spot CLI permits `--quote USD`, `USDC`, or `USDT` when the snapshot instrument matches; stablecoin accounting is refused for non-snapshot inputs and perp mode. Perp funding/borrow and chain fees must not be inferred from unrelated spot candles. No architecture here independently reconstructs historical order-book depth, real fill probabilities, chain-specific execution, or all bot state transitions.

## Streaming oracle or periodic refresh?

Use both as complementary inputs. A continuous stream can capture higher-frequency observations and fresh evidence for forward testing; scheduled source refreshes provide historical backfill, corrected bars and recovery after disconnects. Persist raw stream events with event time, receive/availability time, source, market, sequence where available and explicit gaps. Validate and reconcile each time range against an appropriate historical source, then publish immutable, content-addressed snapshots. A backtest pins one snapshot and runs offline, so a new quote or correction cannot change a run in progress. A correction produces a new revision, leaving the old run reproducible. Streaming alone cannot reconstruct years before recording began; periodic OHLCV alone cannot reconstruct the actual book or every fill.

The existing `soltui/pricefeed.py` recorder is an integration candidate, not a reason to start a second recorder. Its source code records Coinbase `level2_batch` book tops and ticker last prices in gzip JSONL and maintains a recorder lock. Confirm the loaded service, health, products, timestamps, retention, outages and actual SOL/USDC coverage before relying on it. The project previously found that ticker bid/ask can remain stale between trades on thin pairs; book-top freshness and feed sequence/reconnection checks matter. A generic oracle may publish a reference or aggregated price rather than the executable venue price, volume or order book; identify its actual source and semantics before using it as fill evidence. Do not route live streaming into the offline replay loop or infer historical fills from a reference price.

This is a design recommendation, not an implemented integration. Define who owns the recorder and ingestion interface with the forward-testing and signal sessions, then test reconnect, duplicates, ordering, gaps, late arrivals, clock skew, backfill, snapshot publication and backup before enabling it.

1. **Source coverage and revisions.** Build a maintained source registry with exact instrument IDs, venue, quote, chain/mint when applicable, timestamp semantics, availability/retrieval times, license and version. Measure coverage per market, refresh completed bars incrementally, retain raw provider revisions, and report provider gaps separately from unfetched windows and verified no-trade periods. Investigate Binance and other sources without silently substituting their prices. Back up every new revision.
2. **Storage and performance.** Add a stable query/inventory interface over snapshots and segments. Support immutable correction revisions and atomic publication. Benchmark representative multi-year, multi-asset ingestion and reads, peak memory, disk usage, crash recovery and concurrent access. Full snapshot rehash on every read is safe but potentially costly. Verify permissions, isolation, independent backup restoration and recovery after partial writes.
3. **Causality.** Define event time, publication/availability time and decision time separately. Test that changing future data cannot alter earlier decisions across indicators, cross-asset joins, resampling, normalizers, labels, training and strategy adapters. Check bar close boundaries and any provider corrections. Reject unobservable future information.
4. **Ledger and execution fidelity.** Establish a canonical per-order/fill ledger with venue, chain when supported, timestamp, quote/base amounts, balances, fees and explicit valuation. Reconcile realized and unrealized P&L, equity and positions against hand-calculated fixtures. Add historical fee tiers, spreads, liquidity and borrow/funding evidence only when actually sourced. Define partial fills, latency, failed transactions and intrabar ambiguity; refuse unsupported models rather than label assumptions as facts.
5. **Bots and adverse scenarios.** Inventory actual strategy and bot contracts and route each to its compatible engine. Preserve the grid-extension economic parity. Add deterministic seeded outage, latency, slippage, gap, failed-fill and partial-fill scenarios, with explicit assumptions and recorded seeds. OHLCV alone cannot reconstruct depth or all on-chain behavior.
6. **Results and validity.** Bind the exact source revision, snapshot IDs, code revision, dependencies, strategy configuration, cost model, seed, timestamps and artifacts to a run. Add realistic benchmarks, independent review and repeatability checks. Separate exploratory, in-sample and untouched out-of-sample periods; report selection bias, sample size, drawdowns and uncertainty rather than promising future profits.
7. **Integration and operations.** Agree a narrow, versioned history/result interface with the separate signal, forward-testing, UI and orchestration owners. Keep simulation offline and fail closed. Add scheduling only when explicitly designed, with monitoring, retry limits, integrity alerts, fresh GitHub backups and periodic independent restore drills. Avoid modifying other live sessions or their data stores.

reports record reviewed findings and residuals; this page records ongoing limitations.

### 2026-11-08 optimizer residuals

The bounded optimizer repaired 98 findings. Integrated upstream executor work closed two
more original residuals. It stopped at `BLIND-AUDIT-DISSENT` with 13 remaining findings
(seven High, six Medium). These include executor reduce-only admission; raw upstream error propagation; paper
fill ordering; historical triangle replay; research delay/selection/empty-table cases;
and Aero soak, conversion status and concurrent evidence updates. Passing tests do not
close these findings. See [the exact audit and scope](code-deep-optimizer-2026-11-08.md).
The review covered 50 primary sources of 261 at its audited base; final gate coverage
was partial on several files. Owner live-order acceptance remains unavailable.

---

## Extension — the money path

### No live order has ever been placed

The whole live path is unexercised against a real venue. Every test and the headless dry
run go through fakes. Do not present any live-path behaviour as working; read the
**Verification status** section of `extension/README.md` before extending it.

**Consequence:** the first real order is the first real test.

### Trigger contract has offline fixtures, not live acceptance

History pagination and cancellation paths are checked against current public documentation
and offline fixtures. No authenticated wallet response or live order has been accepted.
Incomplete execution valuation, costs or timing holds new planning. The bundled session
signer has no independent transaction-intent verifier, so automatic Trigger writes stay
blocked. See `docs/jupiter-trigger-contract.md`.

Unknown submissions retain their journal hold and are never automatically replayed.

### Fee attribution is unconfirmed

`src/jupiter/attribution.js` has never been checked against a real fill. Reported P&L may
attribute fees differently from the venue.

### Incomplete transport observability

Persistent intent/tick events do not replace per-request transport logs. Jupiter
request/outcome metadata and some failure paths remain outside a common sink.
`docs/logging.md` and the dated code-optimizer report distinguish verified changes from
remaining coverage. Do not infer a complete request history from a tick summary.

### The real-browser e2e covers loading and dry-run only

`npm run e2e` loads the unpacked extension in Chrome for Testing and checks install state, the
service worker, popup, dashboard, a dry-run plan and tick, the rails and secret handling. It never
arms or signs and stubs the network, so it is not evidence about live orders. The headless dry run
(`tools/dryrun.js --ticks 8 --osc 6 --offline 100`) remains the economics gate. Branded Chrome
cannot load an extension from the command line, so the e2e needs Chrome for Testing or Chromium.

---

## Backtester and research

### Historical research artifacts need fresh producer evidence

Sweep and redundancy selection requires current discovery-only provenance, source hashes and
complete prerequisite artifacts. Legacy, tampered or full-history selection artifacts refuse.
The optimizer did not regenerate historical sweeps or change published historical figures.


### The cached data is a snapshot with no freshness contract

`data/` is gitignored and regenerable, and nothing in a CSV records when it was fetched.
`research/decide.py` prints the decision bar's age in bars and says `STALE` past two, which
is a mitigation, not a fix — the underlying cache still has to be refetched by hand.

A historical check found bars behind wall clock despite a current file mtime. That
snapshot is not a current freshness assertion; inspect timestamps/checksum in the
readout for the cache you are actually using.

### Historical `data/SOL_1h.csv` snapshot had two gaps larger than one bar

Reading that snapshot required the loader's `--allow-gaps`. The simulators now refuse
irregular cadence even with that loader flag: missing time is not measured carry or
annualization evidence. Use a complete cache before running a simulation.
The largest gap is 21,600s where 3,600s was expected, after epoch 1761404400. Any
statistic computed across that boundary spans a hole.

### `data/JLP_spot.csv` is not a bar series

One row, columns `timestamp,iso,mint,usd_price,source` — a Jupiter price snapshot from
`core/archive_price.py`, not OHLCV. Bar tools refuse it by naming the missing columns,
which is correct behaviour, but the filename invites the mistake.

### Coinbase is the primary bar and trade-tick source

Binance is geo-blocked from here. That means a single vendor's outage or history revision
affects refreshed price caches, and Coinbase's non-OHLCV row ordering has to be handled
on the way in. Signed funding history uses Hyperliquid with a shallow OKX cross-check;
that does not provide an independent bar history.

### No registry default emits a short

Every registered strategy's default parameters are long-or-flat; only
`ma_crossover(short_when_below=True)` can go short, and nothing constructs it that way.
So `research/decide.py --allow-short` widens the stated exposure bound and changes nothing
else, and `HOLD-SHORT` is unreachable through that CLI. A test asserts this, so a future
shorting default will fail rather than quietly make the help text wrong.

### The full readout is slow on hourly data

Every strategy is replayed over the whole series, so cost is bars × strategies: about 18
seconds for 25 strategies over 8,823 hourly bars. It announces itself on stderr rather than
looking hung. Not a bug — the price of engine parity.

---

## soltui

### Manual Jupiter V2 is preview-only

The manual path has structural transaction checks, but independent economic verification is
incomplete. Submit and quick-submit refuse before key loading, signing or sending. Unsigned
previews require a known input valuation; history and chain reconciliation remain available.
Historical unknown submissions stay blocked until chain proof resolves them. No elapsed-time
rule clears that uncertainty. This limitation does not change separately armed Coinbase orders.

### Legacy recorder Stop metadata

Recorder Stop uses a nonce bound to the active recorder lock and never sends a signal to a PID
from a file. A recorder started by an older version without this metadata cannot be stopped through
that fallback. The command reports the refusal instead of risking an unrelated process.

### The packaging paths have no tests

Unit tests cover signal derivation, state, rendering, launchers and service/plist helpers.
The installed py2app alias bundle and launchd behavior still require acceptance; `soltui/README.md` lists those
checks.

### It is an alias build, so it references this checkout

`setup_app.py` runs `py2app -A`, so the installed bundle points at
the checkout from which it was built. Move the repo and the app breaks — rebuild with
`soltui-service build`. A full freeze would have to embed pandas and numpy.

### Never install a bundle built from a worktree

`.claude/worktrees/` gets deleted, and login startup then fails silently.
`soltui-service install` refuses a worktree target and warns on a worktree source.

### Quit does not stop it

`KeepAlive` necessarily overrides the menu-bar Quit item. The real off switch is removing
`~/Library/Application Support/soltui/supervise.enabled`, which is what
`soltui-service stop` does.

### A py2app launch-error dialog keeps the process alive

So a liveness check alone will report a healthy agent while the app is showing an error
dialog and doing nothing. Check the log, not just the process.

---

## Liquidity

Public RPC and market-data availability can prevent scoring or simulation. Provider
comparison is read-only and includes explicitly labelled quoted rows. A successful
simulation does not establish that a live transaction landed. Preserve partial-sequence
state and receipts before any retry. See `liquidity/README.md` and `liquidity/STATE_FILES.md`.

## Repo-level

### `docs/external-calls.md` is not machine-checked

`scripts/check_docs.py` validates test counts and index paths, but nothing diffs the
external-call inventory against the source. A new `fetch` call will not fail the build for
being undocumented.

### Captured artifacts are checked in

`build/`, `dist/`, `jup.ag/`, `jup.ag.zip`, `pagesource/` and `tradingskilllist` are
scratch and captured material. Nothing imports them. `.gitattributes` marks them vendored
or generated so they do not distort language statistics, but they still inflate the clone.
