# Grover Llorens Activator Strategy Analysis

Version: 1.1.0 (2026-11-08). Delta: v1.0.0 to v1.1.0; explain the complete publication mechanism, objective and source gaps.

**Classification:** trading-strategy. Spec-only; no runnable repository implementation or measured performance.

## Idea and objective

Test whether a price-converging trailing activator can identify reversals early enough to trade trends, while examining the false reversals created by that same convergence.

## How it works

- The Grover Llorens Activator is described as a trailing-stop-like line inspired by Parabolic SAR.
- Closing-price crosses determine direction. Each fresh signal closes the previous position and reverses exposure using constant sizing.
- The central trade-off is early reversal detection versus premature crosses as the indicator converges toward price; a steady trend can itself induce an unwanted crossing.

## Documented rules and trade lifecycle

- Enter long when closing price crosses above the activator.
- Enter short when closing price crosses below the activator.
- Close the old position when a new directional signal occurs; the described experiment does not add a separate money-management overlay.
- The author uses a 1-hour timeframe, length 480 and multiplier 14 for the reported comparison.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Analysis settings: length 480, multiplier 14, 1-hour bars and constant position size.
- The compared market examples use 1,000 EURUSD units and one BTCUSD unit. These are source experiment settings, not repository defaults.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Convergence toward price can force false signals even in otherwise clean trends.
- The author notes that adding spread would make the EURUSD example negative. Reported gross figures are not reproduced or upgraded to evidence here.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- The complete activator recurrence and initialization are not captured; the referenced indicator must be recovered for numerical parity.
- The source does not establish a complete cost model or a robust out-of-sample evaluation.

## Evidence and interpretation

The explanation above synthesizes the complete saved author description. Rules and numerical settings are attributed to that description; failure-mode analysis is our interpretation. > The Innovation Adaptive Kalman Filter (IAKF) is a modern implementation of the Kalman filter that uses its own prediction errors to detect abnormal measurements and adapt its measurement-noise estimate.

> Traditionally, a Kalman filter balances its predictions and observations using predefined noise assumptions that require careful calibration. More recent research has shown how the filter can use its own prediction errors to detect abnormal measurements and adapt its measurement-noise estimate [1]. In self-driving vehicle navigation, this helps reduce the influence of disturbed GPS measurements and limit positioning errors.

> The TradingView community is also no stranger to Kalman filtering. There is already a wide variety of implementations, including price smoothers, trend overlays, oscillators, volume tools, and adaptive bands. In our review of 100 TradingView publications, nine clusters emerged based on similarities in their technical descriptions, as shown in Figure 3. Representative examples include CRYPTIK1’s Algorithmic Kalman Filter, a conventional price smoother with fixed noise settings, and Zeiierman’s Trend Strength Oscillator, which offers optional adjustments based on volume or price range.

> Misses below the threshold: The forecast errors increase, but no error is large enough for the filter to flag the bar as an outlier. No dots appear, and damping stays at zero in this example. Only the blue meter value increases. The filter continues to follow the price changes.

> Single outlier: In this example, one bar crosses the Unusual-Move Threshold. The filter flags the bar as an outlier and marks its candle. The gray curve moves down as the filter reduces its response to the price change. The blue meter remains relatively low because forecast errors on nearby bars are calm. The filter treats this bar as a single unusual event.

## Idea and objective

Volume Footprint estimates how realtime volume is distributed across price intervals inside a candle. ## How it works

- Separate candles into equally spaced price intervals using ATR-based or manual width and accumulate tick-data volume into them.
- Draw the completed footprint on confirmation of a new bar, with selectable box/gradient/regular styles.
- With supplied tick price/volume and caller bin width/origin/edges,assign ticks to price intervals and sum volume. Percent mode=100*bin_volume/candle_total for positive total. This unsigned histogram does not use candle direction as aggressor attribution; automatic width/feed behavior excluded.

- Inspect high-participation intervals within candles; gradient darkness corresponds to larger relative volume and trend colors reflect candle direction.
- Usable scope: Manual-width tick-volume histogram. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

- Method controls ATR versus manual width, Width supplies ATR period or interval size, and As Percent normalizes to total candle volume. Default display uses colored boxes.

## Documented inputs and source details

> Volume is the total amount of assets traded in a specific period of time. The 24-hour Volume indicator is used to measure the total volume of a symbol traded in the last 24 hours, expressed as in currency. It can be used to measure the market's interest in a particular symbol.

> To calculate the 24-hour volume, the indicator uses data from different timeframes; the timeframes chosen depend on the timeframe on the main chart:

> The indicator calculates the sum of the volume for the last X bars of the lower timeframe, where X is the number of bars that opened in the last 24 hours. The indicator works with calendar hours regardless of the symbol session, so if there has been no past trades for 24 hours or more (e.g., on the first Monday bar on a symbol that is only traded on business days), 24-hour volume can be equal to the regular volume data.

> The indicator always displays the 24-hour volume converted to the currency selected in the indicator's inputs. This means that, if the exchange presents its volume data in base currency (e.g., when for BTCUSD, the volume represents the number of BTC traded), the 24-hour Volume indicator converts the base volume into currency volume by multiplying the volume by the price on the chart. The 'Price Source' input can be used to select which specific chart value will be used for this conversion.

> The volume can be additionally converted into a currency different from the one on the chart. This can be done by switching the 'Target Currency' input from Default to a different currency.

## Idea and objective

Realtime 5D Profile accumulates live chart updates into price-level distributions of volume or update counts. It encodes level activity, directional imbalance and age, offering an evolving view of where observed participation occurred. Unlike a historical profile, it starts when loaded and loses its accumulated state when refreshed or re-executed. The source carefully distinguishes chart updates from exchange transactions, so its tick label must not be interpreted as a complete trade tape on aggregated charts.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Independent aggregate activity counts: for ordered chart updates, compare price with the previous update; increment UpCount on higher price, DownCount on lower price, and carry the last known direction when unchanged. Totals are UpCount+DownCount and delta UpCount−DownCount. Use a selected timeframe reset; seed from the first observed price and begin counting once a comparison/known polarity exists. This explicit first-update exclusion is a caller convention because source initialization is not stated.
- Assign each update to up/down using price versus the preceding update, retaining the last direction when unchanged.
- Bin updates around dynamic price levels; rebalance historical updates when the profile range changes. Line lengths scale to the largest level and age comes from average update times.
- Render double-sided down/up profiles or single-sided totals/deltas; reset by selected timeframes or trend changes.

## Outputs and intended use

- Compare participation and recency with line width, thickness, totals, tooltips and Data Window values.
- No alerts are included; the author suggests small-timeframe use with infrequent chart changes.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Four line thicknesses encode age. An example 20-level double profile needs 42 labels against a 500-label limit.
- The author reports handling upwards of 60K updates per profile, not a guaranteed capacity.
- Choose tick/update-count mode and a timeframe reset (chart timeframe resets each new bar). Caller first-update policy is explicitly excluded until direction is known; this is not claimed as default-code parity.

- Live-only state cannot be reconstructed from historical OHLCV.
- Uptick/downtick classification can misclassify true aggressor flow; prolonged accumulation may exhaust memory.

## 2. What was delivered and why

### Request and architecture

The owner asked for one durable application rather than another independent script: defaults for easy creation/control, five strategy families, honest backtests, blind parameter judging, forward paper operation, monitoring, learning and diagnostics, with eventual management of SolTUI and extension bots.

The initial prompt was optimized and executed as a design task. The approved design chose a Python application with one command registry, immutable specifications, SQLite journals, one explicit supervisor, independent workers, pure shared simulation and adapters to existing owners. The owner then approved implementation. Delivery proceeds through eight milestones so that useful controls and recovery arrive before research automation or live operation.

The UI control-room findings were incorporated as backend contracts. A future UI consumes manager state and receipts. It must not add another supervisor, recorder, optimizer, signer or strategy implementation.

### Decisions that shape future maintenance

| Decision | Reason | Consequence or cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Separate stable bot UUID, configuration revision/hash, runtime ID, owner and generation | A saved strategy is different from one executing session | Copies cannot replace workers or allocate a second funded account implicitly |
| Package canonical backtester code as a local dependency | An installed service cannot rely on a temporary checkout or copied algorithm | Build/install both local distributions together; changes need shared-engine parity checks |
| Keep legacy execution with its current owner | The manager cannot fence clients that ignore its protocol | Older owners remain inspectable but guarded controls refuse until verified capability exists |
| Compare and deduplicate inside the legacy owner | A client GET followed by raw POST has a race and an ambiguous retry window | The owner implements the versioned `bots.manager_control` protocol and durable intent journal |
| Use null with a reason for missing observations | Missing price, fee, heartbeat or P&L is not zero or a successful measurement | Consumers must preserve nullability and separate state dimensions |
| Bind receipts to original acceptance context | Later worker generations must not rewrite the meaning of an earlier command | Schema-1 receipts without provable context retain their IDs/bodies but refuse replay; explicit reconciliation is needed |
| Label Coinbase replay as a reference | A target Jupiter specification cannot certify historical route/fill economics | Reference results remain ineligible for live promotion |
| Keep configuration immutable | Installing new defaults or editing a draft must not silently alter a running account | `edit` stages a saved revision; `apply` separately verifies a stopped zero-exposure boundary and archives prior evidence |

`BOT` accepts a UUID or unique display name. An external identity is such as `soltui-local:grid`. The optional `--effective` flag is accepted for config inspection; the returned saved snapshot already includes effective values. `status --why` supplies an explanation within JSON. There is no compact table, CSV export or all-bots control command in this release.

Ordinary command responses have exactly `schema_version`, `request_id`, `ok`, `data`, `error`. The top-level invocation ID differs from a durable control request ID inside a receipt. Preserve the control receipt's request ID when reconciling a lost response. Exit codes: 0 success, 2 invalid input/identity conflict, 3 unavailable capability/input/owner, 4 operational/store/integrity failure. Errors are sanitized and never repeat arbitrary submitted values.

Per-bot receipts distinguish `acknowledged`, `pending`, `skipped`, `failed` and
`unknown`. Acknowledgment does not prove termination or closed exposure. Unknown
outcomes require reconciliation; they never authorize automatic resubmission.
If a legacy owner has no numeric configuration revision, its receipt uses
`config_revision=null` with
`config_revision_unavailable_reason=owner_does_not_version_configurations` and
binds the separately observed configuration hash. It does not invent revision 1.

Common defaults are `mode=paper`, `armed=false`, `venue=jupiter`, `bar_seconds=60`, `capital_usd=1000.0`, `timezone=UTC`, `lot_method=FIFO`, wrapped SOL mint `So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112` and USDC mint `EPjFWdd5AufqSSqeM2qN1xzybapC8G4wEGGkZwyTDt1v`. Only that target mint pair is accepted. Capital is virtual. No observed price, fee, balance, credential or token decimal is fabricated as a default.

`--set armed=false` retains boolean false; `--set deadband_bps=0` retains numeric zero. Duplicate/unknown keys, wrong types, nonfinite values and unsafe ranges refuse before saving. Shared values must match strategy ID/version, venue, both mints, bar duration and execution model exactly. Explicit overrides win and become manual pins. Expected at EOF: `waiting/reference_input_exhausted`, complete cursor and an independently advancing heartbeat. That is healthy historical replay completion, not fresh forward testing. After stop, confirm stopped intent, released worker lock and observed stopped state separately from the receipt. A stop persists even with no supervisor; observed termination can remain pending until the owner is present. Lots, fills and exposure remain visible.

Use an explicit UUID in `--request-id` when a caller must recover a particular control acknowledgment. Generate it once, retain it and use the same operation/identity for receipt inspection. Changed simulator source or NumPy identity invalidates a saved input's engine pin. Do not edit hashes to force recovery or silently treat recomputed results as the original run. Reconcile the old run and create separately attributed evidence under the new engine. Downgrading an executable does not reverse a database migration; retain backups and verify the old version against an isolated restore first.

### Back up consistently

There is no backup/restore CLI. The specification store exposes a backup descriptor through its Python API. Use SQLite `Connection.backup` for each existing database; copying a live database file is not the supported method. Python's SQLite connection context manager does not close the connection, so close it explicitly or use `contextlib.closing`.

1. Prevent new control/registration commands during the backup window. Stop requested work if it must stay stopped; record receipts and observe termination.
2. Stop/uninstall the exact manager service or close its foreground daemon so it cannot restart during the copy. Check the returned label and lock observation. Quiesce external-owner control writers separately if backing up their state.
3. Back up all existing manager databases together: specifications, runtime and external controls. Keep schema versions, package/dependency versions, file hashes and source descriptors in a manifest. Individual SQLite backups are consistent per database, not an atomic snapshot across databases; quiescing writers establishes the cross-store boundary.
4. Preserve original raw recordings and related owner journals for audit/reproduction. The runtime stores its pinned derivative but does not make missing original source evidence complete. Store backups outside source control with restricted permissions.
5. Restore into a new isolated `SOLBOT_HOME`, not over the active original. Check SQLite `quick_check`, schemas, hashes, `list`, `config` and `status --why` before any daemon/service starts. Saved running intent remains running intent in a restore.

A minimal per-file copy, after writers are quiesced, is this Python pattern. It performs no service or restore action and copies only the named default-home databases into a new timestamped private directory:

```sh
/Users/mitch/.venvs/solbot/bin/python - <<'PY'
from contextlib import closing
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path
import sqlite3

source = Path('/Users/mitch/.config/solbot')
if not (source / 'manager.sqlite3').is_file():
    raise SystemExit('No initialized manager store; no backup made.')
stamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime('%Y%m%dT%H%M%S%fZ')
destination = Path('/Users/mitch/.local/state/solbot-backups') / stamp
destination.mkdir(mode=0o700, parents=True, exist_ok=False)
manifest = {'source': str(source), 'created_utc': stamp, 'databases': []}
for name in ('manager.sqlite3', 'runtime.sqlite3', 'controls.sqlite3'):
    original = source / name
    if not original.is_file():
        continue
    copied = destination / name
    with closing(sqlite3.connect(original.as_uri() + '?mode=ro', uri=True)) as reader:
        with closing(sqlite3.connect(copied)) as writer:
            reader.backup(writer)
            assert writer.execute('PRAGMA quick_check').fetchone()[0] == 'ok'
            schema = writer.execute('PRAGMA user_version').fetchone()[0]
    copied.chmod(0o600)
    manifest['databases'].append({
        'name': name, 'schema': schema,
        'sha256': hashlib.sha256(copied.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
    })
manifest_path = destination / 'manifest.json'
manifest_path.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2) + '\n')
manifest_path.chmod(0o600)
print(destination)
PY
```

The snippet is a copy primitive, not an automatic quiesce/restore/migration system. Add the separately captured application versions, raw-source descriptors and owner journal references to the backup record. There is no supported command to discard a held run's inventory or unknown submission history.

### Troubleshoot from observable state

| Observation/code | Meaning | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `runtime_not_available` | Draft lacks registered reference input, or the new strategy runtime is unavailable | Inspect strategy capability and descriptor; do not assume start created a worker |
| Pending start with no supervisor lock | Durable intent was accepted but no runtime owner is observed | Inspect service status; explicitly run the correct home's daemon/service when intended |
| `waiting/reference_input_exhausted` | Immutable historical replay reached EOF | Retain that result; prepare a separate prospective descriptor/account for new observations |
| `heartbeat_stale`, `worker_not_observed`, `tick_stalled` | Separate process/progress observations failed | Read status/events, retained generation and source identity; let bounded recovery act and inspect repeated failures |
| `failed` after repeated failures | Retry budget exhausted | Investigate evidence; no blind reset or automated new-ID replacement |
| `corrupt_checkpoint` / `invalid_spec` | Integrity validation failed | Preserve databases, request IDs and raw evidence; use read-only inspection/isolated backup; fresh stop remains available |
| `input_unavailable` | Missing, stale, incomplete, incompatible or invalid declared data/costs | Inspect the descriptor and exact coverage; never guess missing values |
| `resource_limit` | A bounded admission/input/fill/request limit was reached | Inspect which limit; preserve the original history; no silent truncation |
| `incompatible_owner` | Public health/owner contract does not identify the required SolTUI service | Verify the correct endpoint/loaded owner; do not send a token to another service |
| `credentials_unavailable` | Required existing token is missing or unsafe | Repair the owner installation deliberately; never paste a credential into a bot spec |
| `expected_observation_required` / stale guard | Legacy control lacks matching observed context | Re-read the owner; occupied family slots span coins |
| `unknown/outcome_unknown` | Submit/intent acknowledgment is ambiguous | Reconcile read-only with the owner and preserve journals; never auto-retry |
| `invalid_receipt` on legacy replay | Original acceptance/request binding cannot be proven | Keep the row/ID; explicit reconciliation is needed; a fresh stop is a distinct supported operation |
| `stable_install_required` | Service command loaded source/editable/temporary code | Install reviewed regular packages into the stable environment |
| `service_unavailable` with retained definition | Registration/removal could not be confirmed | Inspect the exact service identity and reconcile; do not claim all workers stopped |

# Efficient Work [LucF]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Measure directional close-to-close displacement relative to an OHLC-based estimate of distance traveled. Efficient Work interprets efficient movement as sentiment strength independent of amplitude, then compares that oscillator across chart and higher timeframes.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Partly disclosed computation.** Exact high/low travel equation, the full coloring conditions, ATR periods and divergence/state update edge cases are absent.

- Exact high/low travel equation, the full coloring conditions, ATR periods and divergence/state update edge cases are absent.

## How it works

- Resulting work is signed close displacement divided by estimated travel through the high and low. Averaging produces the signal; an optional external series can replace the instantaneous oscillator.
- Chart, medium and highest-timeframe values can be plotted separately or combined by weighted average, including only available components. Relative context uses Donchian extrema and saved divergence levels.
- Divergence here means disagreement between the same bar’s direction and signal direction, not conventional pivot divergence. Subsequent movement relative to that saved level determines state; selected coloring conditions must all hold, optionally filtered by short ATR exceeding long ATR.

## Outputs and intended use

- Three selectable lines, divergence dots/levels, Donchian channel, state markers/background and Data Window values support context analysis.
- Alerts and an invisible BTE Signal correspond to displayed markers, letting a separate engine evaluate entries.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Seven average choices, periods, external centerline, two higher-timeframe selection methods/multiples/fixed options, component weights and coloring filters.
- Default aggregate weights are equal; chart value repaints by default while higher-timeframe values are described as non-repainting.

## Failure modes and caveats

- OHLC does not reveal actual tick travel. The author’s repaint controls are source claims, not verified behavior.
- Aggregate composition changes when higher-timeframe history becomes available, affecting historical comparability.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Exact high/low travel equation, the full coloring conditions, ATR periods and divergence/state update edge cases are absent.

## Data requirements

Required inputs: ohlcv.

- Map the minus-lag control to beta and plus-lag to alpha. Adjust their relative values to skew weights toward newer/older observations, or equal values for symmetric weights. Color the output from RSI calculated on the average.

- Reducing lag by emphasizing recent data generally changes noise response. Gradient RSI on a smoothed line is another derived measure, not independent confirmation.

## Idea and objective

Auto Fibonacci and Gann Combo automatically places retracements and fans from detected local extremes. It aims to supply potential support/resistance geometry without manually anchoring every set. A new opposite extreme is needed to confirm the preceding high/low, so automatic anchors inherently arrive late. The Gann component also tries to infer price/time scaling from successive peaks/troughs. That scaling matters more than a screen’s apparent angle; the description’s angle claims are theoretical context rather than proof that levels predict price reactions.

## Documented inputs and source details

> The Composite Manipulation Index (CMI) is a structural integrity tool that quantifies how chaotic or orderly current market conditions are, with the aim of detecting potentially manipulated or unstable environments. It blends two distinct mathematical models that assess price behavior in terms of both structural rhythm and predictability.

> This component assumes that ideal, low-manipulation price behavior resembles a smooth oscillation, such as a sine wave. It generates a synthetic sine wave using a user-defined period and compares it to actual price movement over an adaptive window. The error between the real price and this synthetic wave—normalized by price variance—forms the Sine-Based Manipulation Index. A high error indicates deviation from natural rhythm, suggesting structural disorder.

> Both components are calculated using an adaptive smoothing window based on the Average True Range (ATR). This allows the indicator to respond proportionally to market volatility. During high volatility, the analysis window expands to avoid over-sensitivity; during calm periods, it contracts for better responsiveness.

> The second component estimates how well current price can be predicted using recent price lags. A two-variable rolling linear regression is computed between the current price and two lagged inputs (close[1] and close[2]). If the predicted price diverges from the actual price, this error—also normalized by price variance—reflects unpredictability. High prediction error implies a more manipulated or erratic environment.

> CMI 0.3–0.7: Transitional zone. Caution or reduced risk may be warranted.

# Multi-Layer Volume Profile [BigBeluga]

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Multi-Layer Volume Profile compares where candle volume accumulates across nested historical windows. It aims to show accepted price regions, sparse-volume areas and overlapping points of control, giving discretionary support/resistance analysis a volume dimension. The distinct windows help a trader see whether a dominant level persists across longer and shorter contexts. The author suggests using profile shape for position-building or stop/entry consideration and signed volume as breakout confirmation. Those are qualitative applications; no exact trigger or trade-management system follows from them.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Equal-range bins, close-location volume assignment, maximum-bin POC and signed candle-volume sums define the principal profile. Boundary/tie conventions remain implementation caveats.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Find each window’s high/low, divide that range into equal price bins, and allocate each candle’s volume to the bin containing its close.
- Aggregate bin totals, identify the largest-volume bin as POC, and sum overall volume.
- Calculate delta by signing candle volume positive for bullish closes and negative for bearish closes.

## Outputs and intended use

- Profile polylines, thick blue POC lines, high/low references and total/delta labels expose volume structure.
- Overlapping POCs suggest confluence; sparse regions and signed delta provide discretionary context.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Up to four profiles use full, half, quarter and one-eighth of selected length.
- Bin count is configurable, trading granularity against smoothness; numeric defaults are absent.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Assigning an entire candle’s volume to its close is an approximation of traded volume by price.
- Candle-signed delta is not actual aggressor-side order flow, and a high-volume node does not guarantee support.

## Missing information and implementation boundary

- Rounding of nested windows, doji treatment, bin-edge rules, update timing and actionable entry/exit conditions are not supplied.

  senkou_b: {default: 52, type: int, desc: "leading span B period"}
  displacement: {default: 26, type: int, desc: "bars the cloud is projected forward"}
presets:
  short: {tenkan: 9, kijun: 26, senkou_b: 52, displacement: 26}
  medium: {tenkan: 9, kijun: 26, senkou_b: 52, displacement: 26}
  long: {tenkan: 18, kijun: 52, senkou_b: 104, displacement: 52}

# Ichimoku Cloud

> **Implemented in this session** from spec-only mechanism #21 of
> `research/STRATEGIES.md`. Its stated gap was "implementable now — needs code, not
> data", so the code was written and it was measured on the same 1,875 daily SOL bars
> and the same 70/30 split as every other measured card.
## What it is
Long while the close is above both leading spans of the cloud overhead.

## Equation
```
Tenkan_t  = (max(H, 9) + min(L, 9)) / 2
Kijun_t   = (max(H, 26) + min(L, 26)) / 2
SenkouA_t = (Tenkan_t + Kijun_t)/2      projected 26 bars FORWARD
SenkouB_t = (max(H,52) + min(L,52))/2   projected 26 bars FORWARD
target_t  = 1 if c_t > max(SenkouA, SenkouB) as projected onto t
```

## The displacement trap, and how this avoids it
The cloud sitting at the current bar was computed **`displacement` bars ago**.
Reading a span computed *at* the current bar as if it were the current cloud reads 26
bars of future data — the classic Ichimoku look-ahead error, and it produces
spectacular backtests.

This implementation slices history to what was visible `displacement` bars back and
compares that cloud against today's close. `test_advanced_strategies.py` asserts the
value used equals the cloud computed from the truncated slice **and** that it differs
from the full-history cloud, so the distinction is verified rather than assumed.

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/advanced.py::IchimokuCloud`.

## Measured on SOL

| Leg | Return | Sharpe | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-sample | +336.3% | 0.967 | — |
| **Out-of-sample** | **-33.3%** | **-0.531** | **11** |

For reference on the same split: buy-and-hold made **+565.2% (Sharpe 1.030)**
in-sample and **-70.8% (Sharpe -0.651)** out. That row reproduces the figure the
existing cards document exactly, which is how these new numbers are known to be
comparable to them.


The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: measured-oos.*

**The best-behaved loser among the trend mechanisms measured here.** -33.3% and a
-0.531 Sharpe out-of-sample on 11 trades, against buy-and-hold's -70.8%: it halved
the drawdown of simply holding, through a leg where every trend rule lost. The
displaced cloud is a genuinely conservative entry condition, and 11 trades clears
the evidence floor.

It is still a loss, and the mechanism carries six parameters with heavy component
overlap that no experiment here separated. "Lost less than holding" is the honest
ceiling on this claim.

## Caveats and limitations
- Six parameters; attribution between the components is untested.
- Only the price-vs-cloud condition is implemented. The Tenkan/Kijun cross and the
  Chikou confirmation, both part of the full system, are not.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy ichimoku --interval 1d
```

# Buy & Hold

## What it is
Fully invested, always. No signal, no exit.

## What it looks for
Nothing. It exists to be beaten. Any strategy that cannot beat it after costs is a
cost-generating machine wearing a strategy's clothes.

## Equation
```
target_exposure_t = 1.0     for all t
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/buy_and_hold.py`.

```python
def on_bar(self, history: BarWindow) -> float:
    return 1.0
```

## Parameters
None. That is the point — there is nothing to overfit, which is exactly why it is
the reference.

## Works when
The asset appreciates over the holding period. Structurally unbeatable on *return*
in a monotonic bull market, though not on drawdown.

## Fails when
Any sustained drawdown, because it has no exit. Measured max drawdown on full-sample
SOL daily: **-96.27%**.

## Backtest notes
This is the harness's known-answer test. With zero costs and `fill_delay=0`, total
return must equal `last_close / first_close - 1` **exactly**, to 12 decimal places.
If that identity ever breaks, the accounting is wrong and no other card in this
directory means anything. `backtester/tests/test_engine.py` asserts it.

## Pairs with
Nothing. It is the baseline. `backtester/cli.py` adds it to every run whether you
ask for it or not, deliberately.

## Measured on SOL
Full-sample daily: **+87.61%**, Sharpe 0.617, max drawdown -96.27%, 1 trade.
Walk-forward: **IS +565.2% (Sharpe 1.030) -> OOS -70.8% (Sharpe -0.651)**.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

It is the only card whose mechanism is not a claim — you hold the asset, and the
outcome is the asset's outcome. Rated **low** rather than very-low because SOL did
appreciate over the full sample (+87.61%), and no higher because a **-96.27%** max
drawdown is not survivable at size and the out-of-sample leg lost **70.8%**.
Everything else in this directory is judged against this row.

## Caveats and limitations
- A -96% drawdown is survivable on a spreadsheet and not survivable with leverage or
  with money you need.
- "Beat the baseline" is a weak claim when the baseline lost 71% out-of-sample. Losing
  less is not the same as making money.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy buy_and_hold --interval 1d
```

> The range is highlighted by an area on the chart. By default Start = 9000 and End = 10000, you might not have this amount of data in your chart, as such use the displayed bar index to select Start and End, then set the settings as default.

Linear Correlation Oscillator measures how closely an input series follows a linear sequence over a rolling window. # ATR-Normalised Position Sizing

> **Implemented in this session** from spec-only mechanism #28 of
> `research/STRATEGIES.md`. Its stated gap was "implementable now — needs code, not
> data", so the code was written and it was measured on the same 1,875 daily SOL bars
> and the same 70/30 split as every other measured card.
# ATR-Normalised Position Sizing

## What it is
A risk overlay, not a signal. Exposure is set so that `stop_atr_multiple` ATRs of
adverse movement costs `risk_per_trade` of the account.

## Equation
```
ATR_t          = Wilder smoothing of true range, period p
stop_fraction  = stop_atr_multiple * ATR_t / price
target_t       = min(1, risk_per_trade / stop_fraction)   if c_t > SMA(trend) else 0
```

## What this harness cannot model, stated plainly
**A real ATR stop exits intrabar at a price. Exposure here changes only at bar
boundaries**, so `stop_atr_multiple` sizes the position and never triggers an exit.
Any comparison against a stop-based system elsewhere therefore flatters that system.
The sizing half is what was measured; the stop half was not.

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/advanced.py::AtrSizedTrend`.

## Measured on SOL

| Leg | Return | Sharpe | Trades |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-sample | +5.8% | 0.377 | — |
| **Out-of-sample** | **-2.6%** | **-0.454** | **93** |

For reference on the same split: buy-and-hold made **+565.2% (Sharpe 1.030)**
in-sample and **-70.8% (Sharpe -0.651)** out. That row reproduces the figure the
existing cards document exactly, which is how these new numbers are known to be
comparable to them.


The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: measured-oos.*

**The smallest losses in the directory, in both legs** (+5.8% IS, -2.6% OOS) — and
that is the point rather than a disappointment. With `risk_per_trade` at 1% and SOL's
ATR, the sizing rule holds a very small position: it is risk-normalising, so on a
high-volatility asset it normalises down to near-nothing.

That makes this the one card whose *shape* behaved as designed. It did not lose much
because it was barely exposed, on 93 trades, which is the honest description of a
constant-risk rule applied to an asset far more volatile than the target implies.

Rated low, not very-low, because the mechanism is sound and untested in the
configuration that matters: as a **wrapper around a signal with an edge**. It has no
edge of its own and does not claim one — pairing it with something directional is the
open experiment, exactly as with `voltarget.md`.

## Caveats and limitations
- The stop is not modelled. Do not read this as a test of ATR stops.
- At 1% risk per trade the position is small enough that transaction costs dominate
  the result; 93 trades at 8 bps is meaningful against a 5.8% gross.
- Sizing on trailing ATR de-risks after volatility has already arrived.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy atr_sized --interval 1d
```

Williams %R (%R) is a momentum-based oscillator used in technical analysis, primarily to identify overbought and oversold conditions. The %R is based on a comparison between the current close and the highest high for a user defined look back period. %R Oscillates between 0 and -100 (note the negative values) with readings closer to zero indicating more overbought conditions and readings closer to -100 indicating oversold. Typically %R can generate set ups based on overbought and oversold conditions as well overall changes in momentum.

````text
%R = (Highest High - CurrentClose) / (Highest High - Lowest Low) x -100
````

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** risk-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Per Bak SOC constructs a macro fragility score from options-tail pricing, volatility regime, credit stress and put/call positioning. It uses the sandpile analogy to motivate vulnerability to cascades, rather than predicting the size or exact timing of a crash. The concrete implementation is a weighted normalized indicator basket; its scientific narrative and forward-looking/non-repainting claims are not independently validated by the description.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Raw tail and credit subscores is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Normalize tail, volatility, credit and positioning components with percentile ranks and absolute adjustments, then combine them with configurable weights.
- Tail uses SKEW; volatility uses VIX level/term-structure measures; credit uses LQD/HYG and TED; positioning uses put/call rank and normalized Z-score.
- C_tail=0.7*percentrank(SKEW,252)+0.3*((SKEW-115)/0.5). C_credit=0.65*percentrank(LQD/HYG,252)+0.35*(TED/0.75)*100. Require aligned source-unit inputs. No clipping/composite range is inferred; other components excluded.

- Usable scope: Raw tail and credit subscores. Other advertised outputs remain subject to the listed missing information.

- Default component weights are 0.34/0.26/0.18/0.22 and rank lookback is 252 days. Score regimes are Safe 0–39, Building 40–54, Elevated 55–69 and Critical 70–100.

> # Risk-Adjusted Momentum Oscillator (RAMO): Momentum Analysis with Integrated Risk Assessment

> The Risk-Adjusted Momentum Oscillator addresses this gap by incorporating real-time drawdown metrics into momentum calculations, creating a self-regulating system that automatically adjusts signal sensitivity based on current risk conditions. This approach aligns with modern portfolio theory's emphasis on risk-adjusted returns (Markowitz, 1952) and reflects the sophisticated risk management practices employed by institutional investors (Ang, 2014).

> Maximum drawdown, defined as the peak-to-trough decline in portfolio value, serves as a critical risk metric in professional portfolio management (Calmar, 1991). Research by Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin (2005) demonstrates that drawdown-based risk measures provide superior downside protection compared to traditional volatility metrics. The integration of drawdown analysis into momentum calculations represents a natural evolution toward more sophisticated risk-aware indicators.

> RAMO generates enhanced entry signals through multiple confirmation layers:

> Momentum indicators have been fundamental tools in technical analysis since the pioneering work of Wilder (1978) and continue to play crucial roles in systematic trading strategies (Jegadeesh & Titman, 1993). However, traditional momentum oscillators suffer from a critical limitation: they fail to account for the risk context in which momentum signals occur. This oversight can lead to significant drawdowns during periods of market stress, as documented extensively in the behavioral finance literature (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Shefrin & Statman, 1985).

> The concept of adaptive smoothing in technical analysis draws from the broader literature on regime-switching models in finance (Hamilton, 1989). Perry Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (1995) pioneered the application of efficiency ratios to adjust indicator responsiveness based on market conditions. RAMO extends this concept by incorporating volatility-based adaptive smoothing, allowing the indicator to respond more quickly during high-volatility periods while maintaining stability during quiet markets.

> The momentum effect, first systematically documented by Jegadeesh & Titman (1993), represents one of the most robust anomalies in financial markets. Subsequent research has confirmed momentum's persistence across various asset classes, time horizons, and geographic markets (Fama & French, 1996; Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen, 2013). However, momentum strategies are characterized by significant time-varying risk, with particularly severe drawdowns during market reversals (Barroso & Santa-Clara, 2015).

# Percentage Price Oscillator cross

## What it is
MACD expressed as a percentage of the slow EMA, compared with an EMA of itself.

## What it looks for
Acceleration in trend, in units that do not depend on the price level: a PPO of 2.5 means the same at $20 and $200.

## Equation
```
PPO_t    = 100 * (EMA(fast)_t - EMA(slow)_t) / EMA(slow)_t
Signal_t = EMA(signal) applied to the PPO SERIES
target_t = 1 if PPO_t > Signal_t else 0
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/textbook.py::PpoCross`, over `indicators.ppo`, which rebuilds the PPO history with `ema_series` exactly as `indicators.macd` does.

## Parameters
- **fast / slow / signal** follow MACD's 12/26/9 convention and horizon presets.

## Works when
Directional moves with steady acceleration, the same regime as MACD.

## Fails when
Chop, with the same constant sign flips as `macd`. Fast presets pay more in fees than they earn.

## Backtest notes
Because PPO = MACD / slow EMA, the PPO-vs-signal cross sits at nearly the same bars as the MACD cross on one asset. This card will probably measure as a near-duplicate of `macd`; `research/signal_redundancy.py` is the test of that, and the family label `trend` is a prior, not a finding. If the redundancy score confirms it, the right outcome is to keep the card as documented evidence of redundancy, not to count it as a second bet.

## Pairs with
A volume-flow signal (`obv_trend`), not another trend signal.

## Measured on SOL
Smoke run only, not a sweep row: `python3 -m backtester.cli --split 0.7 --interval 1d`, SOL daily 2021-06-17..2026-08-04, default parameters, 8 bps round-trip costs, one 70/30 split. The split is structurally hostile to long-biased rules (see `research/RANKED_LISTS.md`), so read it as one regime transition, not an estimate. The queue (`soltui/bgqueue.py`) will produce the evaluated numbers; this card stays `implemented` until a sweep supplies them.

Full sample: +822.84% (Sharpe 0.971, 68 trades, fees $8,490 on a $10,000 start) vs buy-and-hold +87.61%. 70/30 split: IS +1,948.5% (Sharpe 1.499) -> OOS -53.30% (Sharpe -0.754). The same in-sample-triumph-then-OOS-loss shape as `macd` (+1,356.5% IS -> -52.8% OOS).

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: base-rate. A rescaled MACD adds no new hypothesis. The nearest card, `macd`, measured among the worst in the sweep out of sample.*

## Caveats and limitations
- Named by the cited trading guides catalogued in `tradingstrategyresults.json` (repo root, untracked source list). The guides give a verbal rule or a formula, not tested parameters; every default here is a convention, not a finding.
- Rated from the sweep's overall hit rate (14% of 311 rankable configurations had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe), not from this card's own result.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy ppo --interval 1d --split 0.7
```

# Slow-MA Regime Filter

## What it is
Fully long above a slow moving average, flat below it.

## What it looks for
A one-line answer to "is this a bull or a bear regime".

## Equation
```
target_t = 1 if c_t > SMA(n)_t else 0
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/signals.py::Sma200Regime`.

## Parameters
- **window** — 168 hourly (one week), 100 or 200 daily. Longer means later turns and
  fewer of them.

## Works when
Regimes are persistent. Its value is less in returns than in *avoiding* the worst
drawdowns.

## Fails when
Price oscillates around the average, producing repeated entries and exits at the worst
possible points. Late by construction at every regime turn.

## Backtest notes
This is the strategy every more elaborate signal should be measured against. If an
eight-parameter system cannot beat "price above its 200-day average", the extra
parameters are not earning their keep.

## Pairs with
**This is the single most valuable partner in the whole set.** Mean reversion's fatal
mode is buying dips inside a downtrend, and this is the only component here that
answers "is there a downtrend". Measured as the top short-horizon pair and the top
triple.

## Measured on SOL
Standalone medium (100): IS +34.8% -> **OOS -35.8%**, 13 OOS trades.
**As a partner it is transformative:** `all(sma_regime + zscore)` reached **OOS Sharpe
+2.572** at the short horizon, against +0.441 for `zscore` alone. `all(sma_regime +
rsi)` reached **+1.456**.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

Standalone it lost 35.8% out-of-sample, which alone would be very-low. It is rated
**low** on the strength of what it does for *others*: `all(sma_regime+zscore)` reached
OOS Sharpe **+2.572** against +0.441 for zscore alone, and `all(sma_regime+rsi)`
reached +1.456. That is a real mechanical story — it vetoes the
buy-the-dip-in-a-downtrend failure — but it is one number from one hostile split, and
the partner effect belongs to the pair rather than to this card.

### The hourly run exposed a three-way degeneracy

On 8,823 hourly bars at short-horizon scaling, `voltarget`, `garch_voltarget` and
`sma_regime` produced **numerically identical** results — median path Sharpe −2.282,
median return −19.9%, 292 trades, all three. That is not a coincidence and it is not a
bug: at `target_vol` 0.8 on hourly SOL the volatility cap binds on essentially every
bar, so `min(1, target/sigma)` collapses to 1.0 and both vol-targeted rules degenerate
into the plain trend gate they share with the regime filter.

The caveat was written on these cards before it was observed. Seeing three separate
"strategies" return one identical row is the cleanest demonstration available that a
sweep's configuration count overstates how many distinct ideas are in it.

## Caveats and limitations
- Standalone it lost money out-of-sample. Its case rests almost entirely on what it
  does for *other* signals, which is a different claim and should not be blurred.
- A pair result built on the same hostile split inherits the same fragility. The
  partner effect is mechanically plausible — it vetoes the exact failure mode — but
  +2.572 is one number from one split.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy sma_regime --interval 1d
```

# TASC 2026.09 Adaptive SuperSmoother

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** indicator. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Adaptive SuperSmoother adjusts a filter’s critical period according to movement in a fixed-period companion filter. It aims to retain high-frequency noise suppression while responding faster to changing market direction. The adaptive line is compared with the fixed line, and their difference is displayed separately. Ehlers’s suggested directional interpretation is long when adaptive is above fixed and short otherwise, with difference peaks/valleys as possible turning-point clues. Those suggestions are signal concepts rather than a full executable strategy with fills and risk controls.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

**Partly disclosed computation.** The complete filter recurrence and adaptive-period normalization are not supplied.

- The complete filter recurrence and adaptive-period normalization are not supplied.

## How it works

- Filter the source with a fixed-period SuperSmoother, then compute its one-bar change and rolling RMS.
- Scale change by RMS and cap the scaled value; square one minus half that value to derive a period factor.
- Multiply the base period by the factor, enforce a minimum, and run a second SuperSmoother with that adaptive period.

## Outputs and intended use

- Red fixed and blue adaptive lines plus a difference oscillator support directional comparison.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Defaults: Close source, base period 20 and RMS length 81.
- Scaled ROC is capped at 2 and adaptive period floored at 2.

## Failure modes and caveats

- The source does not clarify signed-versus-absolute ROC treatment, materially affecting the period factor.
- Filter crossings can whipsaw and do not establish profitable execution.

# Drawdown Distribution Analysis (DDA)

Version: 1.0.0. Delta: individual explanation of the complete saved publication.

**Classification:** risk-tool. Native publication type: study. Review: independently reviewed.

## Idea and objective

Place the current asset-price drawdown within its historical distribution and add return/risk summaries. DDA supports contextual risk monitoring and allocation research; it does not establish a portfolio’s realized drawdown unless the supplied price series represents that portfolio.

## Coin-test readiness: incomplete

No complete standalone coin-test contract or runnable coin-test implementation has been qualified for this card. Source disclosure alone does not establish that readiness.

## Source calculation and gaps

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Raw running-maximum drawdown/nearest-rank distribution is independently defined by the disclosed procedure; other missing outputs do not qualify.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Track the running maximum and express current price decline as a signed percentage. Historical nearest-rank percentiles, mean/deviation bands and z-scores locate the current decline within the selected sample.
- Additional metrics include annualized Sharpe/Sortino, annual return divided by maximum drawdown, drawdown-tail percentile/average measures and volatility-normalized drawdown. A composite score combines Sharpe and percentile rank.
- Percentile tiers classify risk; alerts report tier changes, extreme z-scores, new maximum decline and deteriorating composite/Sharpe conditions.
- Peak(t)=max supplied prices from sample start through t;DD(t)=100*(P(t)-Peak(t))/Peak(t),requiring positive/nonzero peak. ## Idea and objective

EMD Trend builds a volatility-sensitive envelope from exponentially averaged absolute deviations around a chosen moving average. It aims to distinguish bullish/bearish excursions from neutral inside-channel behavior and provide trend/breakout context. Separate risk-on/off alerts identify crossings into and back out of outer regions. The optional historical performance mode is described as a diagnostic simulation with sizing and direction controls, but no fill/cost details are provided. Consequently the channel concept is clearer than either the persistent trend-state engine or the reported performance calculations.

**Disclosed principal calculation.** Usable for caller-parameterized SMA/EMA-centered absolute-deviation EMA bands and explicitly named band-crossing events. Full FRAMA/state/backtest behavior remains incomplete.

No blocking gap was identified for the principal computation described above. Runtime integration and performance remain separate questions.

## How it works

- Narrow ordinary-MA envelope: choose source X and SMA or EMA center M with length L. Let D=EMA(|X−M|,K), Upper=M+mD and Lower=M−mD for selected deviation length K and multiplier m. Risk-on long is a price cross above Upper; risk-off long a cross back below Upper; risk-on short a cross below Lower and risk-off short a cross back above Lower. These are crossing events, not an inferred persistent trend-state machine.
- Calculate selected MA and EMA of absolute deviation from it, then multiply deviation for upper/lower bands.
- Classify excursions above/below bands and track corresponding trend flips/risk-on/off crossings.

# Reliable-trigger trade

## What it is
The execution half of the trigger miner. `research/triggers.py` scores conjunctions of conditions by how often the next h bars go the predicted way; this strategy trades one of them.

## What it looks for
A trigger firing at the close of bar t. Example: `volume >= 10x its rolling median and close at a 2-sigma low`.

## Equation
```
fire_t      = AND(condition_k(bars 0..t))
entry       = open[t+1]              (engine fill_delay=1)
exit        = decided at close[t+h]  (filled at the next open), or close[i] <= entry*(1 - stop) for longs
target      = direction while the context is live, else 0
```
Evaluation in the miner uses entry open[t+1] and exit close[t+h], the same window.

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/trigger.py`; conditions in `backtester/core/trigger_conditions.py`.

## Parameters
- **conditions** which trigger. Funding conditions are refused (OHLCV only).
- **horizon** the context expiry. **stop** is derived from the trigger's discovery-period MAE (80th percentile adverse excursion of winning events) by `research/trigger_backtest.py`.

## Works when
The trigger's hit rate beats the base rate out of sample by enough to cover 12 bps fees, 4 bps slippage and carry.

## Fails when
The trigger was a chance in-sample pattern. On SOL no trigger passed all honesty gates out of sample; see `research/RELIABLE_SIGNALS.md`.

## Backtest notes
Stops are checked on closes and fill at the next open, so a gap through the stop is not rescued. Run through the leverage tiers with `--backtest`.

## Pairs with
`lev_low`, `lev_medium`, `lev_high` wrap other strategies; this one carries its own direction, so run it at a tier through `backtester.core.leverage.tier_config`.

## Measured on SOL
See `research/RELIABLE_SIGNALS.md`.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: base-rate. No mined trigger qualified as reliable out of sample (Stele KNOW-632, KNOW-596, KNOW-617).*

Rated from the sweep's overall hit rate, not from this card's own result.

## Caveats and limitations
- Exploratory unless a trigger passed every gate.
- Exits at the next open after expiry, not exactly the close of bar t+h.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m research.triggers --asset SOL --interval 1d --backtest
```

## Idea and objective

## How it works

- For supplied same-period returns r and periodic risk-free return f, Sharpe=(mean(r)-f)/SD(r). For aligned investment/benchmark returns r,b, information ratio=mean(r-b)/SD(r-b). Caller must select sample/population dispersion and zero-dispersion policy because the description does not fix them. These periodic formulas avoid guessing annual-to-period conversion.
- Request chosen-timeframe percentage changes,compound them into monthly samples when history spans two months or daily samples when it spans two days,and compute excess mean divided by total/downside dispersion. Benchmark-symbol mode uses active-return/tracking-error style ratios with aligned spread requests and dividend/extended-session adjustments.

## Outputs and intended use

- Display return series,benchmark line,new-period highlights and a table/data-window of ratios/sample information. These describe asset price returns,not an actual trading portfolio.

## Parameters and stated settings

- Returns timeframe defaults one month,maximum samples sixty and annual fixed benchmark two percent. Less than two days produces no collected returns. Benchmark choice/timeframe/sample count are configurable.

## Failure modes and caveats

- Yield-valued symbols are unsuitable price-return benchmarks,as the author warns. Results depend on sampling,adjustments and downside convention; a high historical ratio does not establish future sustainability.

# RSI Mean-Reversion

## What it is
Buy when Wilder's RSI is oversold; exit when it recovers past a midline. The position
is **held statefully** between those events, so this is not a per-bar recomputation.

## What it looks for
Short-term exhaustion of selling pressure.

## Equation
```
gain_t, loss_t   = max(dC_t, 0), max(-dC_t, 0)
avgGain, avgLoss = Wilder smoothing with period p
RS   = avgGain / avgLoss
RSI  = 100 - 100/(1 + RS)
enter if RSI < oversold ;  exit if RSI > exit_level
```

## Implementation
`backtester/core/strategies/rsi.py`.

## Parameters
- **period** — 7 hourly, 14 daily, 30 for the slow scale.
- **oversold / exit_level** — the gap between them sets the minimum round trip. Setting
  `exit_level` near `oversold` produces a high-frequency, cost-dominated strategy.

## Works when
Range-bound, mean-reverting conditions.

## Fails when
**In a strong trend RSI stays oversold for weeks, and the reading becomes a
trend-continuation indicator rather than a reversal signal.** Mean-reversion families
show attractive 60–80% win rates that conceal rare catastrophic losses — picking up
nickels in front of a steamroller.

## Backtest notes
**Judge this family on the tail, not the win rate.** A 75%-win-rate equity curve with
one -60% trade is not a good strategy, and average-based metrics hide it. Report max
drawdown and the worst single trade, both of which this harness computes.

## Pairs with
A regime filter — arguably mandatory, since it patches the exact failure mode. Volume,
to distinguish accumulation from distribution.

## Measured on SOL
Medium: IS -9.6% -> OOS -21.9% on only 4 OOS trades (below the floor).
Short (period 7): **OOS Sharpe -0.527**.
`all(sma_regime + rsi)` reached **OOS +1.456** — the filter did the work, not the RSI.

The figures below come from a **single 70/30 walk-forward split**, and
`research/RANKED_LISTS.md` documents why that split is structurally hostile: its
in-sample window ends within one bar of the highest close in the entire series
($261.99 on bar 1311 of 1875). It separated a bull market from a bear leg almost
exactly, so any long-biased rule *had* to look excellent in-sample and terrible
out-of-sample. In-sample rank did not predict out-of-sample rank — the medium-horizon
Spearman correlation was **-0.419**, actively inverted.

Read these numbers as evidence about **one regime transition**, not as a performance
estimate. Across the whole sweep, 45 of 311 rankable configurations (14%) had a
positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 28 (9%) made money. The evidence floor is 10
out-of-sample trades: fewer than that and a row is listed, never ranked.

## Likelihood of success: very-low

*Basis: measured-oos. There is no 'high' rating in this scheme — across 311 rankable
configurations, 14% had a positive out-of-sample Sharpe and 9% made money.*

4 out-of-sample trades at the medium horizon is not a sample, and the short horizon
scored -0.527. The known failure mode is decisive here: in a strong trend RSI stays
oversold for weeks and becomes a trend-continuation indicator. SOL's out-of-sample
leg was exactly that trend. `all(sma_regime+rsi)` reached +1.456 — but the filter
did the work.

## Caveats and limitations
- 4 out-of-sample trades is not evidence of anything.
- The pair result is the interesting one, and it belongs as much to `sma_regime.md` as
  to this card.

## How to run
```bash
python3 -m backtester.cli --strategy rsi --interval 1d
```

# Ecosystem wiki and documentation ownership

The control room wiki collects the Oracle, ecosystem supervisor, Bot Manager and
Backtester documentation in one searchable snapshot. It also includes the
architecture, installation, testing, lifecycle, operating and accepted UI design
guides. Source documents remain authoritative for their stated version and
scope. The wiki preserves their text and authorship; it does not rewrite old
plans as delivered capabilities.

## Find an answer

Search uses every included document's title, source path and full text. The
catalog separates component guides, strategy cards, incomplete references,
architecture, design and historical plans. A matching strategy document does not
establish that its strategy is runnable. An incomplete reference remains an
incomplete reference.

Each page exposes its original file location, SHA-256, source commit when known,
and the snapshot hash. Pages compiled from changed or newly staged source are
labelled `working_tree_snapshot`; they do not claim a commit that contains those
bytes. Committed pages link to their specific GitHub revision. The source path
always points to the canonical checkout under
`/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader`.

The wiki is documentation, not a runtime health probe. Use the control room's
current owner state, lifecycle evidence, freshness and action results to decide
what is running. Historical accuracy and vote agreement do not establish profit.
Forward P&L needs recorded prospective economics and costs; missing accounting
evidence remains unavailable.

## Component and file map

| Responsibility | Source of truth |
| --- | --- |
| Paper orchestration and recovery | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/runner.py` and `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/recovery.py` |
| Control room HTTP interface | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/web.py` |
| Native manager event bridge | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/telemetry.py` |
| Stable external trial registration | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/registration.py` |
| Bot configuration and lifecycle commands | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/botmanager/src/botmanager/registry.py` |
| Bot operation and P&L owner | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/botmanager/src/botmanager/ledger.py` and `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/botmanager/src/botmanager/status.py` |
| Frozen historical matrix and forward handoff | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/f5_batch.py` |
| Prospective calls and outcomes | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/soltui/forwardtest.py` |
| Canonical costed simulation | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/backtester/core/engine.py` |
| Strategy equations, limitations and defaults | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/backtester/strategy_cards/README.md` |
| Oracle observations, forecasts and evidence | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/oracle/engine.py` and `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/oracle/store.py` |
| Oracle vote thresholds and weights | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/oracle/voting.py` |
| Oracle MCP and guide routing | `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/oracle/server.py` and `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/oracle/guidance.py` |

## Architectural choices

The ecosystem coordinates existing owners. F5 retains its backtest queue and
forward ledger. Bot Manager retains bot operation and P&L. Oracle retains
instrument-bound forecasts and their evidence. The shared recorder remains a
singleton. The wiki creates no recorder, optimizer, worker or order path.

The wiki is a packaged snapshot rather than a filesystem browser. The build
command selects only tracked Markdown in an explicit allowlist. Untracked local
notes, private configuration, arbitrary HTTP paths and credential files cannot
be selected through the wiki API. Source Markdown and links are untrusted text;
the browser must render them without evaluating HTML, scripts or instructions.

The snapshot contains two generated files:

- `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/wiki_content/manifest.json` records
  page identities, categories, provenance, content hashes and the bundle hash.
- `/Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/ecosystem/wiki_content/pages.json` preserves
  the original Markdown bodies under deterministic page IDs.

The runtime validates both hashes and each page's content hash before serving
the snapshot. It refuses malformed IDs, unknown pages, changed content and
unavailable bundles. A caller supplies a page ID, never a local path. A rebuild
invalidates the runtime's bounded cache.

## API contract

`catalog(query="", limit=100, offset=0)` returns matching page metadata, total
matches, category names, pagination and `snapshot_sha256`. Search uses all terms,
ignores case and returns bounded text excerpts. The query limit is 256 characters;
page limits range from 1 to 5,000. `page(id)` returns one page with its Markdown
body and provenance. Both return schema version 1. Missing or corrupt snapshots
return `status=unavailable`; invalid argument shapes are rejected.

The HTTP owner maps these functions to `/api/wiki` and `/api/wiki/page`. Normal
control-room origin and authorization rules apply. A wiki page cannot invoke an
action. Documentation links never confer execution authority.

## Rebuild and verify

The generator uses Git's tracked-file inventory and does not fetch, embed or run
inference. Stage a newly created public guide before rebuilding, so it becomes
part of that reviewed inventory.

```sh
python3 /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/scripts/build_ecosystem_wiki.py
python3 /Users/mitch/dev/solmargintrader/scripts/build_ecosystem_wiki.py --check
python3 -m unittest ecosystem.tests.test_wiki
```

Unchanged pages retain their original build provenance, making rebuilds stable
after unrelated commits. `--refresh-provenance` explicitly refreshes source
commit bindings for unchanged content. Content changes always update page and
snapshot hashes. A source reference may be historical; a successful wiki check
proves snapshot integrity and current source coverage, not trading readiness.

## Documented inputs and source details

> <iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/uAuisQGLRVA?&wmode=opaque" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="" class="fr-draggable"></iframe>

> By default, the indicator filters the gaps based on their width and only displays the gaps when they are at least 30% as wide as the average bar range (high - low) for the last 14 bars. The deviation % can be changed in the Inputs section.

> Changes the logic based on which the gaps are closed. By default, this setting is turned off, and a gap is fully closed as soon as a bar enters it, even if that bar only touches a small part of the gap. When the setting is on, whenever a bar enters the gap zone but does not fully cover it, the gap closes partially, and the part that has not been covered by the price movement is extended further (and can be covered by the future bars).

> Additionally, the indicator extends the gaps indefinitely, until they get covered by new price movement. This can also be changed in the settings by enabling the Max Gap Trail Length limit. When enabled, gaps will be closed if they extend past the specified number of bars (300 by default).

> Gaps mark periods when there was a sharp change in prices during the period when the exchange was inactive. This information can be used by traders to profit from the current situation of sudden price changes.

> On the screenshot below, the top chart features Gaps with the Close Gaps Partially turned off. The big down gap that starts at the beginning of February is closed almost instantly because its bottom part is slightly covered by a following bar. In contrast, on the bottom chart, where the Close Gaps Partially setting is turned on, only the small part on the bottom of the gap is closed, and the big uncovered part is extended further right, and is then eventually closed by future price action.
